Narrative: We started our takeoff roll at ZZZ. It was the FO's (First Officer's) leg. Shortly after the 'set takeoff thrust call' my window on the Captain's side started to slide open. I'd estimate our speed at 40 kts. It was barely open so I said 'continue' and reached up to close it. However, the window would not close and actually felt like it was coming out of the track. I assumed the window would easily close and that we still had plenty of time to safely reject at low speed if it wouldn't. At that point I became distracted and was worried that the window was falling in. At that point the FO asked if I wanted to reject and I said 'yes'. He initiated the reject as he saw that I was handling the window. As I brought my scan away from the window the reject was started and I noticed the airspeed was about 100 kts. The aircraft quickly decelerated as it was very light. I expected the airspeed to be less than 80 kts based on the short amount of time we had been rolling. The FO continued to stop the aircraft. At that point I took controls. He called the Tower and I made a PA to the passengers to remain seated. We then taxied off the runway at Taxiway X and coordinated with Maintenance to have the brakes checked. They gave us a thumbs up and we taxied to the gate. At that point the window was stuck in a half open position. We shutdown at the gate and switched to another aircraft. Rejecting immediately when the window started to slide open would have prevented the distraction and the rejection would have started at a slower speed. I assumed two things: that the window would easily close and that we were still below 80 kts when the decision was made. It may have been, but at the light weight the aircraft accelerated quickly and I think by the time the actions began we were over 80 kts.
Narrative_1: At approximately 40 kts during takeoff roll, Captain side window slid open. Captain called continue and attempted to close the window. A few seconds later I looked over and saw the Captain was struggling to get it closed. I stated that I recommend we reject and he agreed. His hands were still on the window to prevent it from slamming back so I initiated the reject procedure. I did not notice the top airspeed, but I would estimate visually about 100 kts, autobraking did engage. Aircraft came to a stop abeam Taxiway X. Notified the Tower. We were instructed to exit on Taxiway. We stopped on Taxiway and called Company. Maintenance met us on ramp and checked the brakes. We taxied in. Window was unable to be shut. When Maintenance came to the flight deck and were able to move the window forward the handle seemed loose and the squeeze grip seemed loose so we all conferred and removed the aircraft from service.I specifically remember observing the Captain check his window just prior to calling for the before takeoff checklist so I think it was secure. We should have rejected as soon as the window slid open to prevent from getting to the higher speed. The aircraft was light so acceleration was very rapid.
Synopsis: B737 Flight Crew reported cockpit window opening during takeoff roll.

Narrative: After takeoff and about 50 ft high, I heard the Yaw damper switch snapped into the off position, with a master caution flight control light on. With time permitting I ran the QRH yaw damper off checklist. When I reset the yaw damper switch back on the aircraft did a abrupt yaw to the left and the yaw damper switch snapped off again. We asked ATC for radar vectors to stay within the Airport area to work out the yaw damper problem. After talking to maintenance and dispatch about the yaw damper failure, Flight planned cruise altitude FL400, thunderstorms and rain at the destination we decided to return back to ZZZ. ATC gave us a visual approach [Runway] XX, on base leg turn 1,300 ft Tower gave us a low altitude alert. We landed safely and wrote up the Yaw Damper.
Synopsis: B737 First Officer reported Yaw Damper failure caused an air turnback and precautionary landing.

Narrative: Enroute on Aircraft X from ZZZZ to ZZZ we were unable to open the flight deck door. The flight deck crew had requested a bathroom break. The Captain went out and returned normally. However, when the First Officer called to return to the flight deck, the Lead Flight Attendant was unable to open the door. The bottom latch was not unlatching, while the upper latch and mid latch were unlatching normally with the door handle. The flight attendant tried using a metal key to pry the latch open. The Captain tried the unlock switch on the center pedestal. Nothing worked. We communicated with the First Officer and told him the flight deck door was stuck locked. The only option left to us was to pull the pins on the emergency/blowout panel on the door. When this was accomplished the opening allowed the flight attendant to exit the flight deck and the First Officer to return to the flight deck. This was done discreetly but was likely witnessed by some passengers in first class. Once the First Officer was inside the flight deck, the panel was reinstalled and secured with the pins. The rest of the flight continued normally. However, both the Captain and First Officer had to exit the flight deck using the panel once the flight was completed (this was accomplished after all passengers had deplaned) as the flight deck door remain stuck closed and locked. A write up was made in the Maintenance Logbook and the aircraft was turned over to Maintenance. Nothing more to add.The flight crew handled the unusual situation professionally.
Synopsis: Pilot flying A320 aircraft reported Flight Deck door stuck in closed position inflight.

Narrative: We were cleared to descend via the arrival except maintain 12,000 ft. We were cruising at 24,000 ft northeast of MOMAR. We began to experience turbulence that resembled wake. At that point in time I was under the impression we were cleared to 12,000 ft. I selected Altitude Intervention to begin a descent out of the turbulence. I selected Altitude Intervention a second time to begin the descent. The crossing attitudes were erased at MOMAR due to selecting ALT Intervene. During both presses of the ALT Intervene the Captain and I VVMI'd. We descended below the published altitude at MOMAR.
Narrative_1: We briefed the arrival/approach as scheduled and then almost 40 minutes later we began our descent, and inadvertently double pushed and deleted the crossing restrictions at MOMAR. I didn't catch it until we were already out of 24,000 ft.
Synopsis: B737 Flight Crew reported overshooting an altitude restriction in descent due to a programming error.

Narrative: The aircraft had preexisting maintenance issues when we received it for dispatch. There was a Class II Flight/Control maintenance message that was defferred. The number 3 IRU was differed from an inbound write up that stated the 'Capt Mach/Airspeed Inop and Nav/Alt discrepancy repeat writeup went to Air Data Capt3 position.' The MEL required that IRU 3 be maintained in the off position. Finally, the First Officer noted a skid mark on the number 1 tire that was subsequently found to be within limits by maintenance. Our Flight was cleared for take off with the Captain flying and Tower indicating that there was a 5 knot tailwind. The 100 knots call out had not yet been made and the thrust levers had been set to FLX/MCT when we received a Level II ECAM. The Captain glanced at the ECAM and noted an Auto Flight Auto Thrust Off ECAM. The Captain elected to continue the take off and to set TOGO thrust. The Captain's thinking at this point was that an Auto Thrust Failure would not affect the ability of the aircraft to fly and that setting TOGO would help with the tailwind. The First Officer then stated that there was another ECAM which indicated an Auto Flight Rudder Travel Limit System Failure. At this point, the V1 call out had not yet been made so the Captain elected to abort the take off. The Captain's thinking at this point was that there was a question now as to the ability of the aircraft to fly since the additional ECAM was potentially a flight control issue and the fact that both ECAMs were received after thrust power had been set. The Captain performed a rejected take off procedure. The aircraft appeared to be under normal control with no other apparent issues so just prior to bringing the airplane to a stop, the Captain instructed the First Officer to make a PA announcement for the passengers to remain seated. The Captain wanted to clear the runway at Taxiway X which is approximately halfway down the 10,187 foot runway but noted to the First Officer that it appeared that the aircraft was not moving forward easily after coming to a stop. At this point the First Officer and Captain discussed the possibility of a tire failure as a potential reason for the difficulty in moving the aircraft but it had not felt like a tire failed. We decided to tell the tower we were going to maintain our position on the runway until we could figure out what the issue was. At this point, we received a call from the flight attendants concerning a faint rubbery/acrid odor that was perceptible in the cabin. The Captain noted that the brake temperatures were still between approximately 450 and 550 degrees Celsius, although increasing, with no other abnormal system indications. The Captain and First Officer discussed that the smell was most likely from the aircraft tires as a result of the rejected takeoff and informed the flight attendants and passengers. The Captain was subsequently able to move the aircraft forward surmising that the aircraft may have been in a low spot on the runway that may have caused the difficulty in moving forward. As the Captain moved the aircraft slowly forward he noted that the aircraft was now moving freely and that there did not appear to be any issues with the tires. The First Officer requested from tower to clear the runway at Taxiway D, we completed our checklists, briefed our passengers and coordinated clearance to hardstand parking Spot 20 so that maintenance could look at the aircraft's condition. Upon arriving at parking Spot 20, the Captain talked with maintenance over the intercom and asked them to inspect the tires and the rest of the aircraft as a result of the rejected take off. Maintenance indicated that there were no visible issues except for the fact that the original skid mark on the number one tire was now larger. After maintenance inspected the aircraft exterior they brought the air-stairs up to door 1L and boarded the aircraft to run maintenance system checks. The wheelswere chocked and the parking brake was released to help cool the brakes. The Captain and Station Manager discussed deplaning the passengers and returning them to the terminal to await the results of the maintenance procedures. The Station Manager did an outstanding job of taking care of our passengers during the deplaning process and also provided our passengers with a complementary meal voucher. The Captain subsequently communicated with Maintenance Control, dispatch and the Duty Manager concerning the rejected take off. The Flight and Cabin crew also debriefed each other concerning the rejected take off. The Captain and First Officer discussed with Maintenance Control what the maintenance plan would be for the aircraft since we were still scheduled to take the aircraft to ZZZ1 and there appeared to be multiple maintenance issues. Maintenance Control indicated that they would perform various checklists and resets. The First Officer advocated that if time permitted that we should attempt to bring in a 320 Systems specialist if possible to answer some of our concerns including why we received the ECAMS after what we thought should have been an inhibited time period after take-off power was set. ALPA Safety reached out to the Captain during this time period so the Captain asked if ALPA Safety could connect the flight crew with an A320 systems specialist to talk about these issues which they did. Maintenance Control subsequently cleared all the maintenance issues with the exceptions of deferring the Auto Thrust system and Class II maintenance messages for Flight/Control and Air Bleed. Maintenance also changed out the number 1 tire due to the skid mark being worse after the rejected take off. We were subsequently dispatched again from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on the same aircraft. Just after take-off roll and beginning the climb out, with the Captain flying, the Captain lost his airspeed and mach indications. The Captain transferred control of the aircraft to the First Officer and the First Officer continued the climb out. The Flight then received a Nav/Alt Discrepancy ECAM. We performed the checklist. In order for us to restore the Captain's Airspeed/Mach indication we had to select Air Data Capt3 for the Captain just like the previous write up. We also had to select the First Officers Auto Pilot 2 since the Captains Auto pilot 1 would level off 500 feet off altitude. We Contacted Dispatch to get a phone patch to Maintenance Control and told Maintenance Control we were still having Air Speed, Mach and altimeter issues for the Captains side and wrote up the issues. We then proceeded to ZZZ1 with no further issues.
Narrative_1: Rejected takeoff due to multiple ECAMs which were triggered and addressed as we transitioned from low speed to high speed regime. The reject actions were as per SOP and the flight attendants thanked us for a prompt Remain Seated, Remain Seated notification. Taxi back to ramp and a multi-hour maintenance delay ensued.
Synopsis: Flight Crew reported recurring ECAM messages after a rejected takeoff and subsequent maintenance action on the next flight.

Narrative: Approximately 3 minutes after takeoff just after clean up received a HYD (Hydraulic) B ELEC PUMP LO PR (Low Pressure) ECAM message. Performed ECAM actions, follow ups, [requested priority handling], and returned to ZZZ. Extended vectors to land below max landing weight. Cleared runway, checked over by ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Fire Fighting), taxied to gate. Additionally APU was inoperative. HYD pump failure.Cause is unknown it was a maintenance issue.
Narrative_1: ECAM Hydraulic B Electric Pump Low Pressure. Ran fix strategy. Decided to return to ZZZ. Delay vectors to burn off fuel to avoid overweight landing. [Requested Priority Handling], safety vehicles inspected aircraft after landing and followed us to gate. Landed underweight runway XX, normal landing. Also APU was deferred.APU deferred. Safest course of action was to return to ZZZ.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported Hydraulic Pump Failure after takeoff.

Narrative: On approach to 35R, we were direct FRONZ, cleared visual approach. We were on an angled intercept to final. Captain asked 7,000 ft. be set for FRONZ, I did and after leaving 8,000 ft., tower advised our callsign and low altitude alert. I replied to ATC that we were ok, meaning level and clear of terrain at 7,000 ft. We intercepted the glide path to a normal approach and landing. During the low altitude alert we had finished slowing from 190 to 170 knots assigned. Several runway changes and speed changes preceded this event. I believe the Captain was trying to have the airplane, on the assigned speed, desired configuration and omitted the class B floor as I did.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported low altitude alert from ATC on approach.

Narrative: While cruising at 38,000 feet in VFR conditions the TCAS RA alert sounded. The First Officer and I performed the memory items and initiated the commanded climb. I advised ATC of our situation and was told by the controller that no other aircraft were observed in our area. TCAS then commanded us to descend and we also complied while looking outside for any intruding aircraft. The alert then said we were clear and went away. We regained our original altitude with no further conversation with ATC. All appeared normal and we determined the alert was false. The TCAS gave us 2 more false alarms. The 2nd was level at 30,000 feet and the 3rd was at 3,000 feet. While being vectored for the ILS Approach. Once on the ground the faulty TCAS was written up. Maintenance and Dispatch were made aware of the problem. After talking to Maintenance I was informed the TCAS system had been a continuing problem with multiple write-ups. I believe we were the first to get an RA alert, but it would've helped if someone had given us a heads up.
Synopsis: A Flight Crew reported receiving false TCAS RA advisories and stated maintenance told them it was a recurring issue with their aircraft.

Narrative: We departed on the RNAV Departure. The Captain was flying. I was Pilot Monitoring. Shortly after takeoff, while in a turn on the assigned lateral profile, Tower asked if we had helicopter traffic in sight at approximately our 2 o'clock position. I responded that we had the green helicopter in sight. The helicopter was slightly higher than our altitude. Shortly thereafter we received an Amber TCAS TA alert followed immediately thereafter by a Red TCAS RA alert instructing us to continue our climb rate. The helicopter had made a left turn directly toward us. We responded according to the RA guidance to climb even though the helicopter was slightly higher than us. Additionally we added a turn to increase visual separation with the helicopter traffic as we climbed above them and they passed below us.Because I don't know what clearance the helicopter traffic had, I don't know what could have been done to prevent this incident. It does strike me as odd that the helicopter was flying so close to the charted SID lateral profile that low to the ground and that close to the departure runway.
Synopsis: B747-800 First Officer reported TCAS warnings during climb.

Narrative: ZZZ Center issued a clearance to climb and maintain 26,000 ft. At approximately 11,400 ft., we received a TCAS descending RA. The Pilot Flying without delay complied with the descending RA. The autopilot and auto throttle were disengaged, and a smooth adjustment to a pitch down attitude was completed to satisfy the RA command. The Pilot Flying followed this planned lateral flight path until approximately 10,500 ft. when the Clear of Conflict was heard. ZZZ Center was advised of the TCAS deviation.Some important points that I (Pilot Monitoring) and the First Officer (Pilot Flying) took away from this event includes knowing company policies and procedures. The Pilot Flying did not hesitate to comply with the TCAS RA. The teamwork between the roles of Pilot Flying and Pilot Monitoring worked. I can contribute this to our TCAS training. This real life TCAS RA with passengers onboard was just like the scenarios we receive in the simulators.[We also had] a concern regarding ZZZ Center. Our flight was never given any traffic advisories to be on the lookout for this aircraft. The TCAS equipment on the aircraft was our first signal that there was a traffic conflict. Only after ZZZ Center was notified of the TCAS RA, did ZZZ Center start issuing traffic advisories to another company flight behind us. This is my first time in XX years of flying Part 121 operations that I have come this close to another aircraft. When ATC asked if I could identify the aircraft, I had no trouble identifying it as a King Air. During this descending TCAS RA, the closest I saw the two aircraft apart was 500 ft.
Synopsis: A B737 pilot reported a near miss after following an automated advisory to descend. Pilot reported ATC did not issue a traffic advisory prior to incident.

Narrative: On short final into ZZZ Runway XXL, we received a GPWS 'Too Low Terrain' warning. We were on glideslope and on PAPI (VMC conditions). We executed a go-around and as we leveled off we received several error messages in the scratch pad [including] 'GPS L incorrect' and a 'Runway/Approach CRS ERROR'. The Captain was flying and could not get NAV data to display on his PFD (Primary Flight Display). He also was unable to tune the ILS frequency for the subsequent approach. We consulted the checklist, then transferred the controls to the First Officer whose displays and NAV data appeared to be reading correctly and hand flew an approach in VFR conditions to a landing without incident. There was a lot of confusion with multiple errors occurring in the cockpit. The GPWS that sounded while we were on the glideslope during short final seemed to be erroneous, but then again with all the errors with the NAV data on the Pilot Flying side, maybe his glideslope was incorrect. In the end, going around and troubleshooting put time on our side and allowed us to determine the best course of action.
Synopsis: A B737 pilot reported several erroneous warnings and display errors on the Captain's side, who was Pilot Flying, during short final. A successful go-around and landing was performed by the First Officer.

Narrative: We were just outside the MNARK waypoint descending via the TBARR1 into Denver when I requested an unrestricted descent in order to expedite down through some turbulence. ATC granted my request and cleared us to descend and maintain 14,000 FT. I took the aircraft out of the managed descent mode and used open descent to descend to 14,000 FT. ATC subsequently amended our clearance as follows; cross BDIVN at or above 14,000 FT then descend via the TBARR1. The next waypoint after BDIVN is KUSHH which has an altitude restriction of 14,000 FT. The Pilot Monitoring (PM) put 13,000 in the FCU as the bottom of the TBARR1 is 13,000 FT at LDORA which is the next waypoint after KUSHH. I acknowledged the change to the altitude in the FCU but failed to put the aircraft back into a managed descent. We were between BDIVN and KUSHH when Denver Center switched us over to approach. As the PM checked in with approach I was expecting the aircraft to level off at 14,000 FT in order to meet the restriction by KUSHH. Just as the aircraft approached 14,000 FT two things happened simultaneously. One, I realized the aircraft wasn't leveling off as I expected, and two, approach cleared us to descend to 10,000 FT and turn left to a heading of 040. I don't believe there was an altitude deviation but I was certainly very fortunate that approach gave us a lower altitude when they did.
Narrative_1: On TBARR1 arrival asked for expedited decent to 14,000 feet to get out of moderate turbulence. I put 14,000 feet in altitude window, captain started open descent. Next ATC transmission was a decent via following BDIVN intersection. I put 13,000 in altitude window. Approaching KUSHH intersection captain realized plane was not going to capture altitude to cross KUSHH at 14,000 feet. Managed descent was not selected. At same time got ATC frequency change and new instructions heading 020 descent to 10,000. I don't think we went below 14,000 feet, but would have if not given new ATC instructions while in an open descent Mode.
Synopsis: A320 flight crew reported failing to engage the correct descent mode upon receiving arrival clearance.

Narrative: In Cruise Flight at FL380 approaching ZZZZZ north boundary of ZZZZ airspace we were denied right deviations for active military airspace. Left deviations at that point were no longer an option and appeared worse. We were on the western edge of a line of weather moving East we were deviating just slightly left of our course to go through what appeared to be the thinnest area of weather on our radar. I had made a PA and had all passengers and Flight Attendants seated. We experienced a brief 10 to 15 seconds of Moderate Turbulence which cause our Altitude to drop 200 ft. to about 37,800 ft. and the a gain of about 300 ft. to about 38,100 ft. and then settled back to level at FL380. We also experienced some airspeed loss and then gain briefly as well as some left bank. It felt much like wake turbulence briefly. Just then MIA center told us to maintain FL380 and contact ZZZZ; before leaving the frequency I stated we had experienced some moderate turbulence which had caused some altitude loss, a couple hundred feet, and that we were now level at FL380 and we were told 'roger' contact Center which we did. The remainder of the flight was uneventful and smooth to destination. [The cause of the event was that] a deviation 100's of miles earlier to the left would have been a better choice and I believe a couple of aircraft behind us after hearing my report to MIA Center deviated into the Military Airspace. I do not know if the aircraft behind me declared an Emergency to do so or not, as we were changing frequency to next center during the radio discussions. That may have been a better choice but I did not expect the turbulence to be that bad, but was very glad I sat the Flight attendants down prior, as well as making a very clear PA to the passengers that we were going to experience some Turbulence since we had to fly in the area of some weather and insisted that they be seated with their seatbelts securely fastened. An earlier plan for weather deviations 100's of mile away if necessary would have helped knowing any right deviations would be denied.
Narrative_1: Level at 380 approaching XXXXX, there was some weather close to the intersection. Requested right deviation and Center informed that Warning Areas were active so unable right deviation. We encountered some moderate turbulence in the clouds for a few seconds. The airplane descended 200 ft. before returning to level. Miami informed to maintain 380 and to contact next center over ZZZZ which we did. Flight continued uneventfully.The cause of deviations was not being able to deviate due to Center's instructions.I suggest deviating ahead of time if known that no deviations allowed.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported moderate turbulence due to weather deviations being unavailable.

Narrative: While at the gate pre flighting, I was informed that we were carrying an aircraft battery to ZZZ1 and was given two copies of the Notice to Captain (NOTAC) to sign. At that point, I had already reviewed our Release and signed it. I gave the Operations Agent a copy of the NOTAC and kept one myself. While at cruise altitude, I received an ACARS message from Dispatch informing me that the HAZMAT was not annotated in the remarks section of the Release in accordance with Bulletin. The Dispatcher and I made a pen and ink change to the Release and the Dispatcher informed he would report the event.
Synopsis: Captain reported in flight notification of Release document missing required Hazmat information.

Narrative: Climbing out, approximately XX00Z, the left engine had loss of thrust associated with compressor stall / surges. Flight attendants rang the call button and indicated they heard loud banging and wanted to verify we heard the same. We shallowed our climb then leveled off at FL 280 and [advised ATC]. Subsequent flight attendant chime indicated they saw flames had extended aft of the #1 engine. We had already begun to tackle the surge / stall QRC followed by QRH checklist when they called advised of flames. We recognized and agreed that ZZZ was our best option due to proximity (80 miles roughly ) off our nose with optimum field capabilities. We coordinated with flight attendants and talked with a non-rev commuting Company Captain who had been sitting on left side of cabin and had seen the flames. During this process, we coordinated with ATC for direct and began a descent to ZZZ [and] fired off a quick message to Dispatch indicating engine malfunction and plan to divert. We coordinated with crew of the precautionary landing and advised passengers of our intentions. In the descent we completed the appropriate checklists, acquired the [weight and balance] data for landing in addition to brake cooling then were vectored for a visual approach to [Runway] XXL. We landed uneventfully and taxied clear of the runway and we were met by Fire and Rescue. We shut down the #1 engine and awaited CFR to evaluate. CFR gave us the all clear and we taxied to gate and began to coordinate with all appropriate personnel.
Narrative_1: Normal climbout passing FL 282. Initially heard banging outside of aircraft followed by a reduction in climb, decreasing airspeed and aircraft vibration. Immediately followed by a call from the A F/A (flight attendant) reporting flame emanating from #1 engine. Engine problem was confirmed in the cockpit by high temp (800 EGT) and diminished N1. My F/O (First Officer) immediately notified ATC that we have an engine issue and need to maintain FL 280. I told him to [request priority] at that time. I reduced the thrust lever to observe changes in engine indications. The vibrations ceased and temperature reduction. We both believed we had a compressor stall. We were holding FL 280 on one engine, albeit with excessive thrust on #2 engine. F/O asked for lower and we were cleared to FL 240. We had two jumpseaters onboard, so I got an experienced set of eyes on the engine. He confirmed all that we knew and that the engine no longer had flames coming from the tailpipe. Assessing the non-normal together, I called for the QRC (quick reference checklist) Engine Limit or Surge or Stall Checklist. The QRH (quick reference handbook) confirmed our assessment. We completed down to Step X (QRH) at that point. An engine shutdown was not required, but thrust lever remained at idle for remainder of flight. ZZZ was 80 miles from our present position and we agreed was the nearest suitable airport. ATC cleared us direct. While I was PF (pilot flying), F/O communicated with F/A's and passengers. I sent a message to Dispatch about our diversion. We ran the Diversion Checklist. F/O ran weight and balance data for a 'One Engine Inoperative' approach and landing data. We planned for and flew a 'One Engine Inoperative Landing'. An uneventful landing in ZZZ culminated with a check of the engine/damage by Emergency Personnel. We taxied under our own power to the gate.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported engine compressor stall and surges resulted in divert to precautionary landing.

Narrative: Unanticipated GPWS warning on approach requiring crew action. We were flying the freighter (tail), second leg ZZZ-ZZZ1 (1.5 hr delayed at start of day), 5-6 hours into the flight duty period (~XA:00 pm local time). Night IMC w/moderate to heavy rain showers in vicinity. I was Pilot Flying PF (Captain).Clearance was ZZZ...ZZZ1. On the ground at ZZZ we planned and briefed the departure and RNAV (RNP) Rwy XX from the ZZZZZ1 transition. De-iced, taxied, departed, climbed to cruise at FL280.Enroute to ZZZZZ1 at cruise, Center warned of areas of moderate to extreme precipitation from ZZZZZ1 fix to the airport and advised of better weather to the Northeast. After discussing a change to the arrival, we both agreed to request radar vectors to the approach segment from ZZZZZ (IAF). Center agreed to vector us around and down to put us on the published portion of the arrival with the stated intention of joining us to the approach path at ZZZZZ2. FO (First Officer) made the changes in the FMS and we briefed and then ran the Decent Checklist Change Triangles.Radar vectors included a descent and vectors resulting in established on published segment near ZZZZZ2 at 5000 and given approach clearance from center (I had directed PM to reset FMS Cruise Alt to 8,000 feet when we were on vectors). Once established near ZZZZZ2 at 5,000 cleared us for the approach. I engaged LNAV/VNAV and set airport elevation, but was high on the vertical path. I continued to slow to final configuration (gear down, Flaps 40) by ZZZZZ1, stable, but still 1,400 feet above the path in VNAV SPD (vertical navigation speed). After the turn at ZZZZZ1 I set 1,600 feet in the MCP ALT window (FAP 1,600 MSL) and at approximately 2,300 MSL, engaged Vertical Speed down in order to regain the VNAV Path before the FAP. As I approached the path, I reset MCP altitude to airfield elevation and engaged VNAV while pitch mode was in ALT ACQ (altitude acquire), resulting in an unrecognized mode change to V/S (2,100 ft/min) and projected vertical path well before the airport. It was at this point, we received a GPWS 'Caution Terrain' followed shortly by GPWS Warning 'Terrain Fly UP.' I immediately executed an escape maneuver/go-around, climbing and flying the go-around flight path to ZZZ2 and mistakenly climbed to 5,000 MSL (missed approach alt 3,000 MSL), entering the hold as published. I requested and was given a descent to 3,000 MSL in holding.We then built and briefed the RNAV (RNP) Rwy XX from ZZZ2, ran the Descent Change Triangles, received our approach clearance, and executed the approach to landing uneventfully. The FO and I thoroughly debriefed the events of the flight. I then called the Duty Pilot and DISPATCH to report the incident. I should have requested radar vectors ZZZZZ1 for the best opportunity to acquire the VNAV path. I allowed the Controller to compress and to keep me high on my approach, and reducing my situational awareness. I configured very early, but it still wasn't enough to regain the VNAV path. In the future, I will not allow the ATC Controller to dictate the terms of my energy management and will give myself the Flight Handbook recommended 3 miles per 1,000 descent planning as a minimum starting point.Because we compressed our arrival and ended up high above the VNAV path I attempted to use the Vertical Speed method on LNAV/VNAV Approach rules to regain VNAV path prior to the FAP. Had I cross-checked my FMA after selecting VNAV, I would have noticed the V/S mode and perhaps executed an uneventful go-around. In the future, I will make sure to always verify my FMA mode on the PFD after making a selection on the MCP.Lastly, after fully configuring and still not descending to the path, I might have been able to acquire VNAV path prior to the FAP using Speed Intervention. There was chance we were light enough (low Ref Speed) to accelerate the idle pitch descent to regain the path, ensuring the pitch FMA remained in VNAV and avoiding the unrecognized and inadvertent V/S mode descent that caused the GPWS Warning. Recommend expanding the understanding of VNAV speed during initial and continuing qualification training in the B737.
Narrative_1: Escape Maneuver occurred at approximately (time) local time on (date). Flight conditions at the time were night, IMC, rain, light turbulence.Leg 2 of a planned 4 leg day. Leg 1 was delayed 1 hours due to cargo loading. The flight was uneventful. Deiced in ZZZ after aircraft pushback. Filed route was ZZZ...ZZZ1. We planned and briefed the RNAV Rwy XX from ZZZZZ. Cruise was at FL280. PF (pilot flying) MFD was in WX Radar mode due to significant weather in the area. PM (pilot monitoring) was in TERR (terrain) mode with VSD (vertical speed) displayed. Cruise was at dusk. Shortly after starting the descent, ATC notified us that he saw an area of Moderate to Extreme precipitation ahead of us. ATC said it looked clearer to the north and asked if we would like vectors to the north for an approach via ZZZZZ1. We responded yes and he started vectoring us north. PF flew while PM loaded the arrival from ZZZZZ1 (via IAF ZZZZZ1). PM briefed the new approach and called for change triangles, which we accomplished. ATC had us do intermediate level-offs at 8,000 feet, then 7,000 feet. PF asked PM to reset the cruise altitude to provide an accurate flight path. In anticipation of being high on flight path, PF configured early to flaps 40. PM was actively monitoring the VSD and flight path, and requested lower when able from ATC. ATC said he would give us lower in a few miles. He then gave us a short vector prior to ZZZZZ2 with a descent to 6,500 feet. At approx 0.5 miles before ZZZZZ2 at 6,500 feet, ATC cleared us 'to cross ZZZZZ2 at or above 5,000 feet, cleared RNAV Rwy XX at ZZZ1'. When cleared for the approach over ZZZZZ2, PF dialed in field elevation in the MCP and descended towards the flight path. Flight conditions were night, IMC, rain, light turbulence. Approximately 1 mile prior to ZZZZZ3, we were still high on flight path so PF verbalized and set Vertical Speed down and reset MCP to 1,600 feet. PM saw the downward vector on the VSD and monitored it for approaching the flight path. Almost immediately thereafter, we received a 'Caution, Terrain' and the depicted island terrain went yellow on PM's MFD. This was quickly followed by a 'Terrain, Pull up' and the depicted terrain on the MFD went red. PF called for go-around and executed the escape maneuver. After aircraft was climbing, PF asked PM to reset MCP for missed approach altitude of 3,000 feet. PF initially had difficulty verifying the missed approach altitude on the EFB due to turbulence, transition to nighttime, and prioritizing monitoring the aircraft state while performing aircraft cleanup. PF put and verbalized 5,000 feet in the MCP window, thinking 5,000 feet was better in case 3,000 feet was incorrect. PMs intent was to devote more brain cells to performing the aircraft cleanup items and monitoring the safe aircraft state as we climbed. Aircraft was cleaned up, leveled at 5,000 feet and continued to holding at ZZZ2. We then queried ATC for a descent to 3,000 feet, setup the RNAV Rwy XX from ZZZ2. Approach was briefed by Captain, flown, and landed uneventfully. Once the aircraft reached parking and shutdown at ZZZ1, Captain and FO debriefed the events. Captain called and briefed Duty Officer, who approved continuing to the remaining 2 destinations. Captain also called and spoke with Dispatch. The remaining flights to were flown with minimal changes. Post flight, the Captain called Quality Assurance to see what they could tell us, so that we could learn further from this experience.Stay on the magenta line, and if vectored off, get back on it as early as possible. Even though the controller had plans to vector us back onto the RNP approach, a better outcome likely would have resulted if we started at the IAP. This way we would have been able to descend on a normal flight path, with adequate time and pacing, vs. having to stay higher due to the controllers higher vectoring altitudes. Request the IAP next time.At nighttime in IMC, I need to have a faster response timecalling for the escape maneuver/go-around. I should clarify this maneuver more, particularly the triggers. I should have been the first to call for it since the Captain was the PF. Instead of trying to salvage a bad or difficult approach, make the decision to go-around earlier. Memorize the missed approach altitude prior to each approach, or ensure my EFB chart is not zoomed-in so far that I cannot see it without a quick glance.Clarify various 'what-if scenarios' on RNP approaches, Escape Maneuvers, Go-Arounds. If I haven't flown as much recently, spend extra time clarifying. Communicate with Center that 6,500 feet at ZZZZZ2 creates a very difficult approach to accomplish. Recommend to them that vectoring to the IAF is likely a better option.
Synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported executing an escape maneuver due to a CFIT event resulting from a compressed approach clearance. Crew completed subsequent approach in an uneventful landing.

Narrative: The number 2 engine did not spool up on takeoff. The takeoff was immediately rejected with maximum speed of 30 knots. Returned to gate and aircraft was taken out of service by maintenance.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported rejecting takeoff due to engine malfunction.

Narrative: The Captain and I discussed not doing a Visual Approach. Passing through about 9,000 feet, we were going direct to the FAF; conditions where ceiling and visibility unlimited. Approach cleared us for a Visual Approach. We accepted and started descending to 7,000 feet, the altitude for FAF. At about 7,300 or 7,200 feet ATC advised us the Minimum Vectoring Altitude was 7,500 feet. The Captain immediately stopped descending and went to 7,500 feet until just outside the FAF. We made a normal stable approach.We didn't want to do a Visual Approach when we briefed it. We were lured in by the visual conditions and the fact that that everything was stable and non rushed. It was late. Lesson is, do not do night visuals at airports that you are not to familiar with, try to do what you brief especially around terrain. I did get distracted when I lost my flight deck WiFi when I was trying to pull up a new ATIS on iPad. Don't do visual approaches at night, especially near terrain. Fly what you brief.
Narrative_1: While descending on the arrival and approximately 10 miles south of ZZZ, ATC asked us to report the field in sight. It was clear and unlimited visibility. So we called it. When cleared visual [Runway] XXL, I began a descent out of 9,000 feet. I felt that we were within the airspace, but when descending to the FAF altitude of 7,000 feet and at approximately 7,200 feet, we got a call from ATC saying altitude alert. Climb to 7,500 [feet] min vectoring altitude. We immediately climbed to 7,500 [feet] and continued approach. ATC handed us to Tower and nothing else said.During cruise, my First Officer and myself went through all company pages and arrival and approach plates. We discussed terrain and even said that we shouldn't accept a visual approach since it was night time. However, we got direct to FAF and not a usual vector outside the FAF. ATC asked us to report the field. We both evaluated that we were comfortable accepting the visual. We should have stayed with the plan because after being cleared approach, we descended below the ATC min vectoring altitude. Bottom line, be conservative and when flying approaches at night, I will no longer accept a visual approach.
Synopsis: B737-800 Flight Crew reported they descended below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude while conducting a night time Visual Approach.

Narrative: On approach to 25L at LAX, ATC vectored a heavy Airbus onto approach in front of us. When I expressed concern for wake turbulence ATC stated only 3.5 miles was required between us. Since there was a tailwind on the approach and calm wind on surface I advised ATC that I'd like to slow to final approach speed to get more spacing with the heavy. On handoff to Tower, Approach Controller again reiterated that 3.5 miles was sufficient with a heavy Airbus. I thanked him and switched to Tower. We ended up with 4-5 miles separation and still experienced wake turbulence on short final.
Synopsis: B737 Captain reported ATC was uncooperative when he requested more spacing to avoid wake turbulence on approach to LAX.

Narrative: ATC cleared us for a visual approach to Runway 16R into Denver after turning us on to a right base approximately 5 miles from MERYN intersection on the ILS 16R. After being cleared for the visual approach the First Officer (FO) selected the approach mode and a selected a slower speed. The FO was slow to turn towards MERYN and over shot the final approach course. I instructed to FO to turn immediately toward the runway and then back to the final approach course. The approach controller asked if we need a vector and I declined. The FO had previously briefed the ILS to 35R. During the approach briefing we discussed threats that included high elevation, an MEL that restricted RNAV approaches, and that we were tired. The flight was cleared to descend via the TBARR 1 RNAV Arrival with the Runway 16R transition. The transition ends at CLFFF intersection at 11,000' with a speed of 210 knots. ATC was informed that we could not accept an RNAV approach and we were told to expect a visual approach, which we backed up with the ILS approach. The flight was turned to a right base heading at 210 knots. While turning the FO requested a slower speed which ATC approved. ATC asked if we had the airport insight. When I replied that we had the runway insight we were cleared for the visual approach. The FO selected the approach mode. As the FO was selecting a slower speed I mentioned that she should turn toward MERYN intersection. She slowly selected a heading toward MERYN and over shot the final approach course. I think this was due to the angle in which the course was intercepted. I would suggest adding a discussion about accepting visual approaches to the approach briefing, as a possible threat.
Synopsis: Captain reported overshooting final approach course on a visual approach into Denver.

Narrative: Captain's window opened and detached from aircraft during climbout. All checklists were completed, perhaps they were not completed in normal sequence due to severe noise associated with window detachment. Aircraft configuration was fulfilled after much consternation due to nearly nil communication due to wind noise and headset loss.
Synopsis: B737 Captain reported that the Captain's side window opened and became detached during climbout.

Narrative: There was a line of storms crossing ZZZ. We were told to expect holding at ZZZZZ. We ended up holding. We did one turn and then we got sent back on the arrival. We ultimately got vectors from ZZZZZ1 and were following one Company aircraft. The plan was to fly northeast about 30 miles at 5,000 ft to go around the weather and then come back south to land. We couldn't get in front of it or through it. Company turned around to try to get around the weather from the other direction. We did the same thing. We got a 270 heading and a descent to 4,000 ft and an assigned speed of 170 knots. On that vector, I noticed airspeed decreasing and added some power. Then the airspeed dropped to approximately 140 knots and the autopilot and autothrottles were disconnected. I announced to the PM (Pilot Monitoring) that we were in windshear and I added power and started a climbing turn to the left. The aircraft started accelerating and climbing, and we retracted the flaps. The highest speed I saw during the recovery was 220 knots. During this period, airspeed, pitch attitude and altitude was very difficult to control and we encountered what we believed to be severe turbulence. The PM told ATC that we had severe turbulence and windshear and that we were turning to the left and climbing. We tried to level at 5,000 ft and flew southwest. ATC told us to climb to 6,000 ft for traffic. I added power and the aircraft responded poorly. Eventually, we got a climb going, but we were unable to stop the climb at 6,000 ft. The aircraft continued to about 6,450 ft and ATC asked us what altitude we were going to. PM told them that we were trying to get to 6,000 ft but were having a difficult time maintaining altitude with the turbulence. On our way back down to 6,000 ft we got a TCAS TA for traffic at our 1-2 o'clock at 700-800 ft above us. I continued down to about 5,800 ft to make sure we avoided that traffic. We continued southwest and diverted to ZZZ1. If we had asked to stay in holding until we saw that the line had passed even further northeast of the field, it would have prevented this. We had about 13.0 of fuel when we entered holding, so we had the time. [We were] unable to maintain assigned altitude, heading, and airspeed due to windshear and severe turbulence.
Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported the flight encountered wind shear and severe turbulence associated with a line of storms resulting in altitude/airspeed excursions, a conflict and a divert.

Narrative: While departing ZZZ Runway X on the RVAV departure, we experienced a wind shear ahead alert shortly after rotation and after the gear was selected up. While climbing through approximately 500 feet AGL, we entered an area of moderate to severe turbulence followed by a gain and loss of 20+ knots of airspeed. Airspeed excisions were brief in nature, and climb rate decreased from near 3,000 FPM to 1,000 FPM and momentarily less while we transited the wind shear. During this time we also experienced multiple quick rolling and yawing moments that required nearly full control deflection to counter. Both myself and my First Officer agreed that the aircraft was at times momentarily out of control. It is my recollection that the maximum intensity of the turbulence occurred from 500 feet AGL to approximately 3,500 feet AGL. Again these excursions were very quick left and right rolling and yawing motions. During the event, the aircraft energy state never decayed to a dangerous level, however, we were in a lightly loaded -700 with max thrust selected for wind shear avoidance. Above 4,000 feet, we experienced continuous moderate turbulence and icing up to 14,000 feet, and only light turbulence above that. There were no injuries reported, and we did not suspect any aircraft damage. The flight attendants and passengers were briefed before takeoff. Before departure, both myself and the First Officer consulted the Airport Wind System reports as well as reviewed the required wind limits for the departure. The ZZZ Tower and Dispatch were contacted to get a better assessment of what they were seeing with the winds as well. At the time of the beginning of the takeoff roll, the Tower reported steady state wind from the south east 28 KT gusting to 38 KT. The Airport Wind System alert was not functioning, however, [other weather station's] wind and the gust 2-6 Airport Wind System was reporting. All wind reports were within limits at the time of takeoff, and had been for most of the morning. The Dispatcher reported the 8 High Airport Wind System Alert was intermittent all morning. Both myself and my First Officer briefed the departure and took steps necessary to mitigate the perceived threats. Wind shear take off procedures and power settings were used during the take off. After level off, myself and the First Officer consulted the FOM and we were in agreement that we experienced a situation where the aircraft was momentarily not in positive control. A pilot report of MOD to SEV turbulence was relayed to ARTCC as well as company. Dispatch was consulted at this time, and a plan was made to divert to ZZZ1 for maintenance inspection as Maintenance did not want the aircraft stuck in ZZZ2. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. Ensuring Airport Wind System has full functionality and wind profiles are working to the greatest extent possible.
Narrative_1: Preparing for departure from ZZZ we looked at weather reports including the ZZZ Airport Wind System and PIREPS. Nothing indicated that we would encounter anything greater than moderate turbulence as we took off from Runway X. Shortly after liftoff we encountered moderate turbulence and at about 1,000 ft AGL received a 'Windshear Ahead' alert. We then experienced approximately 30 - 45 seconds of severe turbulence. We gave ATC a PIREP and overflew our original destination of ZZZ2 at the request of Dispatch and Maintenance control to get the plane to a maintenance base.
Synopsis: B37-700 flight crew reported after encountering severe turbulence and wind shear, it was decided to overfly the destination airport and divert to a maintenance base.

Narrative: While preflighting a stub flight we received an amended flight plan from Dispatch. The Dispatcher said that there was a bend in the flight plan and that he wanted to remove that. Because this was a stub flight our application struggled to upload the correct flight plan. It kept wanting to upload our original flight plan. The PACOTS east routing (Pacific Organized Track System) for that day was our original flight plan which had us departing the 130W longitude for DACEM onward to pick up the IRNMN arrival into LAX. However the Dispatcher rerouted us to fly from 140W bypassing 130W to begin an arrival using the RYDER arrival. This confused not only us but departure Area Control who had our original flight plan in their system. We departed the gate with the correct uploaded ATC flight plan but possessed on our iPads the amended flight plan from Dispatch... in addition our FO (First Officer) refused to coordinate with Dispatch to revise our our flight plan to its original format which resulted in erroneous flight progress forms from ACARS. To be clear the flight plan only deviated towards the latter end of the flight with the confusion resulting from the Dispatcher uploading an erroneous flight plan to remove a bend in the flight however that was not loaded to the PACOTS east routing for the day. Our FO contacted SFO radio to confirm our routing was correct with our FMS but neglected to inform Dispatch who thought we were still flying the amended route he had given us. It would be helpful if the company would provide guidance regarding how procedurally they would prefer crews coordinate changes to flight plans with ATC. Do they prefer we coordinate with ATC directly or would they prefer that we contact Dispatch and ask that they upload the correct route and that we check it with ATC. It would seem there is a loophole in regards to keeping Dispatch up to speed on changes to flight plans. I believe there is language in the FOM regarding any changes to the flight plan to notify Dispatch of those changes. In this case the changes were minimal however the arrival time differed by about 6-8 minutes from the original flight plan and the amended one from Dispatch. Dispatch was unaware that this stub flight was not flying the amended flight plan they sent us. When I, as the relief pilot, arrived from my break on the flight deck I noticed the erroneous flight progress forms and notified Dispatch who then sent us the revised flight plan. Dispatch was unaware that we were back on our original PACOTS routing. This was accomplished 2+45 into the flight. However if I had not done this it would not have gotten done as the FO refused to contact Dispatch to clear up the confusion. please advise. The First Officer refused input from both the Captain and myself, the relief pilot, to contact Dispatch and get them in the loop regarding discrepancies from filed flights from amended ones. Stub flights caused more confusion than necessary. Clear guidance is needed from company on how they prefer the crew to remedy route discrepancies from Dispatch versus filed. Do they prefer the crew to contact ATC and fix the problem ourselves or do they prefer Dispatch to get involved and fix the discrepancy.
Narrative_1: Just prior to pushback, we received a message from Dispatch with regards to a change in our flight planned route. We delayed pushback until receiving new flight plan. Only change was to end of route after waypoint at 140W. We then called Clearance Delivery and did a full route verification. They still only had the original, unchanged route. Since the only discrepancy between the flight plans was at the end of the flight, we opted to depart. After departure, we received the flight progress report that showed the modified route (after 140W). During flight, after checking in with San Francisco ARINC, we asked for a verification of our cleared routed. ARINC verified it was the original flight planned route. We then sent a message to Dispatch with our cleared route and received an update. Dispatch believed we requested a look at modifying our route to remove a 'dog leg' segment from our route which we hadn't. We were a STUB flight and that might have been a factor as the original flight was near to the arrival time. The change to our flight plan wasn't requested and wasn't essential to safety. Unless critical to flight safety, last minute changes to flight plans (especially international) can cause miscommunications and errors in navigation and should be avoided.
Synopsis: B-777 flight crew reported difficulty resolving discrepancies between the flight plan provided by Dispatch and the received clearance for a trans-Pacific flight.

Narrative: Traveling in level cruise at FL370, smooth air, Mach .80 we experienced an aircraft Mach speed exceedence. With no noticeable wind change the aircraft accelerated, uncommanded, up to Mach .84. The A/T system made minimal, if any, changes to the cruise power setting. The Captain (PF) immediately spun the Mach speed way back and extended full speed brakes. This was the point at which the A/T finally brought the power back. We stabilized the aircraft, configured the automation and continued to the destination with no other abnormalities.We possibly could have reacted more aggressively and sooner, but we fully expected the A/T system to respond correctly to the speed increase and reduce power accordingly. Aside from that, I cannot see anything else that could have prevented the situation.I don't know what we could change to prevent this situation again.
Synopsis: Air carrier First Officer reported a Mach speed exceedance during cruise. First Officer stated the increase in speed was uncommanded and there was no noticeable wind change either.

Narrative: I was the Pilot Flying. On climb-out I noticed my electric trim was not working. The First Officer's electric trim was also inoperative. We leveled off to assess the situation and complete the QRH checklist. We elected to return to ZZZ.
Synopsis: B737-700 Captain reported the Electric Pitch Trim failed on both the Captain's and First Officer's control columns.

Narrative: While on the RNAVM XX in ZZZ1 we encountered a GPWS event. At the beginning of the approach we had a tailwind and the descent angle of the approach caused us to be a little fast starting the approach. As the pilot monitoring I should have caught this issue sooner and brought it to the attention of the PF (Pilot Flying). Because of the speed the PF disconnected the autopilot/auto throttles and slowed the plane to the proper approach speed. During the turn onto final the PF was visual with the runway and let the nose drop which caused a momentary don't sink. He corrected and the warning went away. Still with the airport visual he tried to correct on the VASI and received another momentary don't sink call at around 700 ft. We continued the approach and the landing was normal. I don't have anything to add for [this report].I have learned many lessons from this very short flight. I haven't had much ZZZ experience and my FO (First Officer) who was PF has had very little. We tried to mitigate the possible issues by having a slow cruise speed of 210 kts. and trying to get ready for the approach early. We briefed the 3.4 GP and felt we were in a good position for the approach. With the unfamiliarity of the situation and the weather in ZZZ this day I missed the strong tailwind that was making our situation worse. This put us behind and we had to play catch up. It was turbulent the whole flight and when he disconnected the AP/AT my [situational awareness] went down because I was worried about his flight path at that time. As I look back at the event and if I could do this again I would have us discontinue the approach early and come around to try again. Once we continued and got out of the [weather] and had the runway visually climbing back into it in that terrain did not seem the safest option. But if we had bailed early it would have made the situation easier the second time.
Synopsis: B737 Captain reported an uneventful landing after two GPWS alerts during approach due primary weather conditions.

Narrative: Have more of a warning from ATC of the turbulence expected to encounter. We did not know of the severity of the turbulence until we were in it ourselves. Experienced continuous moderate turbulence between 8,000 feet to 3,000 feet on descent on the RNAV arrival. We landed without incident.
Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported unexpected moderate turbulence during descent.

Narrative: Be fast to recognize an air quality event.I was flying an A320 from ZZZ to ZZZ1. During the arrival we had an air quality event. The estimated duration of the event was 5 minutes. During the event the power levels did not change. I have experienced this in the same type of aircraft before. There was no evidence of smoke or fire in the cockpit and it was localized. The odor smelled like dirty socks and were mild. It was only in the cockpit. During the time of event, our air supply was the engines. I was able to turn off Pack 1 and isolate the problem within about 15 seconds. I reserve the right to change my statement as more informant becomes available.
Synopsis: A320 Captain reported a fumes event during descent which was described as a 'dirty socks' odor. The flight continued to its destination after the number 1 Pack was turned off.

Narrative: On climb out to ZZZ both airspeed disagreement cautions came on with +/- 10 knot difference between the Captain and FO (First Officer) airspeed [indicators]. Once at cruise all cautions went away and we continued. Upon descent and on the arrival we again got the 'airspeed disagreement' caution for about 5 minutes then it again disappeared. Continuing on the descent at around 16,000 ft. and in icing conditions the Captain's airspeed went to +/- 50 knots causing the throttles to chase the airspeed. I turned off the autopilot, autothrottles and both flight directors as per the QRH and quickly realized the FO side was working fine. The FO continued the descent.
Narrative_1: Climbing out, passing approximately FL280 in IMC conditions, with the CA (Captain) flying, we received an 'IAS DISAGREE' indication. There was a split of approximately 10 KIAS between the CA and FO (First Officer) instruments with a corresponding split in Mach. I, the FO, got out the unreliable airspeed checklist in the QRH to look up the possible indications. After a few moments the indication disappeared and the IAS returned to normal. After beginning a descent the same indications returned and then disappeared as they had before. Passing approximately 16,000 ft. there was a large fluctuation in the CA's airspeed causing a large fluctuation in the autothrottles. The CA disengaged the autopilot and autothrottles. We transferred aircraft control since my indications seemed normal. The CA ran the QRH for unreliable airspeed [and] I flew the approach using the autopilot with the autothrottles disengaged to an uneventful landing.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported the Captain's airspeed indicator became unreliable and control was transferred to the First Officer.

Narrative: I was PF (Pilot Flying) and received an RA about 20 NM SW of ZZZ. Descending from 7,000-5,000 feet, I received a TA and immediately reduced my rate of descent. I received an RA while leveling off at 5,000 [feet] regarding traffic 500 feet below, I complied and cleared the conflict. The aircraft was landed safely without issue.
Synopsis: Air Carrier First Officer reports an NMAC during descent.

Narrative: I was CA (Captain) and PM (Pilot Monitoring). Departed late due to ELAC (Elevator & Aileron Computer) 1 MEL (Minimum Equipment List). South of ZZZ at FL390, we had ECAM for HYD (Hydraulic) G RSVR (Reservoir) LO AIR PR (Low Air Pressure). I ran the ECAM and told ATC we had a HYD issue. ECAM put us into ATL LAW (Alternate Law) and FO (First Officer) had to hand fly. We asked for lower altitude and told ATC we wanted ZZZ1 and I sent ACARS to Dispatch. I was running the COM and getting ATIS and found out ZZZ was showing 002OVC (200' Overcast) and 1 1/2 vis (Visibility). I asked ATC if there was anything better for weather and he said the region was all the same. We decided to go to ZZZ. Once the COM was complete I called and briefed the FA's (Flight Attendants) and made PA to the passengers. We decided that I would take over and fly the approach and landing. We briefed the ILS 11 Approach and the FO hand flew the Aircraft until about 15-20 mile final so I could take my time and take a few minutes to 'gather my thoughts.' We started to configure early and we had to gravity extend the gear. Now we were in direct law and started to fly the approach.. We saw the approach lights and continued and saw the runway at minimums. We landed. We taxied to the gate and briefed the passengers and deplaned. I made the phone calls to Company, Dispatch and Maintenance. Maintenance looked at the issue and found out there was HYD fluid all over and we had a bad O ring. They fixed the issue and we were about to land in ZZZ1 about 5 hours late.
Synopsis: A320 Captain reported a Hydraulic System Failure inflight resulting in a diversion.

Narrative: Great weather, normal fuel burn. Entering terminal area we were vectored around then low and slow which created more fuel burn in terminal area. Did go-around for XXL due to an animal on runway. Aircraft in front of us did same. Declared minimum fuel on go-around in order to expedite landing since fuel now was an issue with extra fuel burn and not much to play. Controller was going to extend us downwind behind an arriving aircraft which would have added more time and fuel so I elected to [request] an immediate turn to the FAF for XXC. I didn't want XXL because of animal issue and another possible go-around. Controller vectored preceding aircraft off their approach and cleared us for visual XXC. Landed uneventfully with 3.9 fuel.....2.10 left tank and 1.8 right tank. Reserve Fuel on Flight Plan was 3.78.Cause: Dispatched with normal arrival fuel with very good weather. Controller vectored us low and slow which increased fuel burn. Suggestions: Next time I will not accept so many vectors and low and slow increasing fuel burn when I do not have extra fuel to play.
Synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported a low fuel situation developed following a go-around to avoid an animal on the runway.

Narrative: Enroute ZZZ-ZZZ1 on the red-eye at FL 33,000 ft. into the flight we had an ANTI ICE STBY PITOT ECAM. QRH was used. later we were at FL 35,000 ft. and Autopilot 1 disconnected, I attempted to reengage #1 or #2 autopilots and neither would engage. The FMAs went blank on both the F/O and my PFDs. Autothrust disengaged and went into Thrust LK. Thrust levers were matched with power setting and IDP switches used. We had our route displayed in the ND on both sides and MCDUs were operating normally. ECAM displayed:AUTO FLT AP OFF (RED)AUTO FLT A/THR OFF (AMBER)L/G SHOCK ABSORBER FAULT (AMBER)Indications looked similar to an FMGC Dual Failure except we had both NDs displaying our route, our MCDUs did not go into a subsystem page and no FMGC (Timeout) was observed. The Shock Absorber Fault ECAM had me thinking this may be a different malfunction that I have never witnessed or a coincidence. We contacted Dispatch/Maintenance via phone patch using the 'CALL ME' function on ACARS. Maintenance was perplexed of what was causing our malfunction. They had us reset the Auto Flight C/B's B1 (MCDU 1) B2 (FMG 1) and hold. C/B's were reset with no change. We attempted the Long Reset in the QRH Dual FMGC Failure with no success. Mintenance had no other options available.ATC was advised of our equipment malfunction and our inability to remain in ZZZ airspace. We were cleared down to FL 27,000 ft.. Review of our fuel, weather and capabilities with my F/O. Dispatcher we agreed to continue to ZZZ1 with the caution that if we had additional malfunctions, we would consider ZZZ2 as a divert airport. ATC was given our new suffix with the inability to operate in RVSM airspace.Purser was informed of our status.Prior to touchdown at FL 27,000 ft. both FMAs began to populate. Autopilots and Autothrust became available. All malfunctions except for the STBY Pitot cleared. We reengaged the Auto flight functions and remained at FL 27,000 ft. We landed on Runway XX at ZZZ1. Malfunctions were recorded on in the ELB, including a information writeup of what happened. Technician met the plane and we explained what happened.
Synopsis: Captain reported failure of aircraft display systems, causing aircraft to descend out of RVSM airspace.

Narrative: After we were clear for takeoff on the Runway XX, at ZZZ airport. The Captain applied power; he waited for the engine to stabilize, then he pressed TOGA. As the plane started moving, it suddenly started veering to the right. He tried to correct it by pressing the left rudder, but the aircraft did not respond right away. After a few seconds, the plane veer back to the left, but it only went about 45 degrees to the left. After that, the Captain pressed the right rudder and was able to bring it back to control. Furthermore, we stopped at the runway; then, I called the tower to abort the takeoff. Finally, we were able to taxi off the runway and went back to the gate.
Narrative_1: Cleared for takeoff Runway XX. Engines spooled up 'taxiing' up to takeoff point on Runway XX. With engines at 40% N1 pushed TOGA button and throttles advanced. We observed the white arcs advancing but the plane didn't seem to be accelerating normally. As I glanced inside to ensure the auto throttles were engaged (they were) the aircraft started to drift right. I tried to correct back with the rudder as we always do but it had no effect. As the right drift continued I rejected the take off and had to use almost full nose wheel tiller to correct back to centerline. We smelled burning rubber, so we taxied clear of the runway and had ARFF (Airport Rescue Firefighting) come inspect the gear and wheels. No problems found by ARFF. Tower had the runway inspected. Nothing found. I had ARFF follow us to the gate where we made an AML entry and had a lengthy discussion with Maintenance. During the takeoff roll the throttles never made it to Takeoff Thrust and I was looking outside the whole time, but the speed achieved was well below 80 kts. Probably around 40-45 kts. In addition, on taxi out when brakes were applied to stop in line they often 'chattered.'We suspected a brake problem or asymmetric thrust.I'm not sure why it happened. I've seen asymmetric thrust before and it is easily corrected with rudder to steer back to centerline. This plane was very difficult to get turning back to the left.
Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported the takeoff was rejected after the aircraft drifted to the right and was not responding to rudder inputs.

Narrative: Ten minutes into the flight, we received an ACARS message. It stated that oxygen cylinders were on-board. We did not receive a Dangerous Goods Form on the ground. Once we landed in ZZZ1, we reached out to Dispatch and received a copy of the Dangerous Goods form. I signed it, and it was faxed back to ZZZ.
Narrative_1: Approximately ten minutes into our climb out from ZZZ, we received a message from Dispatch telling us we had four oxygen bottles in the cargo area. We did not receive a Dangerous Goods Form from the Ramp prior to our departure. We continued on to our destination. In ZZZ1 we were given the proper paperwork. Captain signed it, and paperwork was sent, via fax, to ZZZ.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported in flight notification of Hazmat cargo onboard without proper flight crew documentation. Required Hazmat documents completed upon arrival at destination.

Narrative: Upon gear retraction, after departure from [Runway] XXL at ZZZ, we heard a loud bang in the nose wheel well with an associated yaw of the aircraft. A burnt rubber smell was also detected and dissipated after 5 minutes. My thoughts ranged from, 'something hit us' to 'we blew a nose tire.' All engine and hydraulic indications were normal and the plane was flying fine with no control problems. I decided we had no immediate safety of flight issues and we continued the climbout. At 25,000 feet I had the First Officer take the radios and I messaged dispatch that I wanted to talk to Flight Operations. The Dispatcher and I talked briefly on the SATCOM and he put me on hold to get Flight Operations online. While waiting I ran through the QRH to see if there was a procedure for this issue and found 'Tire Failure.' That seemed to most agree with the possible problem and I was pleased to see that it called for us to proceed normally to the destination since that's what we were doing. Discussing what we knew with Flight Operations we all agreed that the problem was probably the tire and proceeding normally was the action we would take. Flight Operations also said they would call the Tower and Approach control to let them know we might have an issue.After level off the 'A' Flight Attendant came to the cockpit and asked if we heard a bang on takeoff. She said some of the 1st class passengers asked her if we were alright and she said that she was able to reassure them that we were. I told her what we suspected and that I would brief the FA's (Flight Attendants) near top of descent.We had plenty of time and I didn't want to get caught unawares so the FO and I briefed various scenarios and reviewed checklists including 'manual gear extension' and ' partial or all gear up landing'. By the time we were ready to brief the arrival I felt prepared to handle any scenario.Unrelated to the wheel issue, about halfway to ZZZ2 the FO fwd window overheat-light illuminated. We ran the checklist and never got it back so, knowing we had clouds and probably ice to descend through I opted to do the landing. I had considered it anyway, but that clinched it. Sure enough the FO's window was opaque until about the outer marker.ATC was ready for us thanks to the Flight Operations phone call. They set us up for [Runway] YYL and slowed us to 170 around ZZZZZ [Intersection]. I put the gear down at that time to give us some breathing room if it didn't come down. The nose gear was the first to show down and locked and I relaxed a bit. We told tower we anticipated a normal landing but they still asked for souls and fuel, which we gave them. They had an operations vehicle shadow us to check for debris. Touchdown was normal and the nose wheel felt fine when it made contact so we told Tower we could taxi in unaided.We were met by the ops manger and several mechanics. Disappointingly, the nose wheel and the well area looked perfectly normal. After all that build up, I admit I wanted to see some torn metal or bits of tire. It will be interesting to see what maintenance discovers.What I can say I learned from this, is that we have a solid system of communication at (Company). The call to ATC by Flight Operations and Dispatch saved us a lot of on air negotiation for 16L. My FO contributed many helpful thoughts that aided our preparation for just about any gear scenario. The FA's took the news of a possible irregular landing calmly and knew what roles they would play should things get sticky. Although it all turned out to be much ado about nothing, it was a good test of the system and the system works.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew aircraft reported aircraft yaw and a loud bang in the nose wheel well during gear retraction. Additionally, the FO's forward window had an overheat issue.

Narrative: Departing ZZZ1 for ZZZ2 I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring) and the CA (Captain) was the PF (Pilot Flying). We planned a low altitude flight due to the shortness of the leg. Some altitudes in the legs page were edited to allow the lower cruise altitude to be selected. The flaps 10 takeoff went as normal (LNAV/VNAV). The PF called for flaps 1 as near as I can recall. I believe this is the case as most if not all of our previous legs had been flaps 5 takeoffs. I was distracted with a radio call or frequency change and I moved the flaps to 1 and did not catch the error. Shortly after that, the FMC changed to the descent phase and the speed bug moved to the flaps 5 maneuver speed, and the A/T (Auto Throttle) mode went from N1 to FMC speed, which resulted in the flaps 5 maneuver speed being the A/T target. As, or just prior to this happening the PF called for flaps up. I moved the flap lever to the up position, and since we were no longer accelerating got a momentary stick shaker. The PF instinctively lowered the nose reducing the AOA (Angle Of Attack). I increased the speed in the MCP window to get the A/T to command acceleration. The remainder of the flight was normal.Suggest crews be alert for unusual mode reversions when using low altitudes for cruise. I would probably use non VNAV takeoff procedures in the future. The big lesson is not new, vigilance absolutely has to be maintained during the 'red' parts of the flight path. The PM job is challenging and can be intolerant of errors.
Synopsis: Air Carrier flight crew reported a procedure error during flap retraction.

Narrative: We were cleared for a visual approach following a Boeing 777 to Runway 25L at LAX. On short final we encountered what was most likely wake turbulence from the proceeding aircraft on short final ~300 feet AGL. This presented as a roll and shear to a headwind. This apparent shear to a headwind along with an addition of some thrust put me high on the profile and ~15 knots above target speed. The severity of the event was below what I would describe as an 'upset'. When the turbulence subsided we appeared to be in a good position to land, so I continued the approach and landed. Being high on profile and bleeding off the excess speed in the flare resulted in a touchdown that was most likely beyond the touchdown zone. Despite this we were in position, with normal braking, to exit at taxiway H8. Tower instructed us to exit at H9.
Narrative_1: Upon landing on Runway 25L at LAX we landed outside of the normal 3000 feet of the touchdown zone after being preceded by a 777 to landing during light tail wind conditions. The briefing and approach were completely routine. We had originally planned to land on 24R but we were prepared for a possible change to Runway 25L. We were told on downwind that we would be following a heavy 777 and could expect 25L. Conditions were clear and we had the aircraft in sight. As I reconfigured the aircraft for landing on the south runway, the Captain made the comment that he would be prepared to fly a dot high. The Captain flew as he briefed and we experienced mostly calm winds all the way down the glideslope. By 200 feet AGL, we were back on glide slope. The aircraft sank somewhat and by 100 feet we were almost a half dot low when we started to feel some of the wake of the 777. The winds were still light, about 300/7. The plane was very controllable and the Captain pitched up and added power slightly to stay on top of the wake. In doing so, the speed increased almost 15 knots and I considered calling for a go around. It still appeared that we were going to be touching down in the first 3000 feet so I allowed the approach to continue. The Captain flared the aircraft so that it looked like we would touch down right at about 3000 feet. Without trying to hold the aircraft off, the plane continued down the runway at what seemed like 1 foot. The aircraft finally settled a couple hundred feet later and we turned off the runway and proceeded to the gate without any further issues.This was a case where one limit almost being crossed led to another limit being crossed. It looked like it was all going to work out. We have all encountered 'disturbed' air from a wake before on landing especially at busy airports like LAX. The question is how much of an adjustment do you have to make and at what point do you go around. This looked very doable. We had plenty of runway and performance. This looked familiar with a landing in the touchdown zone. I only thought later and realized that the Captain had elected to do a flaps 40 landing in a 737-900ER. I know I have not done many flaps 40 landings in a 900ER in the last couple years, so I think my sight picture was off a bit for the flare and the touchdown. We may have also gotten a bit more of ground effect than what I would have imagined. The speed did not bleed off as fast as I had anticipated.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported encountering wake turbulence from preceding B777 on approach to LAX that resulted in a long landing.

Narrative: I was the Captain on Flight XXXX, ZZZ to ZZZ1.During the climb, passing FL330 to FL 350, ECAM ADR1. Complying with instructions from ECAM, additional ECAMs: AP 1& 2, A/THR, RUD TRV LIM and GPWS. We also lost both FD (Flight Display).[Advised ATC] and asked for vector to divert to ZZZ2.
