ZZZ2 weather was clear, ZZZ had thunderstorms.Phone patch with Dispatch and [Maintenance Control] and advised of situations and intentions.Descended into ZZZ2. Asked for delaying vectors to get under landing weight.Raw data landing was normal. Completed [Maintenance Manual].
Narrative_1: I was the First Officer on Flight XXXX, ZZZ to ZZZ1.During the climb, passing FL330 to FL 350, ECAM ADR1. Complying with instructions from ECAM, additional ECAMs: AP 1&2, A/THR, RUD TRV LIM and GPWS. We also lost both FD (Flight Display).[Advised ATC] and asked for vector to divert to ZZZ2. ZZZ2 weather was clear, ZZZ had thunderstorms.Phone patch with Dispatch and [Maintenance Control] and advised of situations and intentions.Descended into ZZZ2. Asked for delaying vectors to get under landing weight.Raw data landing was normal. Completed [Maintenance Manual].
Synopsis: Flight Crew reported diverting caused by loss of ADR1 and associated NAV and FLIGHT Displays.

Narrative: We were at cruise when we noted the right engine oil pressure at 6 (normally around 12). We see that the number was going down, showing that we are losing oil. I started to go through the iPad QRH for an appropriate checklist. While looking, the Captain said 'your aircraft' so I took over pilot duties (it was his leg). He was looking at the Low Oil checklist when the oil qty went to zero, and the Captain decided to just shutdown the engine before it got worse. We [advised ATC] and a turn back towards ZZZ. We ran the engine shutdown checklist. I was flying, he was doing the checklists, radio, and the procedures, as recommended by our training department. We were still over max landing weight, and needed time to run all the supplemental checklists and procedures, so we decided to land at ZZZ and burn fuel to get under max landing weight at the same time. The single engine ILS into ZZZ was textbook. We taxied off the runway, was inspected by CFR, and then taxied to the gate.The Low Oil Quantity checklist is not easily found, as it is not in the index as 'low oil quantity' or 'oil low quantity' and it only reference oil pressure in the index.There was no audio or visual alert, when the oil quantity was half what it was supposed to be. We just happened to catch the small indication on the lower screen, and watched it drop to zero. I don't think we could have caught it any faster than we did.
Narrative_1: Oil quantity on the Number 2 engine went to 0.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported loss of engine oil, causing an in-flight shut down and a diversion to a precautionary landing.

Narrative: Loss Blue Hyd system. Applied QRH procedures and advised ATC.
Narrative_1: Approximately 200 nm south of ZZZ we received our first indication of any issue with the blue hydraulic system. In level cruise flight we received an ECAM for HYD B SYS LO PR. While running the ECAM we noticed that the hydraulic quantity was low. The procedure calls for the Blue Electric Pump to be shut off, and as we did so, we monitored the quantity indicator. As it dropped, we received an ECAM for Hyd B RSVR LO LVL. After running the ECAM, finishing the QRH and conferring with dispatch we advised ATC for the loss of redundant systems. We chose to divert to ZZZ for a multitude of reasons including the nice weather, long runways, availability of ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) and the fact that it's a maintenance hub. We immediately received vectors and a descent from ATC for an arrival into ZZZ. The Captain finalized his briefings to both the flight attendants and passengers. We then updated the FMC, applied the landing distance procedure and landing calculations and briefed the descent and approach. We completed the RNAV to [Runway XX], landed and had ARFF inspect the aircraft for any potential hazards or safety concerns. Once complete, we taxied to the gate and completed the diversion safely.
Synopsis: A320 flight crew reported a loss of hydraulic pressure that resulted in a diversion.

Narrative: We were on a visual approach to Runway XXL at ZZZ at 3,000 feet. Approach cleared us for a visual approach about 7 miles out and we were giving a heading towards the FAF following an airbus. PF set 2,000 feet in the MCP and we began a slow descent heading inbound to the airport. ATC issued a 'low altitude alert' at about 2,300 feet. We leveled off and intercepted the G/S just past the FAF. In addition, we had to rapidly slow since the airbus in front slowed rapidly and ATC wanted us to slow to approximately 150 knots or less. They really did not leave us much lateral room. We slowed and configured while descending. We were never near an obstacle, nor were we a threat to another aircraft. We were still above the 1,000 feet stable approach criteria (1,300 to 1,500 feet) and met the criteria proof to reaching 1,000 feet. We were lower than what was normally flow for that area but still seamed safe. Again on a visual approach. PF stated that he read 2,000 feet at the FAF and misread the altitude. The FAF altitude is 2,800 feet. I did not reverify it since we were visual and I was working on setting up radios and configuration for landing. I assumed he saw it correctly.I can't find where we violated anything. We were a little low for the area but still in a safe position to land and had visual clearance from all obstacles. I know next time to verify the altitude in the MCP from the chart myself. That is that only thing that may have stopped the lower alt in the first place.
Narrative_1: On receiving landing clearance, I set 2,000 feet in the altitude window and planned to descend to that altitude at ZZZZZ, the FAF. I misread the approach plate. The correct altitude at ZZZZZ is 2,800 feet. The Tower gave us a Low Altitude Alert at 2,200 MSL in VMC and we maintained that altitude (we were nearly at glideslope intercept) until glideslope intercept. We landed uneventfully.
Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported entering the wrong altitude in the MCP and descending below FAF altitude which resulted in Air Traffic Control issuing a low altitude alert.

Narrative: Noticed slight airframe vibration in the climb. At FL300 it was much worse. Getting even more vibration as speed increased. Called up the flight control page and saw the R FLPRN was almost all the way up with the L in a normal position. The control column was 2 degrees right wing down. Called Operations Control and discussed. Had the Tech Pilot on the phone also. All agreed it was not normal. Decision was to return to ZZZ. Had to dump fuel. Did this in coordination with Center. Arrival was normal until landing flaps were selected. When flaps started past 20 the airplane shook violently and rolled to the R. Re-selected flaps to 25 and added 15 knots. At the gate the maintenance tech could see the Number 6 spoiler was up. Wrote up the discrepancies and debriefed the mechanic. Crew did a phenomenal job. Great back up.Cause - Spoiler float not locked down.
Narrative_1: Aircraft X did a block turn back for a spoiler issues when I first sat down. After nearly 5 hours on the ground, we received a duty extension and the flight departed. (XA16z) At approximately XA55z crew sent ACARS message:...ALT AIRFRAME VIBL ENG 1.0 R ENG .9R FLPRN IS UPVIBWORSE AT HIGHER SPD.I spoke with the crew on the SATCOM for over an hour bringing in Operations, Tech Pilot, Maintenance Control and Maintenance Control talked to mechanics that did the spoiler work. We determined it was odd behavior for B777 controls and this aircraft usually flies straight. Determination was made to bring the flight back to ZZZ as this may not be an easy fix.
Synopsis: B777 flight crew and the flight Dispatcher reported airframe vibrations during climbout which worsened as the speed increased. The crew contacted the company and decided to return to their departure airport. Reportedly, the cause of the issue was a spoiler float was not locked down.

Narrative: I was the Captain on Aircraft X from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on Date. Just about top of descent both the FAs (Flight Attendants) and both pilots heard a high pitched squealing sound and the FAs believed it was coming from Door R1 near the floor.The FAs also reported a vibration in the floor at the bottom of Door R1.The FAs never reported smelling anything.About a minute after the sound started the FO (First Officer) thought he might be smelling something coming from his gasper vent on the forward instrument panel. I couldn't initially smell anything but possibly a few minutes later might have briefly but if we did it was very brief and minor. The FO described it as a hot plastic type of smell but very faint and for just a couple of minutes.The squeal and vibration lasted about 10 minutes and the rest of the flight was uneventful.I filled out an odor form for MX (Maintenance), they said it would help them troubleshoot our issue and therefore I also am filing a report.
Synopsis: A320 Captain reported experiencing a 'brief' fumes event at the top of descent. Simultaneously, the flight Attendants reported a temporary 'high pitch squeal' accompanied by a floor vibration.

Narrative: Flight crew noted a slight rumbling vibration on climb out. The vibration increased with airspeed and as we reach cruise at FL300 and increased speed we noted the increased vibration and that there was a control yoke displacement of approximately 2 units right in straight and level flight with all other trim neutral. After discussing the situation as a crew, we decided to contact [Operations and Maintenance] for further discussion and possible solutions. Due to a known history and MEL addition affecting spoilers, we selected the flight control schematic page and noted that the right flaperon indicated a near full upward deflection in level flight. Through our discussion with [a] tech pilot, it was suggested that we try utilizing rudder trim to determine how much was needed to neutralize the control yoke, and we determined that 4 units of rudder trim was required. Without being able to fully determine what was causing the vibration we decided that a 13 1/2 hour flight and oceanic crossing would not be prudent, and most likely would not be possible due to fuel over burn. We discussed possible alternate airports and [Operations] ultimately requested that we return to ZZZ. We were North West of ZZZ1 when we coordinated with ZZZ2 Center for our return to ZZZ. We coordinated with ZZZ1 Center to jettison fuel in order to be below max landing weight. The fuel jettison of 78,400 lbs. was accomplished just south east of ZZZ3 VOR at FL200. Arriving back into the ZZZ area, we coordinated for runway 36C. As we configured the aircraft for landing, we noted a drastic increase in vibration as the flaps were extended from 20 to the planned setting of 30. We adjusted to flap 25 for landing and flap 25 speed. Although the vibrations and roll control were abnormal on final, the landing was uneventful. After landing we elected to leave the flaps at 25 until mechanics at the gate could verify that retraction would not cause further damage. After block in it was discovered that the number 6 spoiler was up. We could not see indications for the number 6 spoiler on the flight control page due to the MEL deactivation. Initial indications are that the number 6 spoiler which was deactivated under MEL was 'floating' or extended when it should have been down.
Narrative_1: On taxi out, during the control check a 'spoilers' EICAS message displayed. PDM (Programmed Depot Maintenance) procedures were attempted, but we had to return to the gate for maintenance, as it was a 'flagged' item. Spoilers were MELed. After takeoff, we felt airframe vibrations that got worse at higher altitudes and airspeeds. We found the right flaperon was indicating all the way up, the left flaperon was indicating slightly down. Additionally, the control wheel was right wing down about 2 degrees. After consulting Maintenance and [Operations], everyone decided that the best course of action was to RTB (Return to Base) ZZZ. Fuel jettison checklist was executed in order to land on 36C. Due to excessive airframe vibrations at flaps 30, a flaps 25 landing was made.Uncommanded asymmetric spoiler deployment.
Synopsis: B777 flight crew reported uncommanded asymmetric spoiler deployment in flight.

Narrative: The incident took place at ZZZZ on runway XX, where aircraft must back taxi to use full length. The CA (Captain) and I had just deadheaded down, with our first flying leg of the trip being from ZZZZ to ZZZ. I was feeling refreshed as I had napped for about 2 hours on the [deadhead] down. We had 1.5 hours on the ground, so did not feel rushed, even though it was my first time to ZZZZ. Boarding, preflight, briefing, clearance, pushback, start and taxi to hold short of Rwy XX were uneventful. The CA briefed language as a threat, but the clearance and ground control went smoothly. Initially we held short at taxiway E. Following a departure by another AC we were cleared to back taxi down to Runway XX approach end, and lineup and wait. While in our turn around, an aircraft checked in on final for our runway, I visually identified that aircraft and said aloud that he looked to be on a 6 mile final. Tower told that aircraft to continue.Once aligned with the centerline, I confirmed with the Captain that he was ready to depart, then told Tower "Aircraft X in position, ready for takeoff'. Tower responded that we were cleared for takeoff runway XX, and to contact departure when airborne. I replied that we were cleared for takeoff, runway XX, and echoed the departure frequency we were just given.The Captain and I confirmed with each other we were both ready to go and he pushed up the throttles. As we both were watching the engines spool up, we began to roll forward down the runway. Tower then said something to the effect of "Aircraft X, please do not takeoff, there is an aircraft...' As I started to look up, my first thought was about the aircraft on final. The CA and I both looked at each other, confused about the nonstandard radio call. Tower sounded a bit flustered, and then I saw 2 strobe lights at the far end of the runway. I said 'Reject' aloud, then answered tower "Aircraft X rejecting takeoff.' The CA executed the rejected takeoff, but at only 40 knots or so, was really just bringing throttles to idle stopping the aircraft. I called 'Remain seated, remain seated' on the PA.At that point I started to see an aircraft that went with those strobe lights and a white twin engine civilian airplane lifted off our runway. Somehow this aircraft had gotten onto or been cleared onto RWY XX for an intersection takeoff. There had been Spanish being spoken on the frequency but I did not connect that discussion with an aircraft on our runway. The same frequency is used for clearance, pushback, ground, and tower control.As we stopped...perhaps 500-1000 ft. down the runway, tower then told us we were cleared for Takeoff again. We replied negative that we would need to taxi clear or do a 180 turn and go to the approach end. Tower then told the aircraft on final to go around while we taxied. The CA called for the Rejected takeoff checklist, which we ran. We used the card first then QRH back cover. The CA also used the PA to briefly explain what had just happened. We quickly discussed our options, and decided that we could do a 180, and rerun the before takeoff checklist. Subsequent lineup, and takeoff were uneventful.
Synopsis: B737 First Officer reported rejecting takeoff due to ground conflict with departing aircraft.

Narrative: Aircraft X in ZZZ with pilot discrepancy 'F/CTL FLAPS FAULT. ECAM OCCURRED ON APPROACH WHEN MOVING FLAP LEVER FROM 1 TO 2. AFTER RECYCLING FLAP LEVER PER ECAM, FLAPS OPERATED NORMALLY.' Post flight report indicated flap jam in flight phase 6 cruise. 4th shift started troubleshooting per TSM and I was assigned to continue. TSM stated both flap actuators were required to be changed in the event of a jam with no faults due to known icing problem. Concurred with Maintenance Control that this was desired and safest step to continue. Gave all information to my crew chief, and supervisor and that the plane needs to be taken out of service until the parts are removed and replaced. Supervisor outlined that his boss argued that it's not the problem and proceeded to find any way to keep aircraft green. Both myself and work partner were pressured for well over the night to not ground Aircraft X and call it good. We raised the fact the TSM explicitly states with no faults both actuators must be changed. Due to ongoing peer pressure I reluctantly agreed to sign Aircraft X airworthy on the technicality that although the aircraft is reporting a flap jam, the phase of flight it occurred was in cruise and probably an indication error. However, prior to Date on Date-1 the exact fault and exact write up was entered. Corrective action from ZZZ2 base was a reset of LH #1 torque limiter. The TSM for this faults states that when resetting a flap torque limiter, the TSM refers to lubricate drive system, do a detail inspection and replace rotary actuator which have a tripped torque limiter. This was not done in ZZZ2 when an indicator was tripped, reset, and signed off. See [Logbook Entry]. I advised Maintenance Control and supervision of this oversight and advocated for replacing flap actuators.Event occurred because management doesn't take un airworthy as acceptable.Keep management where it belongs. Managing their supervisors and leave the technical aspect to the mechanics with the proper steps and actions from the manuals.
Narrative_1: Plane arrived in ZZZ with Flight CTL flap slat fault, was written up previous day for same thing. Contract maintenance with Maintenance Control guidance troubleshot fault - no faults where found, we ran engines and cycled the flaps per Maintenance Control request, no faults occurred. Approaching ZZZ1 at 2,000 ft. at flaps 2 selected we had a ECAM FLT CTL FLAPS FAULT message. Did go around and followed vectors to 3,000 ft., advised ATC and followed QRH, We did all steps but were both misinterpreted the checklist. Should have put lever to flaps 3, instead of flaps full and calculated the wrong approach speed as we now believe we misinterpreted the max speed chart for approach speed. 190 kts. instead of 165 kts. Report said we were 185 kts. I believe. On the approach I knew something was not right, thought about going around but was worried about the fuel time. During approach we had full slats no flaps. We requested longer runway (12,000 ft.), Landing was normal I let plane slow to 100 kts. before applying breaks. Never heated up beyond 150 [degrees] more or less. After firefighters looked over the airplane we proceeded to gate. Should have referred to SOP in performance for added info but thought we were right and worried about fuel. I have done this procedure in training, I ran the checklist and made the mistake that I was warned about. I believe frustration with a reassignment, irritated with a broken airplane (multiple problems) that was delivered to us and worried about fuel during checklist all added to my distraction and lead me to misinterpreting the checklist.Slow down slow read checklist slower, have more fuel to run all the way through.
Synopsis: Multiple repeat flap failures caused a no flap landing and subsequent errors during maintenance trouble shooting and repair of the affected system.

Narrative: Ops normal from pushback to takeoff roll. I was flying pilot, [the] Captain non-flying pilot. Power was set and autothrottles and FMAs all had normal indications. At approximately 60 knots there was a loud bang and the jet swerved to the right. I steered the jet back to centerline with rudder and the Captain initiated the abort. We stopped quickly on the runway and told ATC we'd aborted and instructed the passengers to remain seated. After quickly assessing the risk, and talking with the Lead Flight Attendant, Captain determined it was safe to taxi clear of Runway XX and we stopped on the parallel taxiway. We requested assistance from [the] Fire Department to look at the landing gear to ensure we hadn't blown a tire or had smoke/fire coming off the brakes. After getting the all-clear, we coordinated with Operations/Tech Ops to return to Gate X. We closely monitored brake temp indications during the taxi back and saw that they were all decreasing in normal fashion as expected. We were met by many company personnel at the gate and Maintenance was able to quickly determine we had an Engine Number 2 compressor stall during takeoff roll. Passengers deplaned in normal fashion through Door 1L, and the flight crew was then escorted up to ZZZ Flight Ops to discuss our readiness and ability to continue flying the trip. Captain and I then proceeded to fly as scheduled.
Narrative_1: During takeoff roll, heard a loud bang and aircraft swerved to the right. Executed rejected takeoff procedure. Exited runway. Personnel inspected aircraft externally. No visible damage and no fires were detected. Returned to gate. Maintenance data showed engine stall on Number 2 Engine. My compliments to the First Officer and Flight Attendants for their professionalism during this unexpected event.
Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported that an engine compressor stall occurred during takeoff roll, causing the aircraft to swerve and the crew to reject the takeoff.

Narrative: On climb out, after pressing the ATTEND CALL button as part of my flow, the A Flight Attendant immediately called the flight deck and complained of a loud squeal coming from the main door (L1) and that they could 'see daylight' coming from the door seal. I could hear the squeal in the background on the interphone. I looked on the overhead panel and verified that there was NO door light illuminated, I then went to verify pressurization and noticed that the cabin altitude was approaching 9,500 ft. I immediately instructed the First Officer to level off and then called ATC and reported a 'pressurization issue' and requested 10,000 ft.. We did not get a CABIN ALTITUDE WARNING at any point. I then requested to return to ZZZ and they gave us a further descent to 5,000 ft. and direct to the field. I made a PA and let the Passengers know that we were returning to ZZZ because of a pressurization issue and that we would be on the ground in ten minutes. I never requested priority handling because I didn't feel like it was necessary because we had already received an immediate descent clearance, but ATC declared one for us and had the trucks standing by on arrival. We had just enough time to run all of the checklists and get our landing data. The arrival and landing was uneventful. I called the Flight Attendants and asked how everyone was. The A and B Flight Attendants said they felt a 'little dizzy' but they said all Passengers seemed fine and there didn't seem to be any issues. Before opening the main door on arrival I inspected the seal and on the aft part of the door from top to bottom I could indeed see daylight and could run my hand in between the seal and door frame from top to bottom.
Narrative_1: Loss of pressurization in the climb, due to forward entry door not sealed properly due to malfunction. Climbing through 10,000 ft. and beginning the Climb Checklist, the Flight Crew received a chime from the Cabin Crew that the forward entry door was squealing loud and air rushing through the front area enough causing the Flight Attendant's hair to be circulating with the flow of air. No indication of the event on the flight deck. Cabin pressurization reached 9,500 ft. The aircraft reached a peak altitude just over 12,000 ft. before descent. Returned to ZZZ uneventful. ATC themselves gave us priority handling for our return to ZZZ. Upon landing and at the gate, all Passengers were removed and no indications of any medical distress.
Synopsis: Flight Crew reported a diversion caused by an L1 door leak that prevented the cabin from pressurizing.

Narrative: I wish to report a near mid-air collision. We were operating Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZ1, on a 737-900ER. The FO (First Officer) was the PF (Pilot Flying). I was the PM (Pilot Monitoring). Our IFR clearance was [SID]. Upon takeoff clearance from Runway XXR, we were given a heading of 290 with a initial climb limit of 3,000 [feet]. We received no notification of any traffic that we should be looking for upon takeoff clearance or during our initial climbout. As we were climbing out and cleaning up the aircraft, we received a TA at out 1 to 2 o'clock and high. I stopped my PM duties to search for source of the TA. As I searched, we got the altitude alert for the level off. I found the aircraft. He was not moving in relationship to our direction of travel. I told the PF to stop his climb. As I was saying that, we received the RA. The PF lowered the nose the slow the climb, as he was doing that the TCAS annunciated 'monitor vertical speed.' I glanced at the MFD to see the aircraft was only +200 feet above us. I was still on the 5 mile range and the symbol was inside the 2.5 mile tick mark at our 1 o'clock. The PF executed the RA escape maneuver to comply with the RA. I then told ZZZ Departure that I had the GA aircraft in sight, as we still hadn't been given any traffic alerts. The TCAS announced 'clear of conflict' and we resumed the climb uneventfully.
Narrative_1: Aircraft X, ZZZ-ZZZ1 I was the PF (Pilot Flying). Our clearance was [SID]...off Runway XXR heading of 290 with a initial climb limit of 3,000 [feet]. We received a TA at about 2,200 [feet]. There was an aircraft approximately 2,500 feet. No notification from ATC about the traffic. TCAS told us monitor our vertical speed which I did. I performed an RA escape maneuver and TCAS said clear of conflict. We notified approach about the traffic and TCAS RA. It seemed as if there was something going on at ZZZ or surrounding airport with an emergency at the time...rest of the trip was without incident.
Synopsis: B737-900 flight crew reported taking evasive action after receiving a TA and RA.

Narrative: For the ILS Runway 04R at ZZZ, performance numbers were run for a Flaps 30 landing with a good stopping margin at Autobrakes 3. ATIS winds were calling approximately 070/13 - no gusts. Upon switching to Tower at ZZZZZ on the localizer course and tracking the glideslope, Tower cleared us to land with winds now gusting to 20. As PF (Pilot Flying), I elected to add 4 knots to the Vtarget and as an added Safety measure at ZZZ, I selected Autobrakes MAX to compensate for a slightly increased approach speed. The PM (Pilot Monitoring) attempted to quickly re-run the performance data, but the gusts were not yet accounted for in the METAR. Rather than going heads down any longer inside 1,000 feet AGL, we agreed a 4-5 knot addition to VTarget and using Autobrakes MAX would be more than sufficient to account for the gust factor.At approximately 500 feet AGL, we received a GPWS Too Low Flaps Alert. The PM immediately called for the go-around and it was initiated. A quick scan of the flap handle and I realized that I had neglected to call for Flaps 30 from a Flaps 15 setting, and the Before Landing Checklist was not run. We were quickly vectored around for another uneventful ILS. The minor distraction of adding a gust factor and changing the Autobrakes setting sent me out of a normal approach configuration sequence and we ended up both missing the final flap setting and subsequent checklist.With the normal ZZZ procedure of not contacting (and often not switching to) Tower until reaching the fix at about a 5-mile final, it's possible for us to miss out on cues to changing weather on the ground. We were number 3 or 4 in a sequence of landings on 04R. Had we switched to Tower five or more miles sooner, we may have caught the gusting winds earlier and had more time to type in the adjusted winds and send away for the performance numbers prior to 1,000 feet AGL. This was another series of events combined with mild fatigue that led to poor task prioritization on our parts.
Narrative_1: The short version is that we got 'Too Low, Flaps' at 500 feet because we were at Flaps 15. We went around. Planned winds were 070/7. Tower winds were 070/12G20. I re-ran the performance landing numbers at 1,500 feet, but did not override the METAR and got back the numbers for 070/7. The PF (Pilot Flying) chose to add 5 knots to VTarget and we agreed to go from Medium to Max braking and continue.There is no guidance I am aware of as to when we would be required to re-run our landing numbers. I should not have tried to re-run the landing numbers at that point. That would have eliminated the distraction that led to not selecting our planned final flaps or running the Before Landing Checklist.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported executing a go-around due to improper flap setting on short final.

Narrative: During climbout from ZZZ, above approximately 2,000 feet AFL, an amber GPS-L enunciated. I continued to hand fly the jet as we climbed into IMC conditions in the pre-dawn darkness. The GPS-L caution distracted me from calling 'flaps-up' at the appropriate speed. The Captain called my attention to this as we approached 240 knots IAS. I called for flaps up and the captain retracted them normally. I engaged the autopilot after flap retraction. At no time did we exceed the 250 knot flap placard limit. Maximum speed I remember seeing was 244 knots IAS with flaps not up. The rest of the flight to ZZZ1 was uneventful. I believe my recency of experience was a factor; this being my first unsupervised flight since re-qualification. Also, night, IMC in low marine layer clouds while hand flying the initial portion of the RNAV departure. The GPS-L caution was a nuisance warning that served as the distraction. I was focused on hand flying smoothly and lost situational awareness of aircraft configuration.Earlier use of automation may have helped with my situational awareness during the nuisance GPS distraction. My habit is to hand fly the aircraft until clean.
Synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported a GPS-L annunciation on departure which distracted flight crew from calling flaps up at the appropriate speed.

Narrative: In cruise received notification from Dispatch that due to dry ice loaded with live animal in Forward Cargo divert recommended. Almost immediately after digesting message from Dispatch received call from a Flight Attendant indicating medical [situation]. Diverted to ZZZ2 without incident. Required overweight landing, followed QRH and landed without incident. Made required logbook entries and notifications. Maintenance accomplished requisite checks and entries proceeded to ZZZ1 without incident.The cause of the Hazmat violation [Cargo Illegal Load] was that flight crew received ACARS message to anticipate NOTOC (Notification to Captain) but did not receive NOTOC until departure time through window. Reviewed NOTOC indicating dry ice but did not trigger my mind for live animal loading in same compartment. Same during review of closeout. Captain suggest a normal procedure of receipt of NOTOC with normal inquiry of live animals boarded. Live animal notice of some kind to trigger mind about carriage restrictions.
Narrative_1: While enroute to ZZZ1 we received a message from Dispatch that we had dry ice loaded in the forward compartment bin with a live animal and recommended a divert to ZZZ3. The Captain and I discussed that we would be extremely overweight for ZZZ3 that was right under us so we were discussing ZZZ2 as a diversion airport. As we were discussing, we received a call from the #1 Flight Attendant that a passenger was having a medical [situation]. We diverted to ZZZ2, elected to land overweight, followed QRH, and landed without incident. Captain made the required logbook entries and notifications. Maintenance eventually accomplished the required inspections, dry ice was taken off airplane, and we then proceeded to ZZZ1 without incident. The cause was that we received a message to anticipate a NOTOC (Notification to Captain), but we did not receive the NOTOC until departure time through the Captain's window. Captain reviewed NOTOC and said we were good so I overlooked the fact that we had a live animal in the same bin. When I reviewed the load close out, I saw there was a live animal, but I did not know the restricted articles were dry ice so it did not trigger me that something was amiss. Flight crew suggests Crew Chief stating there is restricted articles, what it is, and if there are live animals. A more thorough review of the NOTOC on my part as First Officer.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported an uneventful Hazmat diversion which happened to coincide with a passenger medical event.

Narrative: At approximately 100 kts, I noticed and called out a IAS Disagree warning indication on my PFD. I immediately looked at the First Officer and the STBY Airspeed indicators to compare speeds and saw the same warning on his. The difference in speed between both was about 5-7 knots (see FM, Airspeed Disagree Alert (amber) Indicates the Captain's and First Officer's airspeed indications disagree by more than 5 knots for 5 continuous seconds), and took about 5 to 10 seconds before the warning went away. My decision was to continue the takeoff since the IAS discrepancy was small and we were in the High-Speed regime. Following the disappearance of the warning indication, I closely monitored the speed differences which was reduced to 1-1.5 knots. Throughout the rest of the flight. An ELB write-up was made and local maintenance contacted to give a full description of the event after landing.Once we were at a safe climbing altitude, we discussed the situation further. I mentioned that if the difference in IAS had been larger I would have opted to reject. Interestingly; the First Officer expressed relief that we did not reject, and that we could have taken off even with the stick shaker going off, similarly as we experienced in a recent MAX training session (during climb), and that the company does not want us to reject other than for the exceptions stated in the FM. His honest answer left me to ponder and wonder if I made the right decision, and to take a closer look at our Normal and Non-Normal procedures, guidance, and its implications, and if any further clarification is needed or due. With that said, I would like to review on how would they apply in the following scenarios. For ease of page reference, I utilized FM dated XX-XX-XXX, however the manual date at the time of the event was [on] YY-YYY-YYYY. The information appears to be identical with the exception of a slight page numbering difference. As a point of reference to determine a reliable airspeed indicator, the checklist states 'An airspeed indication that differs by more than 20 kts or 0.03 Mach from the airspeed shown in the table should be considered unreliable.' Also, there is NO guidance for pitch attitude on takeoff for this situation other than an initial pitch to 15 degrees followed by the immediate actions, which would call for a pitch and thrust reduction just off the ground following gear retraction. The immediate above action items seems contradictory to safe and sound practice of flying away from the ground and executing an emergency procedure at a safe altitude. Should safer guidance be included?It seems very clear, as always, that excellent flying skills and judicious Captain's Emergency Authority will be needed.
Synopsis: B737 NG Captain reported an airspeed split on takeoff roll and elected to continue. Post flight and reviewing the incident, Captain described misgivings over published policy.

Narrative: Captain was pilot monitoring. FO (First Officer) was pilot flying. Passing through 4,000 feet MSL on climbout from ZZZ we noticed a fuel imbalance developing - right wing main tank fuel indication already 400 pounds lower than left wing. Right wing main tank fuel appeared to be feeding at approximately twice the rate of the left and it appeared that the center tank fuel was not feeding at all. Engine fuel flow readings appeared normal and equal. By 10,000 feet MSL the imbalance had increased to the point that the IMBAL alert was activated. We coordinated with ATC to level off at 12,000 feet MSL in order to reduce fuel flow and begin taking appropriate action. Upon leveling at 12,000 feet MSL we observed the right fuel tank quantity feed rate appear to normalize and then observed a 50 pound increase in right main tank fuel quantity. Fuel imbalance at that point was 1,100 pounds. We initiated the IMBAL checklist in the QRH. Observing what then appeared to be normal tank quantity indications for a crossfeed operation, we coordinated with ATC to continue our climb and proceed on course to the destination knowing we would also coordinate with Dispatch and maintenance promptly to determine if proceeding to ZZZ1 was advisable. As soon as we established climb fuel flow settings and pitch attitude, the right main tank quantity began to decrease again at what appeared to be the same abnormal rate observed during the initial climb. We then requested priority handling initiated the return to ZZZ (nearest airport) and started the APU as a precaution. I advised Dispatch, the cabin crew, and the passengers of the situation using SOP. As soon as we stopped the climb to initiate the return to ZZZ the right main fuel tank indication again stopped decreasing at an abnormal rate. We concluded the IMBAL checklist and for the remainder of the flight we observed no further indications of abnormal rate of decrease in right main wing tank fuel. During the descent, I spoke with the flight attendants and they confirmed that there were no visible indications of fuel leaks on either wing or engine. We landed uneventfully at ZZZ with a total imbalance of 1,220 pounds with 8,370 pounds in the left wing, 7,150 pounds in the right wing and 13,470 pounds in the center tank - 29,000 points total. The aircraft was below max landing weight at touchdown. ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) personnel were standing by as requested. After landing and before further taxi, ARFF personnel inspected the aircraft closely and reported no leaks, no visible damage, and no abnormalities. We shut down the number 2 engine as an additional precaution and requested that the ARFF vehicles follow us to our gate. Maintenance personnel were debriefed in person at the gate upon arrival.Captain suspects suspect faulty fuel crossfeed valve.Reporter recommends company consider revisiting the IMBAL checklist in light of this particular malfunction.
Synopsis: B73-800 Captain reported an uneventful air return due to an airborne fuel system malfunction during initial climb.

Narrative: All crews should be informed and knowledgeable about emergency procedures in order to be prepared for such unexpected events in flight.After an uneventful preflight preparation and exterior inspection we departed ZZZ, myself as Pilot Flying and the Captain as Pilot Monitoring. We climbed to planned cruise altitude without issue. Shortly after reaching cruise and just south of ZZZ1, an ECAM message and associated chime presented on the lower ECAM screen indicating 'ENG 1 SYSTEM FAULT'. We worked through the indicated actions and referenced the COM procedures. As the engine was reduced to idle thrust only, we began a descent and began diversion planning as it became clear that we could not continue to ZZZ2 with this issue at the lower altitude required on a single engine at ZZZ3. Initially ZZZ was selected, but while I was flying and communicating with ATC the Captain in consultation with the dispatcher elected to divert instead to ZZZ4. With plenty of time to prepare we did all necessary tasks for the diversion and proceeded to an uneventful landing on ZZZ's longest runway, XXR, with fire/rescue services on standby. After landing with no issues we taxied to the assigned gate and shut down the aircraft without issue.
Synopsis: A320 First Officer reported an in-flight engine problem required a diversion and single-engine approach and landing.

Narrative: On a descent into DEN, we were cleared to descend via the CLASH 3 Arrival. I confirmed that the final altitude was 9,000 ft. and selected it in the altitude window. About 10 miles from EVRLY, we experienced wake turbulence for about five seconds, and then experienced it again. I selected Vertical Speed and leveled off the descent to get above the wake turbulence. After we were clear of the wake turbulence, I selected a 2,000 FPM descent to get back on my vertical path. At that time, we were told to switch to Denver Approach. Upon checking in with Denver Approach they changed our runway to 35L. At this point I was concerned about changing the approach in the FMC. I forgot to re-engage the VNAV. Because I forgot to re-engage the VNAV, the aircraft did not slow down to 250 kts for EVRLY. The aircraft also continued a descent below 12,000 feet., which was the lowest altitude at TWNSN. The aircraft continue to descend until I notice the deviation. By this time I was leveling at 10,000 feet. and was below the 11,000 feet. altitude required for PNBAL. ATC advised me to slow the 210 knots, and gave me a vector for the final approach to Runway 35L. They also gave me a descent to 9,000 feet. The rest of the arrival went as planned.
Synopsis: B737 Captain reported distractions from a wake turbulence encounter on arrival into DEN contributed to altitude and speed deviations.

Narrative: At 800 feet AGL, clicked autopilot off for a visual landing. At 500 ft., FO called 'Stable, cleared to land Runway XX Center.' I replied 'Landing.' Between 500 and 400 feet AGL tried to make small lateral correction with aileron but aileron movement was limited. Used a touch of rudder for correction. Clicked autopilot button again and crossed checked then confirmed that 'Flight Director' was displayed in PFD. Landed uneventfully but elevator movement was very heavy in flare. After landing at taxi speed, I tried to move the yoke left and right and there was very limited movement. The First Officer tried as well with the same result. We checked the Flight Control and Hydraulic Displays and both were normal.I considered a go-around but quickly [determined] a go around would be extremely difficult with big power changes and limited flight control capability. The flight path was set up to touch down in the landing zone on speed so I elected to land.Unsure what caused the flight controls to be limited. After landing, I debriefed Maintenance in the cockpit and put a detailed write up in the logbook.
Synopsis: B777-200 Captain reported aileron flight control stiff during landing and limited movement after landing.

Narrative: While descending on the CLASH Arrival just prior to EVRLY we encountered a wake turbulence event 2x in short succession with roll deviation. Autopilot disconnected, was immediately reconnected by the Captain (PF). He disconnected VNAV and initiated Vertical Speed mode to reset our descent path to be slightly above the previous aircraft path, to prevent a third event. About this time, ATC offered us a runway change from 35R to 35L, additionally they requested us to slow to 210 kts. The Captain went to reprogram the FMS for Runway 35L, I was confirming the Captain inputs at this time. The aircraft was still in Vert Speed rather than VNAV, neither of us noticed this and we descended below the STAR required altitude and did not slow to 210 kts. as directed. A query from ATC as to our speed brought us back to reviewing our flight path, at which point we leveled off and reduced speed. ATC made no further comments as to our flight path deviation and at that point broke us off from the STAR with a vector to intercept the LOC. No loss of ATC separation was reported to us.
Synopsis: B737 First Officer reported speed and altitude deviations on arrival into DEN, citing distraction from a wake turbulence encounter as contributing.

Narrative: On approach to ZZZ gear was selected down but normal gear indications did not appear and there were no associated noises such as gear extending into slipstream, etc. PF (Pilot Flying) executed a missed approach and while being vectored we tried to lower the gear normally with the same indications and we got the L/G Gear Not Down locked ECAM. Accomplishing ECAM led us to the L/G Gravity Extension QRH and after accomplishing checklist the gear safely extended. We (advised ATC) and coordinated with Flight Attendants and Dispatch and ZZZ for subsequent runway closure and tow to the gate.
Synopsis: A320 Captain reported a landing gear malfunction.

Narrative: Aircraft X was uneventful leading up to the approach at ZZZ. We had been cleared for the approach to Runway XX and were established on the localizer and glideslope. The autopilot and autothrust had been disengaged earlier in the approach and the aircraft had been configured to Flaps 3 when Gear Down was requested. When the gear lever was selected down the three indicators on the landing gear panel indicated red UNLK (UNLOCKED), no noise from the landing gear doors opening was heard. Captain [Name] and I communicated and confirmed on the Landing Gear Systems page that the landing gear had not extended. We decided to level out at 6,000 feet MSL while we confirmed the situation and attempted to cycle the gear. We communicated to the tower we would be going around for a landing gear failure approximately 3mi prior to the runway. Tower provided vectors and a climb to 9,000 feet, we initiated a go around over the threshold per ATC instructions and cleaned up the aircraft per SOP. The autoflight was re-engaged after the go around. During this time after the failure of subsequent attempts to cycle the gear and with the lever still down, we eventually got the L/G GEAR NOT DOWNLOCKED ECAM. The ECAM was run according to SOP by Captain [Name] while I flew the aircraft and handled radio calls. We [received priority], stated our intention to return to land on Runway XYR and requested CFR (Crash Fire Rescue Equipment). Gravity extension was successful and we were vectored to the approach. Approach and landing were normal with the exception of the gear doors remaining open. We landed with 8000 lbs. of fuel. We stopped on the runway and Operations was standing by to tow the aircraft back to the gate.
Synopsis: First Officer reported a Go Around and precautionary landing after landing gear lock problems.

Narrative: I was deadheading in the cabin when I was asked by the Captain to come to the flight deck due to an [urgent situation]. By time I reached the flight deck the number two engine was already shut down. I assisted the primary crew anyway possible to lessen the workload and stress. I assisted with cabin and airport operations communication, checklist completion, and any other tasks the crew needed help with. The primary crew did a fantastic job and needed very little assistance.
Synopsis: Deadheading Pilot reported being asked to come to the Flight Deck and act as an ACM (Additional Crew Member) during an inflight event.

Narrative: Arriving at the aircraft and checking the logbook, I noticed that the last crew had written that the Takeoff Configuration light and horn activated on takeoff (speed of activation was not noted). I surmised that the crew rejected the takeoff and subsequently swapped out of the aircraft after returning to the gate and the aircraft was not flown afterwards. The corrective action was a check of the Takeoff Configuration Warning System with no faults noted. Since nothing was actually corrected, the Captain and I discussed the possibility of it activating again on our takeoff. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the Forward Cargo Bin C. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. We were relatively full on this flight and our V1/VR speeds for Flaps 1 on Runway XXR were 125/135. The engine start and taxi out were uneventful with the throttle burst yielding no takeoff warning. On the takeoff roll at approximately 130 knot (5 knot after V1) the takeoff warning horn and light activated. We elected to continue the takeoff. The initial climb was normal and we discussed that we would be writing this up in ZZZ1. The Captain called for 'flaps up' at the appropriate speed and I moved the flap lever to UP. We had a few distractions from ATC due to hold-down altitude that was cancelled. Before I moved the landing gear handle to OFF, I checked the flap indicator and noticed that the flaps were still at 1 with the LE FLAP EXT green light illuminated. After confirming that the flap handle was up, I told the Captain the issue and that we need to keep our airspeed below 250 kts. and level off to handle the problem.After notifying ATC that we would need to level off, they gave us vectors for terrain while we ran the QRH for Trailing Edge Flap Disagree. Since the QRH doesn't really address the disagreement when attempting to RETRACT the flaps and only deals with setting the flaps for landing, we turned our attention to coordinating the air return. Dispatch was advised of the return as well as Station Ops in ZZZ. Our current gross weight was a little over 130,000 pounds so we extended the gear to add drag and burn off excess fuel for landing. The F/As (Flight Attendants) and passengers were notified of the return. Since this was a flight control issue, we [received priority handling] and notified ATC that we were requesting [Runway] XYL but would need time to reduce our landing weight to 128,000 pounds. We felt this was the safe option as time was not an issue. We then ran the QRH, ran the performance calculation for the Trailing Edge Flap Disagree QRH, and then the brake cooling module. The flaps extended normally with the Alternate Flap system to 15 degrees. The only slight issue was although I read the section directing the flap lever to be moved to the final flap position (15), we were sidetracked by discussing slowing during the extension and this was not done until after the QRH was completed. This allowed us to see our Flaps 15 maneuvering speed. After the delay vectors were complete and we were below the maximum landing weight, we made an uneventful landing on [Runway] XYL. Brake cooling allowed us to take right to the gate and the ARFF (Airport Rescue and Fire Fighting) trucks followed. No other issues occurred. We swapped into another aircraft and continued the pairing.
Narrative_1: The aircraft was an originator. The previous day a takeoff had been rejected because of a spurious Takeoff Config Warning and the maintenance resolution was no faults noted. The F/O (First Officer) and I discussed possible reasons for a false warning lasting a few seconds, which refreshed our memories of the warning system and thankfully prepared us for a repeat occurrence. We pushed late due to an unrelated finding of damage in the floor of the forward cargo bin. The bin was deferred and bags transferred to the aft bin. On takeoff, approximately two seconds after the F/O's V1 call, the configuration light illuminated and the warning horn sounded. The F/O called VR, and we lifted off. The light went out and the horn stopped about the time the wheels left the ground. The F/O's performance and adhering to procedure during this event was flawless, which combined with our earlier discussion allowed the situation to be handled easily. We briefly mentioned writing the issue up again in ZZZ1. I called for Flaps Up, from their takeoff '1' setting. F/O moved the flap lever to Up, and then moments later told me the flaps didn't go up, and instructed me not to go over 250 [kts.]. We were still at about 200 knots, so no airspeed issues. I told F/O to tell ATC we needed to level off and maintain low airspeed. Initially we told ATC we would follow the SID and get back to them. ATC gave us a terrain clearance altitude. We confirmed the flaps were not up. I called for the QRH and we agreed that 'Flap Disagree' was the appropriate checklist. The checklist starts off by saying 'to prepare for landing' so we paused the checklist, agreed we were not going to ZZZ1 with flaps out, and I messaged Dispatch we were returning to ZZZ, told ATC, and received clearance to return to ZZZ. I notified the F/A (Flight Attendants) and told the passengers we were returning to ZZZ. We ran the QRH for Flaps Disagree, the procedure went mostly uneventfully. We were at 130,000 pounds, so we took delaying vectors to burn fuel to 128,000 [lbs.]. We checked the brake cooling for Autobrake 3, no issues. We did [receive priority handling]. We landed Flaps 15 and taxied to the gate. Positive takeaways. The CQT training from (year)?, (year)? that emphasized flap malfunctions prepared us well to handle the stuck flaps. Negative takeaways. The QRH for Flap Disagree was obviously written with a failure occurring during approach in mind. For our situation of failure on takeoff, the procedure kept us with the flap handle up until we had returned to ZZZ and were preparing to land, which meant we had flaps out, but no maneuvering speed. We know that Flaps 1 speed is 180 knots approximately, but it would have been one more item in our favor if we had moved the flap handle to match the flaps to give us the normal sight picture on the displays. While we were extending the flaps with the alternate switch, between watching the flap gauge and calls from ATC, we momentarily missed the instruction in the QRH to move the flap handle with the flap movement. We followed proper flap speeds as flaps were extending, but that that was because of our experience, not the display. The QRH should have the instruction to move flap handle with flaps before the actual instruction to move the flaps so that crews can discuss the handle in advance. We ran the brake cooling for Autobrake 3, and then tried to run again for Autobrake 2. The brake cooling module did not work the second time. We recalled a recent (Company communication piece) about Dispatch doing something to mess up performance calculation results, which could be rectified by requesting landing data again, but that did not work. Something in the performance calculations needs to be corrected so that brake cooling can be run more than once. Brake cooling was not an issue, even with Autobrake 3, so this was a small nuisance. Based on passenger comments, F/As did a great job. F/O's performance was excellent, our teamwork together allowed the situation to be handled easily.
Synopsis: Flight Crew reported a repeat failure of the Take Off Warning System and a failure of trailing edge flaps to retract caused an Air Tun Back and a precautionary emergency landing.

Narrative: We were at FL320 on the HLYWD arrival into LAX, and we had been given a vector off course for spacing. Upon rejoining the arrival we were given slower speeds until we actually saw an aircraft 5 nm in front of us. We were then assigned a speed of 250 kts indicated, then descend to FL240, followed by a clearance to descend via the arrival. I was concerned as we started our descent as we were clearly descending at a higher rate than the aircraft ahead of us and would be flying through their flight path at a close proximity plus winds at altitude were approximately 110kts. Suddenly our airplane began a roll to the right, I would estimate 20-25 degrees of bank, then it began rolling to the left at least 30 degrees of bank if not more and the autopilot disconnected itself. We were having an upset due to wake from the aircraft ahead of us so the Captain quickly recovered and I advised ATC what was happening and that we needed something different. They approved an offset to our course, and then advised the aircraft ahead was a B777. 5nm is inadequate spacing between a heavy aircraft and others. Fortunately we recovered well and landed safely. 99 percent of the time our folks in ATC do an absolutely outstanding job, and we couldn't do this without them! This event is unusual, but highlights an opportunity we can improve.I would also like to see better communication from ATC and a better understanding of the safety ramifications of wake turbulence - I frequently get the impression that they don't understand this risk adequately. I want to know if I'm in trail of a heavy aircraft! Sooner than later! It matters, it changes my expectations and I'm not consistently getting this information. I recommend more spacing, more and consistent communication about heavy aircraft ahead, and if I need to be vectored for spacing then let's address speed at the same time so I'm not constantly changing my configuration when I need to focus on flying.
Synopsis: B737 First Officer reported encountering wake turbulence on descent into LAX in trail of a B777.

Narrative: Prior to departure Maintenance was called due to FOs (First Officer's) MAP failure on navigation display. Maintenance did a reset and signed off logbook as reset ok for service. FOs MAP was restored. Approximately 2 hours into flight and approximately 30 mins from ZZZZ1 enroute to ZZZZ, FOs MAP failed, followed by Captain's CWS (control wheel steering) fail, autothrottle failure, and SINGLE FMC operation message. Very shortly later, approximately 10 seconds, LNAV/ VNAV failed, both FMCs failed. Opposite autopilot selected, autopilot B. Captain's CWS was restored and one FMC was restored allowing for the engagement of LNAV/VNAV, and autothrottle was restored. FOs MAP still indicated a failure. Within approximately 60 seconds we had another dual FMC failure, followed by another LNAV/ VNAV failure, autothrottle failure, Captain's CWS failure. At this time with over two hours left to ZZZZ and navigating by raw data we decided it was the best course of action to divert to ZZZZ1 where the weather was favorable for landing with these navigational failures. We notified ZZZZ1 Center of our issues and intent to land in ZZZZ1. Around this time the Captain's FMC was restored automatically and we were once again able to navigate with LNAV/VNAV and the autothrottle and Captain's CWS was restored and autopilot was operational. As we neared ZZZZ1 we informed ATC of the need to hold to burn off fuel due to being overweight for landing which took approximately 10 minutes. The remainder of the flight was uneventful, we landed on Runway X and commenced the ILS approach in VFR conditions. The FOs MAP warning flag remained in view for the rest of the flight. My FO, Fas (Flight Attendants) did outstanding jobs. Great communication. ZZZZ1 ATC also very professional and helpful. In the 21 years I've been on the 737 both as an CA (Captain) and FO I've never experienced a dual FMC failure. I've experienced several single FMC failures, but not dual failures leading to several other navigation failures.
Synopsis: Captain reported a diversion to a precautionary landing following the loss of both Flight Management Computers which caused the loss of Cockpit Display Units and most navigation systems.

Narrative: Captain (CA)=Pilot Monitoring (PM), First Officer (FO)=Pilot Flying (PF). Discovered pressurization outflow valve in the full open position during the after takeoff checklist (no Auto Fail lights, both Packs, ISO valve and bleeds all in proper position). Discussed with the FO and advised ATC we needed to level off at 10,000 ft to investigate an issue and asked for straight ahead to avoid terrain (initially assigned 15,000 ft on the SID). FO was PF and had them take the radio. Pulled the QRH and referenced AUTO Fail or Unscheduled Pressurization Change 2.2. At this point we discussed and surmised we did NOT have an AUTO Fail issue nor and unscheduled pressurization change as the Cabin appeared to be modestly, although suspiciously pressurizing, as we were building some differential and the cabin altitude was relatively low. Troubleshooting forbids switch manipulation unless inclusive of a QRH or other written procedure hence we chose not to manipulate cabin pressurization controller from AUTO to ATLN. Additionally, we recalled a bulletin from Standards Department dated 7/xx/2020 titled 'Cabin Pressure Controller Blinking/Blanking issue'. This bulletin states that on our 900ER fleet from (tails)(we were in tail) the digital controller can blank and or blink or become so dim its unreadable. Additionally, the bulletin states the controller should right itself shortly...We did not have any blinking/blanking or dimness. Our outflow indicator was bright and solid indicating full open and remained so for the duration of our flight. In an attempt to determine if the cabin would hold we elected to continue our climb to 12,000 ft at which point we got a significant bump felt by the entire crew.... At this point I attempted to contact Dispatch via ACARS to establish two way radio communications. We had plodded along south at a low altitude for a good duration in an attempt to solve the issue. I became concerned with our flight plan fuel. We were dispatched with no reserve for ZZZ1 (weather severe clear at arrival time). Was there enough to complete the mission or might we find ourselves having to divert for fuel 'if' we felt the cabin psi was solid enabling us to continue? We we're now down near (mountain) at 12,000 ft IMC picking up a fair amount of ice as weather was now an issue. After multiple attempts to get a hold of Dispatch to no avail, Flight Attendants complaining about ears, a QRH procedure that didn't quite fit, no ability to troubleshoot, a bulletin that didn't match enough to convince me and a possible fuel stop with an open maintenance issue stranding passengers....in consultation w/ my FO I made the command decision to return to ZZZ. In my mind, this was the safest option and provided our passengers an opportunity to reset. Additionally, it brought the aircraft back to a maintenance base for investigation and repair. We informed Dispatch via ACARS and setup to return and received an amended release via ACARS. We did not declare an emergency as it did not appear warranted/necessary. We ran performance including our LTP (landing threshold point), discussed our TPC and landed significantly under max landing weight as we had a light load. During block in as L1 was opened we felt another pressure bump despite the outflow valve remaining in the full open position. I greeted all deplaning passengers and answered questions, debriefed full crew and discussed scenario and concerns. Flight Attendants met with supervisor and were replaced. No crew members/ nor passengers asked for medical attention. Swapped aircraft, checked duty time and pressed on.Lesson learned:I should have used SATCOM to raise Dispatch in lieu of ACARS. We traveled a fair ways south and company frequency became weak. We switched to XXX.X and sent a message but never could get radio contact. We became distracted by the accumulation of ice buildup at that point in the journey. Bulletin concern: If it is related to the digital controller bulletin why would the company continue to allow problematic controllers be installed? NOTE: The original design Pressurization Control Panel may be installed in any 9ER aircraft from (tail) and subsequent as a repair for a Pressurization Control Panel issue. Therefore, even though (tail) and subs were delivered with the upgraded panel, this issue may occur on these aircraft if the upgraded panel has been replaced with an original panel.
Synopsis: Captain reported aircraft failed to pressurize correctly on takeoff and after trouble shooting, elected to do an Air Turn Back.

Narrative: I was pilot monitoring on this flight. ATC was giving us vectors for a visual approach to RWY XX at ZZZ. We were at 2,000 feet on a right base between waypoints ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 (1,500 feet MSL) when we told Approach we had the airport in sight. We were cleared for the visual and told to contact Tower. I said 'glide slope alive' and the First Officer asked for gear down flaps 15. I looked down to select the Tower frequency (which I didn't have preselected) and told them we were on the visual for RWY XX. We were cleared to land. When I saw we were capturing the localizer I noticed that the glide slope was now full scale deflection (low). The First Officer had selected a lower altitude (1,100 feet) on the MCP without telling me and so we were below the final approach fix altitude of 1,500 feet at ZZZZZ1. I called for a go around and we were vectored back around for a successful landing. The cause was a long flight across the country with last minute vectors to final for a visual approach led to the First Officer thinking we were high nearing the FAF and incorrectly setting an altitude lower than glideslope intercept altitude without verbally advising the Captain.
Synopsis: B-737-800 Captain reported an uneventful 'go around' due to a CFIT event during final approach.

Narrative: I was Pilot Flying. Just after liftoff, the nose trim ran high speed nose up on its own. I waited a quick moment and told the Captain that I was not doing that trim command, and then pushed forward on the yoke to stop the runaway. After retracting the flaps, I relaxed forward pressure and the trim continued nose up runaway at slow speed. I pressed the electric time nose down on the yoke, and the up trim stopped its uncommanded nose up runaway. Then we ran the Stabilizer Runaway Checklist and returned back to ZZZ uneventfully.
Narrative_1: During takeoff from ZZZ, at approximately 300 ft. AGL, the aircraft trim began running continuously, high-speed, in the 'Nose-Up' direction. The F/O (First Officer) stopped the trim by pushing forward on the yoke. This action stopped the trim movement. At 1,200 ft. AGL, after retracting the flaps, the trim began running again, continuously 'Nose-Up' in the slow-speed mode. This time the F/O used the Electrical Trim switch in the opposite direction and this action stopped the movement. We ran the Runaway Stabilizer Checklist and returned to ZZZ for an uneventful approach and landing.
Synopsis: Pilot reported a runaway stabilizer trim system and elected to air turn back and make a precautionary emergency landing.

Narrative: Moderate turbulence below 14,000 feet. Heavy winds as well. 290/19 G29 on the ground. Cleared Visual Approach 34L. Approach was normal, but Captain very busy dealing with speed fluctuations and turbulence. I was double checking the winds with Tower. Watching terrain as well. Adjusted REF speeds for gusts and prevailing winds. Captain called for flaps 30, I inadvertently moved flap handle to 25 and did not know it. Everything was good until short final, we got "Too Low Flaps" aural alert. We executed go-around immediately. Need to look down and see if correct flap detention is selected.
Narrative_1: On flight to RNO we received a Too Low Flaps warning from the GPWS around 500 feet AGL on an approach to Runway 34L. We had continuous moderate turbulence below 13,000 feet MSL on our approach and that was distracting. We were on a high right base leg because of the terrain. We were cleared for the visual on the right base leg. Also, on base we were gear down flaps 15, and near flaps 15 approach speed. I called for flaps 30 and the Before Landing checklist well above 1,000 feet AGL, because I wanted the extra drag. I did not notice the flaps were at position 25 during the Before Landing checklist. Our REF speed was plus 9 and then increased to plus 15 with the new Tower winds. At about 500 feet AGL we received the Too Low Flaps warning and I did a go-round. We were vectored for another approach to Runway 34L and did a normal landing.I felt task loaded on the approach. I was concerned about the turbulence, terrain, and changing surface winds. I let these additive condition distract me while doing the Before Landing Check List. I should have bought myself more time by asking for a longer down wind on the approach.
Synopsis: B-737 flight crew reported executing a go-around upon receipt of a configuration GPWS warning.

Narrative: Visual to 27 at SAN using RNAV Z. Ceiling was BKN015. Crew briefed visual procedures at altitude but was informed that ATIS had changed late in the descent, crew adjusted minimums to account for the updated ceiling. Earlier I had queried the Captain if he preferred flaps 40 for SAN and he said he wanted flaps 30. Vref was 141 knots, wind component added 6 knots for a VTARGET of 147 knots. Captain configured early and we were stable at 1,000 feet AGL with a slightly high VVI (Vertical Velocity Indicator) due to SAN Runway 27 3.5 degree approach and the high weight and subsequent high approach speed. We were visual at that point, I think we broke out at 1,000-1,200 feet. Every time I crosschecked the speed and VVI, the Captain was stable, with the knowledge that the 3.5 degree approach and speed (as mentioned in the Safety Alert) would result in VVI rates over 1,000 feet. I was crosschecking radar altitudes and glideslope guidance more than I usually do, but this is my personal habit for SAN. As I did the normal 'in and out' visual crosscheck, nothing seemed amiss. Directly over or slightly after the parking deck on short final, the Captain slightly adjusted his visual aim point as is common technique at SAN. My eyes were outside at this point. We both heard a 'sink rate...'. I don't know what the second phrase was, as the Captain acknowledged the first sink rate forcefully and almost instantly. I quickly looked inside and I think I saw 'pull up' on the bottom of the PFD for what seemed like an instant. I can't be certain, however, and it can't be understated how fast it went away if indeed it was there. I looked back up and we were two red and two white on the PAPI, slightly fast, and Captain was in what looked like a good position to land. We made a safe landing and applied moderate braking and exited the runway. In the postflight, the Captain and I disagreed about what the second term was at the aural system annunciated. He thinks he heard 'sink rate, sink rate.' I actually don't know what the second term the aural system annunciated was, as I didn't hear it clearly due to the Captain's acknowledgment of it. I do think I saw a very fleeting 'pull up' on the PFD, but I can't be perfectly certain, and Captain is adamant that we didn't get the GPWS warning, only the sink rate caution. I want to be clear that I understand the limitation with regard to the warning annunciator. In hindsight, I can see now that a go-around could have been a prudent decision even though the aircraft appeared to be a safe and normal position for short final at SAN. I want to highlight this issue for a few reasons. It bears repeating that phase of flight, temporal distortion, and flight deck confusion can all conspire to create a situation where two trained and alert crew members can see different things. The other thing I want to highlight is how heavy -800's, going into SAN, can potentially be affected by a flaps 30 approach. I don't know why we don't have recommended flap settings for certain situations. We've all been flying light aircraft for almost a year now and perhaps it would help to remind crews about heavy aircraft with higher approach airspeeds and subsequently higher VVIs in higher altitude environments or steeper approaches like SAN.
Narrative_1: On approach to SAN when transitioning outside, we briefly received a sink rate call. At the gate, the First Officer was unsure if it was just a sink rate call or sink rate pull up. I adjusted sink rate and landed normally.
Synopsis: B737-800 Flight Crew reported on an unstable approach receiving two cautionary messages the were missed by flight crew.

Narrative: During climb out of SMF, everything was normal with some occasional light chop. We had asked the Flight Attendants to remain seated due to crossing the Sierra Mountains. We were climbing at approximately .76 Mach. Upon leveling at FL 370, we experienced moderate bordering on severe mountain wave. Our airspeed began decreasing rapidly and the F/O (First Officer) disconnected the autopilot, applied full thrust, and began a shallow descent to regain airspeed. The airspeed decayed to about .70 - .71. It was about a 30 knot decrease. I may be a little off on the Mach numbers. We descended about 500' and the airspeed began increasing. I reported the encounter to ATC and we began climbing back to FL 370. The wave climbed us to FL 375, and at that time we requested a descent to FL 350. The Controller cleared us to descend to FL 350. We did not encounter any additional mountain wave and nothing more than a little light chop. We checked with the Flight Attendants to make sure everyone was alright, and the remainder of the flight was uneventful. I would like to add that the F/O did an excellent job of recognizing and reacting to the situation.
Narrative_1: We had just leveled off at our cruise altitude of FL 370. (Filed for FL 390 but we were too heavy at that time.) During climb we had anticipated and encounter some light turbulence. Nothing more significant was encountered. WSI (Weather Service International) and Jeppesen weather showed areas of turbulence covering about the first 45 minutes of our flight. Our clearance was on the SCTWN 3 RNAV Departure. We were level at FL 370 when suddenly our airspeed had dropped from M.76 (250 KIAS) to 220 KIAS this was approximately 10-15 above the yellow maneuvering bar on the airspeed indicator and the green vector bar was indicating that the slowing was continuing and at a significant rate. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle and pitched down to keep airspeed. I also increased thrust to max and I was able to recover airspeed about 500' low at FL 365. In my attempt to climb back to FL 370 we started climbing at a significant rate and stopped the climb at approximately FL 376. The Captain reported to ATC that we were in MVA (mountain wave activity) and that we were unable to hold altitude. I continued to hand fly until I was sure we were passed the MVA and re-engaged the autopilot. The rest of the flight was uneventful.
Synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported encountering moderate to severe mountain wave for which led to a rapid decay of their airspeed.

Narrative: Departed ZZZ without Dispatch release remark of 'HAZMAT on flight - refer to [Dangerous Goods Form]'. When I discovered the error I notified Dispatch via ACARS.
Synopsis: B737-700 Captain reported Dispatch release missing required Hazmat information.

Narrative: About one hour from landing, we started to smell a faint burning scent from the packs. It was very faint, but noticeable. It smelled like glycol or plastic burning. It remained constant until we initiated a descent from FL390-FL370. The smell became more pronounced. For lack of another checklist or procedure, we ran the smoke fire and fumes QRH. The smell was only in the cockpit and not the cabin. Since we could not determine the source. We deemed it appropriate to take the safest course of action to expedite getting the aircraft on the ground with no undue delay. We [advised ATC] and asked for CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) to meet us to check for anything out of the ordinary upon landing. We initiated a high speed descent and approach, and performed a safe landing. CFR met the aircraft and checked it over and we taxied to the gate.
Synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported a flight deck fumes event during cruise. The crew ran the appropriate QRH checklist and continued to destination.

Narrative: I was Pilot Flying. On approach to Runway XXR at ZZZ, after calling for the landing gear down and flaps 15, we noticed that we had three green and three red landing gear indications. The overhead panel showed three green indications. We were able to complete the QRH and Landing Checklist and determined that the landing gear was down and locked. We continued the approach with the intention of landing. At approximately 500 feet AGL, we received the oral warning 'TOO LOW GEAR.'I was no longer sure that the landing gear was down and locked. I called for the go-around and executed the go-around procedure. We decided to leave the landing gear down and cleaned the flaps up to 5 degrees. The Captain was working the radios and informed ATC of the go-around. ATC gave us a heading and cleared us to 2,000 feet. They asked for the reason of the go-around. The Captain informed them that we were having landing gear indication problems. The Captain then decided to request priority handling.We completed the QRH and were able to get three green indications without red indications. The Captain informed ATC we had solved the problem and could continue for another approach and landing. ATC assigned us Runway XXL. We set up the FMC, re-briefed the approach, completed all of the appropriate checklists, flew the approach, and landed uneventfully on Runway XXL. We taxied to the gate, shut down the engines and completed the Shut Down Checklist. While at the gate we had realized that due to workload, we had forgotten to inform the flight attendants of the priority handling situation.To prevent this from happening again, we need to slow down, and complete all briefings to the Flight Attendants and Passenger cabin prior to landing. Just because we were able to solve the landing gear problem and workload was heavy, does not alleviate the duty to inform the Cabin Crew.
Synopsis: B737-700 First Officer reported a landing gear indication issue during approach resulting in a go-around. The flight crew ran the QRH procedures, resolved the issues and landed safely on their second attempt.

Narrative: We were cruising at FL390 and we called the back for a break. I was the second pilot to exit the flight deck and while in the main cabin I noticed the pitch of the aircraft. I then made a brief break and called to return to the flight deck. Once the flight deck door opened and the A came out I noticed the thrust levers advancing to max power and the airspeed indicator slowly approaching the amber band. I then immediately called for a lower altitude as I took my seat and once I was in my seat I looked at my First Officer and said we need lower now. My First Officer then dialed a lower altitude on the FMC and selected descent via V/S (Vertical Speed). I then gathered all info on what we were experiencing and thought either we had an unreliable airspeed or runaway stabilizer. As I looked back at our altitude, I realized we weren't descending and our airspeed was slowly approaching amber pole. At that time I disconnected A/T (Autothrottle), A/P (Autopilot) and started a slow descent and requested my First Officer to call in our descent to ATC. ATC then notified us that we needed to stop descent at FL370 due to lower aircraft. My training kicked in and I figured if this went back we would need around 10,000 feet to recover so I then requested a vector off course. We then were given 10 degrees left and I leveled off at FL370 continued to hand fly and one by one acquired A/P, HDG, VNAV. Our Airspeed gained approximately 30kts and we were stable at FL370 on a heading. ATC asked why the need to descend and I replied we encountered mountain wave and could not hold altitude. ATC then replied that we were the first to complain of mountain wave. Seconds later an aircraft at FL470 notified of +/- 1000 gain/loss and another airliner requesting lower due to mountain wave. We were then given direct to a waypoint on our flight plan and landed at destination without further incident. Be more vigilant while single pilot operations.
Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported altitude and airspeed deviations as a result of mountain wave activity in cruise.

Narrative: This flight was a planned departure from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Weather was overcast, rainy with relatively calm winds and temperatures decreased during preflight from around 10C to 4C prior to departure.
