Pushback was delayed due to ramp congestion but only delayed takeoff slightly. The Captain was operating as Pilot Flying (PF) for this flight. The First Officer was Pilot Monitoring (PM). Takeoff was uneventful. The departure was flown autopilot off. While heading toward ZZZZZ and climbing at 280 KIAS, sometime after passing FL180 and climbing to FL230 in Instrument Meteorological Conditions (IMC), Boeing 737-800 aircraft experienced extreme airspeed indicator swings on both sides of the cockpit. Indications wildly fluctuated between 300 KIAS down to 180 KIAS. The PF asked the PM if his indications were normal and the PM responded that his indications appeared erroneous as well and he had an airspeed disagree indication. The pitot heat was verified ON. The autothrottles started to chase the airspeed fluctuations and were subsequently turned off. PF maintained the climb power and pitch angle and asked the PM to get a higher altitude from ATC. ATC responded with a 'standby for higher' response. The PM attempted to select Vertical Speed and it would not engage. All vertical guidance was unavailable. The PF asked the PM for a groundspeed and the PM responded that he did not see one. There was no groundspeed on the Captain's (PF) side as well. The Standby Flight Instruments were difficult to read as they had been dimmed for the takeoff and now the sun was coming up. Simultaneously, we were approaching a turn from ZZZZZ to ZZZZZ1. PF elected to maintain wings level and continued straight ahead as to not compound the problem by turning in IMC conditions with obvious airspeed errors. Since the sun was just rising we could see the top of the weather was very close. As we approached FL230 we continued to climb and notified ATC. ATC cleared us to FL380. After reaching an altitude, probably FL240/FL250 in Visual Meteorological Conditions (VMC) the aircraft returned to nominal limits. The flight continued under VMC to ZZZ1. The aircraft flew normally after the event and landed safely. Discrepancies were noted in the Aircraft Maintenance Logbook (AML) and maintenance personnel were debriefed by the Captain. Recommend a third air data inertial reference unit (ADIRU) on the B-737 so the bad ADIRU can be removed from the equation during a failure and still have a comparator feature.
Narrative_1: Early morning departure out of ZZZ to ZZZ1. During climbout on the SID just after passing through the transition through FL180 I noticed we had lost the flight director and a yellow 'speed disagree' flag on the PFD (Primary Flight Display). I then looked at the MCP and VNAV/LNAV was off. Tried to re-engage and it wouldn't due to the PFD flag. About that time I noticed the speed had dropped from 280 KIAS to about 260 KIAS and we were off course having missed a slight turn on the SID. The Captain then said his was not right and asked me what mine said. I had said mine didn't seem correct either. Then he asked me what our ground speed was and I looked and mine was blank, not showing and wind/GS/TAS. At that time I told Center that we were having a problem with our instruments since we were off course and altitude. He came back and gave us present heading and FL230. The Captain then asked me to see if we could continue our climb since we weren't far from being on top of the weather, I asked and was told to stand by. A few seconds later Center gave us FL380. At this time I notified ATC having noticed we were getting further off our heading and the situation was getting worse. As we started to climb everything came back, air speeds matched, flag went away, was able to re engage LNAV/VNAV and flight directors. Few seconds after that we were on top in VMC. Everything came back just as quickly as we lost it. We were cleared to our next fix and resumed normal operations. We discussed our options and mutually decided that since there was clear weather for the rest of the way to ZZZ1 and everything was working that it was best to continue rather than turn back into the weather and return to ZZZ. The rest of the flight was uneventful and sent an ACARS message to let Maintenance know we would be writing the aircraft up when we landed. We landed in ZZZ1 and the Captain made the entry in the logbook when we got to the gate.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported Air Data Computer malfunction inflight.

Narrative: Turning final ZZZZ fully configured at 150 knots I armed the Localizer first than the Approach mode. First Officer inquired and received the landing clearance. I noticed that the glide slope didn't capture and that we were going above the path. I tried to descend in Vertical Speed, but it didn't come active, so it wouldn't work. Approach mode light still on. I disconnected the Autopilot, lowered the nose and started a descend using the VGSI (Visual Glideslope) path indicator and the outside PAPI (Precision Approach Path Indicator). During the descent we tried to reset the Approach/Glideslope unsuccessfully. The approach was pretty bumpy with some good downdrafts. The aircraft went below the glide slope and I started to correct back when the pull up warning came on then stopped right away. Then the glide slope warning followed. I was just under the path recovering and had 3 red lights and 1 white on the PAPI. Speed around 10 knots above Vref and decreasing toward Vref. I was very focused on the approach and continued to an uneventful normal landing.We were configured early, ready for approach, but the Glideslope not capturing and the uncertainty concerning the landing clearance created a distraction that put me behind the aircraft and I developed some tunnel vision trying to remedy the approach. I became fixated and continued when I should have discontinued the approach and gone around. After landing the First Officer said to me that she had mentioned going around, but it hadn't registered with me during the approach. I tell First Officers that there is no mission, but today I didn't follow my own advice. It's easy to become over focused without realizing it. When in doubt, go-around.
Narrative_1: The event began while beginning the ILS Approach. The company notes on the approach dictate not to arm the ILS until reaching a certain position because of the possibility of false localizer signals. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and I was the Pilot Monitoring. I remember thinking that the Pilot Flying armed the approach later than I would have since we were well beyond the designated point. My best guess on what happened is that because of the delay the localizer armed but the glideslope never captured because we were already too high. Whatever the reason for the automation not doing what we had expected, the result was that we realized that the Glideslope never captured and were trying to get the aircraft to come down.Not only were we distracted with being above the intended glide path, but we were handed over to tower late and I was busy with getting clearance to land while the Pilot Flying was flying the plane trying to get back to a stabilized approach. As the aircraft was getting back to a normal glide path (3 red, 1 white on PAPI) around the 500 foot mark I gave my stabilized approach callout and realizing we were slightly above speed and correcting, but the vertical speed exceeded what is acceptable. At this point I said 'I think we should go around'. I can't remember if it was just before or after I said this that we got a 'PULL UP' alert. The Captain elected to continue the landing. Later after discussion, I learned he may have had tunnel vision to the point where my go around call didn't register with him.My unfamiliarity with ZZZZ did not help our situational awareness as well as being distracted with getting switched over to tower (late) and attempting to get landing clearance around the same time we realized the automation did not perform as expected. As a FO/PM not being assertive enough when a go-around was needed.Abiding by company SOP to the letter. No matter what, at 500 feet if stabilized approach criteria aren't met, it's an automatic and firm 'GO AROUND'.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported they descended below the glidepath on their approach resulting in an unstable approach and a terrain warning but the flying pilot continued the approach and landed.

Narrative: We were cleared to FL 230. Passing through 17,500 feet, #1 engine rolled back to approximately 30%N1. The N1 and EGT had flashing red and yellow arcs and the lower section had a red flashing box around both engine indications. Our initial analysis was engine failure. We requested to level at FL 180, communicated to ATC our situation and requested vectors to return to ZZZ. Upon further analysis of the engine condition, the Captain (Pilot Flying) stated the engine was still running but noted the indications were not normal. We also saw the EEC in ALTN mode. Captain continued to fly and directed me into the QRH for the EEC ALT MODE checklist since the engine was running and not surging, stalling, or any indications dictating complete failure or the need to shutdown. We completed the QRH for the EEC ALT MODE according to our situation and indications. We discussed and agreed to also reference and ran the QRH [for] One Engine Inoperative Landing. I continued communications with ATC, while the Captain communicated with F/A's and made a PA to passengers. I computed [landing] data and set up the FMC. Captain flew the approach and landing, taxiing clear of the runway to a safe location. Autobrakes were used and no manual braking activated until slowed (approximately 50 knots) and prior to the exit of the runway. Based on our weight and configuration [calculations] prior to landing required the use of autobrakes and brake cooling calculations. I calculated the [landing data] for Non-Normal One engine Inop with 15 Flaps landing. Brake Cooling calculations returned a 58 minute cooling period, which we accomplished at the turnout abeam runway. Emergency Rescue Crews communicated to us no visible smoke from brakes and heat signature negative. After the 58 minute cool down, we were given clearance to taxi and proceeded to our gate.
Narrative_1: When we arrived at the gate, Maintenance was working on the #1 engine. The previous crew that had the aircraft had returned to the gate. When they started the number one engine they got the Engine Control light. Maintenance cleaned the cannon plugs did an engine run and returned the aircraft to service. Our engine start and initial climb were all normal. We were on radar vectors for our route and climbing through 17,500 feet or so when the #1 N1 Gauge flashed yellow twice. We both saw it, then the #1 engine rolled back to 31% on the N1 but the engine didn't quit. We leveled at FL 180 and requested vectors back to ZZZ. We ran the EEC ALT Mode Checklist and the Engine Failure or Shutdown Checklist from the QRH. Landed Flaps 15, autobrakes 3. We ran the brake cooling calculation prior to landing. We had a 58 minutes of break cooling.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported returning to departure airport after experiencing #1 engine anomalies that reduced thrust to idle.

Narrative: I was the First Officer and the pilot monitoring. We were cleared to descend via the ZZZZZX. Approaching FL200 on the descent, I noticed my airspeed start to decrease rapidly without any change in airplane thrust or pitch. I called out 'airspeed' while inspecting the standby and Captain's airspeed indicator. We called unreliable airspeed and started the QRC (Quick Reference Checklist). We followed the QRC followed by the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook). We were able to confirm that the Captain's airspeed indicator was accurate based on the pitch and power settings and correlating with the standby airspeed indicator. The QRH instructed us to reengage the autopilot and change the ALT SOURCE selector to the Captain's side. This allowed my airspeed indicator to correspond with the Captain's and standby airspeed indicator. After we dictated which airspeed was accurate, ATC had given a heading and altitude to continue into ZZZ. I completed the QRH checklist for Unreliable Airspeed but kept the unreliable airspeed tables open to make sure the pitch and power settings correlated with our speed. We continued to fly the ILS approach into ZZZ without any further incident. The Captain notified Maintenance and Dispatch once we were blocked in and the door open. We were unable to conclude the cause that created the unreliable airspeed situation. But, I will become more familiar with the airspeed unreliable checklist and table so that I may refer to it and utilize it more efficiently in the event of another similar occurrence.
Synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported unreliable airspeed indications on Captain's side during arrival descent.

Narrative: As we arrived in ZZZ, the First Officer and myself had planned on the ILS to RWY (Runway) XX as the winds had favored that runway. The winds had shifted and favored RWY XY as we were handed off to approach control. As I was the flying pilot, the FO (First Officer) hastily entered the RNP to Runway XY. This was also our first time into ZZZ. As the aircraft captured Final App... it looked as if we were on profile... and we were also visual. I soon realized that the altitude constraints had not been loaded due to the fact that the approach via had not been entered. I arrested the descent, however, we did get the 'pull up" warning ....a go around was performed followed by the published hold. We then performed the ILS to RWY XX, circle to [Runway] XY to a normal landing.
Synopsis: Air carrier Flight Crew reported GPWS Alert on approach.

Narrative: During cruise STAB OUT OF TRIM light illuminated intermittently. Complied with STAB OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure. Maintenance notified via ACARS. Descending with autopilot and autothrottle on, aircraft did not level off at the preselected 4,000 feet. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottle and began to return to 4,000 feet. I tried the electric trim and found it to be inoperative. I notified the Captain of the inoperative electric trim. The Captain tried his electric trim and also found it to be inoperative. Captain conferred with me about disconnecting the STAB TRIM CUT OUT switches. I agreed and the STAB TRIM CUT OUT switches were disconnected. Captain opened the QRH and we complied with the STAB OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure. The STAB OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure directed us to the STABILIZER TRIM INOPERATIVE procedure, which we complied with. I tried to operate the manual trim with my left hand could not move the trim wheel through a full rotation. I notified the Captain of this and he tried the manual trim. Captain seem to require both hands to operate the manual trim. Captain notified ATC and we requested delay vectors. We requested the longer Runway of XXR. We performed a flaps 15 landing on XXR. Descended below assigned altitude of 4,000 feet due to malfunctioning elevator trim.
Narrative_1: This report is being submitted to cover the altitude deviation on approach into ZZZ. The altitude deviation was a direct result of a malfunction of the stabilizer/stabilizer trim system. The other required category reports will be covered in a separate irregularity report.Approximately two hours after departure and level at FL350, the STAB OUT OF TRIM (amber) light illuminated. We ran the STABILIZER OUT OF TRIM QRH procedure. Autopilot B was engaged and remained engaged while the light was eliminated, the aircraft maintained altitude and airspeed in light mountain wave and light chop conditions. Since the auto pilot appeared to be trimming the aircraft normally and in accordance with QRH, we continued normal operation. We notified maintenance control and Dispatch via ACARS and made a maintenance logbook entry for the condition. Dispatch acknowledged receiving the message. The light remained illuminated for approximately 10 mins. During this time both the first officer and myself reviewed not only the QRH, but Stabilizer Trim Inoperative QRH procedure in the event that these stabilizers stopped trimming at some subsequent point. We also reviewed be available information in both the flight handbook as well as the systems handbook.The STAB OUT OF TRIM light continued to illuminate intermittently in durations that ranged from several minutes to just a few seconds. We also climbed to FL370 with no abnormal indications and with the B autopilot remaining engaged. I observed some movement of the trim wheel at various times.During the cruise portion of the flight, the light was extinguished most of the time, but we did have the intermittent illuminations periodically. We informed dispatch and maintenance control that the light was illuminating intermittently.On the arrival into ZZZ we were given several intermediate level offs as well as crossing altitude and airspeed restrictions all of which were met with autopilot B engaged.While being vectored around some weather, for a visual approach to Runway XXL, we were kept somewhat high on the profile and were in a fairly aggressive dissent to 4,000 feet. Autopilot B remained engaged throughout this descent. At 4,000 feet the flight directors commanded a level off but the aircraft continued to descend below 4,000 feet and did not capture the altitude, the first officer (pilot flying) immediately disengaged the auto pilot and auto throttles and began to correct The flight path, but due to the out of trim condition of the stabilizer the aircraft descended to approximately 3,500 feet before being able to level off the aircraft with considerable back pressure on the yoke.We informed ZZZ Approach that we had a stabilizer issue and were attempting to correct back to 4000 feet. They directed us to maintain 3000 feet. At about this time, the first officer informed me that 'I don't have any trim' and I saw him activate the yoke stabilizer trim switches for nose up and nose down trim with no movement of the stabilizer trim wheels. I attempted to trim the stabilizer using the yoke switches on my side with no effect as well. The first officer was holding a great deal of back pressure on the yolk and stated 'I need nose up trim' at this point with his concurrence after having verified that neither yolk could trim the stabilizer electrically, I selected both stabilizer trim cut out switches to cut out.At this point I told the first officer that he was going to continue to be the pilot flying and also have the radios while I reviewed the QRH procedures. After I verified that we had accomplished all of the steps and had been directed to the next QRH section. Well I was reviewing the QRH procedures the first officer attempted to trim the aircraft manually and stated 'I can't move the wheel'. It was at this point I believe where I [requested priority] with approach and told them that we had a stabilizer trim failure and we were attempting to trim the aircraft manually we requested and receiveda vector to do this and we reported our souls on board as well as fuel and requested ARFF assistance at the airport. At this point I attempted to trim the stabilizer nose up manually from my side but was unable to turn the stabilizer trim wheel. I directed the first officer to attempt to slow the aircraft to clean maneuver speed in an attempt to unload the stabilizer so that we could trim the aircraft manually. At some point approaching clean maneuver speed I was able to begin moving the trim wheel nose up but it was still quite difficult and required a significant two-handed effort to move the wheel at all. I managed to get several turn nose up trim and the first officer said 'that's good'. At this point, we were in a more or less in trim condition at clean maneuver and clean. We continue to execute QRH and requested the longer Runway (XXR). It was at about this point I believe that I informed the flight attendants of our situation and that we would be landing in about 5 to 10 minutes, to expect a normal landing but that there would be fire trucks standing by.We completed QRH and had a normal flaps 15 landing on Runway XXRWe rolled out normally and cleared the runway and informed ground control and the ARFF captain that we did not require any further assistance.We taxi to the gate and shut down the aircraft, debriefed the flight attendants, and spoke with maintenance on the ground about our situation.
Synopsis: B737-900 flight crew reported Stab Trim failure resulted in an altitude overshoot and limited control ability.

Narrative: Received a climb RA while flying the [Runway] XXL RNAV X. We climbed at 1500-2000 FPM, a small civilian aircraft flew under our aircraft and missed us by 400 feet. We heard approach control give traffic advisory to the other aircraft for a '737'. We received no traffic advisories. I consider this event a near miss.No traffic advisories received from approach or vectoring to either aircraft to avoid the conflict.The Approach Controller needs to do their job. Not vector another aircraft into our aircraft. The pilot of the other aircraft should not take climbing vectors into a 737. (Day VFR Weather, 10 miles plus visibility)
Narrative_1: Cleared RNAV (RNP) X [Runway] XXL at ZZZ and subsequently received a TCAS RA approaching ZZZZZ. A light civil aircraft called us in sight and approach told them to maintain visual separation. Light civil aircraft was being vectored by approach control when RA commanded a climb to which the Captain (Pilot Flying) executed. We never saw the aircraft but the TCAS display showed them 400 feet below us. When resolved we were cleared a visual approach and landing without further incident.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported an uneventful landing after an NMAC event requiring evasive maneuver during approach. No traffic information provided to flight crew.

Narrative: We were flying the ILS 27R to ORD. When cleared for the approach level at 4,000 ft, we twice had to disconnect the autopilot from the aircraft wake ahead of us. Spacing was the usual 3 miles and winds were straight down the path at 40 kts. Other aircraft were radioing similar issues with wake. I decided to hand fly the approach the rest of the way to better control the speed and avoid the wake. The Final Controller told us to slow to 170 kts and contact Tower. We were cleared to land by Tower and continued the approach at 170 kts. Spacing was holding at 3 miles, but as we approached the marker I noticed our spacing was closing faster than normal. At about 2.5 outside the marker I made the decision to start slowing to avoid going around. (Full disclosure, I have been in the exact situation before and had to go around twice on this approach.) What I misjudged was how fast the 737-700 slows down. We were at approach speed too early and the Tower asked our speed and instructions. We made the aircraft behind us go around from my error in speed control.
Narrative_1: While on ILS 27R into ORD, we were experiencing wake turbulence from the aircraft ahead of us and appeared to be quickly closing the distance between us. We had been assigned 170 kts until the final approach fix 'SIBLY' and began slowing 2 miles prior to the fix to stop the closure. The Tower Controller queried our speed, and emphasized we were to hold 170 until the fix.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported slowing below assigned airspeed to avoid wake turbulence from aircraft ahead on approach to ORD, forcing traffic in trail of them to go around.

Narrative: Cleared to line up and wait Runway XX. When cleared for takeoff, pushed power to approximate 40% then selected TO/GA. As the thrust levers advanced, there was a very loud bang and yaw to the left. We had just started rolling. The thrust levers were brought to idle and we stopped on the runway. Initially, with the bang and yaw I thought we hit something or ran over something. As I was looking out the window, the First Officer stated we had a #1 Engine failure. Tower asked if we wanted equipment. We asked if they saw smoke or damage, and they replied 'No', along with another aircraft on the taxiway. I made a PA for everyone to remain seated. I then called the F/A's (Flight Attendants) and asked them to look at the Captain side engine for smoke or flames. They reported it looked normal. We ran the Engine Failure Checklist, and discussed running the Rejected Takeoff Checklist. Since the event happened as the aircraft had just started to roll (probably less than 10 knots) we didn't run the Rejected Takeoff Checklist, knowing that brake energy and cooling wouldn't be an issue. After we taxied to the gate, I made calls to Dispatch, Maintenance, and the Chief Pilot on call, while the First Officer went to the ramp to inspect the aircraft. He discovered bent and broken turbine blades with metal pieces loose in the engine. He came back upstairs and called ZZZ Ground to do a runway check for engine debris. I made a PA to the passengers explaining that we had an engine failure at power up, and the aircraft would be taken out of service. They would receive more flight information in the terminal. After the passengers had deplaned, the crew got together and debriefed the event. I informed the F/As of what had happened and let them ask questions.
Synopsis: Captain reported engine failure on take off roll causing a rejected take off and a return to the gate.

Narrative: After the addition of thrust for T/O (takeoff) and selection of TO/GA (takeoff go-around) and N1 attaining T/O power, the aircraft was already rolling and had achieved approximately 15 knots of forward motion. At that point we heard a very loud bang followed by a hard left yawing motion. The PF (Pilot Flying) immediately retarded the throttles to idle, and applied smooth breaking, which brought us to a complete stop. We were angled left by about 30-40 degrees in relation to the center line of Runway 4, just prior to taxiway. I immediately informed ATC that we had stopped on the runway, the PF informed the PAX (passengers) to stay seated. At that point we began to assess the situation. Initially we thought it was a blown tire or nose wheel steering issue. In that moment of assessing I noticed the #1 Engine Fail Caution illuminate in the #1 EGT Gauge. I informed the PF of the indication. It was the only indication we saw. No fire, no red lines only the engine failure alert caution. We reviewed the Rejected Takeoff Procedure, completed the QRH for Engine Failure. We then assessed the rolling and breaking capability of the aircraft and we found it to be normal. We got clearance to exit the runway and return to the gate. As we pulled in to the gate, we remembered that we had not run an After Landing Checklist and quickly completed that, followed by the Parking Checklist. Then, the jetbridge malfunctioned and we had to wait until Airport Ops came to fix it. Once the jetbridge was attached I exited the aircraft to inspect Engine #1. I found the N1 fan blades and the stators directly behind them to be in a normal appearance. When I looked into the tailpipe of the turbine section, I found metal debris from the engine and both the aft fan blades and stators in front of them to be damaged and missing pieces. I hustled back to the Flight Deck to inform Ground Control that they needed to do a FOD check of the runway as we had, had and engine failure and that they needed to check for small engine parts.
Synopsis: First Officer reported engine failure on take off roll, resulting in engine damage and a return to the gate.

Narrative: All preflight items complete INCLUDING Main Electric STAB TRIM CUTOUT switch with normal results. Student Captain was Pilot flying for this leg. Shortly after Takeoff the PF commented that his electric trim switch was not working and asked me to try mine, which also did not work. I asked him if the elevator was working and he replied that it was and felt normal. We asked ATC to level off at 12,000 ft to work on a flight control issue and was approved. We did not ask for priority handling at this time...we engaged the A Autopilot successfully but shortly after the 'STAB OUT OF TRIM' light came on. As we began to look up the appropriate Non-normal, the PF disengaged the autopilot and tried to manually trim the stabilizer. Although he was successful it looked like it was difficult to rotate so I asked to give it a shot to feel the force required to rotate. The force required to rotate was abnormally high but did provide results and we were flying a trimmed aircraft at 240 knots. By now I was considering that a Jammed Flight Control (the stabilizer in this case) was the source of our STAB OUT OF TRIM problem. So the first checklist we addressed was the Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls Non-normal and also the Jammed or Restricted Flight Controls procedure (the script/expanded explanation). Around this time we requested priority handling with ATC because checklist called for landing at nearest suitable airport. We were hoping that we might get electric trim back when moving STAB TRIM switch on pedestal to OVERRIDE. Did not happen. Called Dispatch with Maintenance Control on the line hoping for some systems expertise. Ended call with where we started. We began to discuss possible value of running STAB OUT OF TRIM checklist. We did. But before doing so we noted the hazard of running multiple checklists and capped our STAB TRIM OVERRIDE switch to normal. The Jammed Flight Control non normal resulted in moving both STAB TRIM switches to CUTOUT but also called for landing at nearest suitable with Flaps 15. About this time we got on radio again with Maintenance Control, Dispatch and also the Flight Operations. Our hope was that Flight Operations might be able to get a Hydraulics of Flight Controls Maintenance expert on with us. We discussed both checklists and Flight Operations talked about the potential effect of slower speeds. This call ended with general consensus we were on the best track and we discussed whether to land sooner or burn down to below Max landing weight. Because we felt the aircraft was stable and our condition was not likely to get worse we chose to burn fuel. I talked to PF and told him it would be prudent for me to do landing since that would be his first one from left seat in aircraft. We briefed our arrival plan which included our trim plan as we reduced airspeed and extended gear and flaps. As we descended and slowed we reminded ATC of need for priority handling equipment. Only significant thing to report was that by the time we had fully configured and slowed to final approach speed it was extremely difficult to trim manually. In fact, with one pilot exerting maximum effort, you could maybe get the manual strection about a quarter turn. All of this led us to believe that the Stabilizer was DEFINITELY jammed. Landed uneventfully, had equipment check us out then taxied to gate. Flight Attendants were given TEST brief and told there was no need to prepare for evacuation.
Narrative_1: All systems checked ok at gate, but after rotation we discovered our electric stabilizer trim was inop. The aircraft was controllable, but required moderate yoke pressure.We got vectors over the water and stopped our climb at 12,000. We engaged the autopilot momentarily, but the Stab out of Trim light led us to complete that non-normal checklist.We used the Manual Trim Procedure, but felt the force required was excessive, and the trim wheel was not rotating freely.Dispatch contacted and priority handling requested. We completed the Jammed Flight Control and the Stab Trim Inop checklists, both which call for Flaps 15 landing.After again contacting Dispatch, Maintenance Control, and Flight Operations, we planned to divert back to ZZZ.We burned down to max landing weight and landed uneventfully.
Synopsis: B737 NG flight crew reported a jammed horizontal stabilizer trim system and elected to make an Air turn Back and precautionary landing.

Narrative: While being radar vectored to the visual final for Runway XX at ZZZ, Approach Control issued a descent to 6,000 feet MSL. We read back the clearance and proceeded to descend to 6,000 feet MSL. The Captain did observe that we seemed closer to some radio Towers on a hill than what would appear normal, but we received no GPWS Alerts. We continued on vectors and flew an uneventful approach and landing. After a call from Tower a few hours later, it was explained that the descent clearance to 6,000 feet was issued to a (other carrier X) whose readback was on a different Approach Control frequency. Our readback to that clearance as Company A (very similar sounding call sign) must have occurred at the same moment as (other carrier's) reply. Since the (other carrier X) aircraft had been on a different approach frequency, we had yet to hear any other communications to or from that aircraft, and ATC had not issued a caution for the similar sounding call signs. Additionally, ATC did not issue a low altitude warning if we had gone below the Minimum Vector Altitude in the sector we were within.When managing multiple frequencies, ATC should ensure that aircraft with similar call signs are alerted to possible miss interpretations. Furthermore, ATC should minimize the use of simulcasting on multiple Approach frequencies and consolidate traffic to one radio frequency.
Narrative_1: We were being vectored for the visual approach to Runway XX at ZZZ from the east. ZZZ Approach Control issued a clearance to 6,000 feet MSL. We were later contacted that the clearance was for (other carrier) X, on another frequency and not for Company A. The clearance apparently took us below the MVA for that sector. The Controller was controlling multiple frequencies (he was busy) and never advised us of similar sounding call signs. We did not receive any terrain cautions from the aircraft or Controller. The subsequent approach and landing were uneventful.Listening during communications is always the most important. Being advised of similar sounding call signs is an important step to help alleviate threats and for Crews to be more vigilant.
Synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported a CFIT event during a visual approach due to an ATC communications breakdown between flight crew and Approach Control who was working multiple frequencies with similar callsigns.

Narrative: Flying Aircraft X on a ferry flight from ZZZ - ZZZ1. Climbing out of FL350 for FL390 the flight crew was alerted of a bleed trip off of the No.2 Pack. The Bleed Trip Off QRH was called for and completed with no resolution as we leveled at FL390. As directed by the QRH the No.2 pack was turned off. At this moment ATC gave us a clearance up to our cruising altitude of FL410. The crew declined the request and relayed the need for a lower altitude (initially FL310). The request was granted and the crew began descending the aircraft to assure the single pack could maintain adequate cabin pressure. Passing FL380 the crew received a cabin altitude warning light. The appropriate memory items where accomplished, requested priority handling and descent to 10,000 was initiated. During the descent, the high cabin altitude and decent QRH procedure were accomplished by the First Officer while the Captain negotiated the descent. Passing through 27,000 feet the cabin altitude reached a level which activated the automatic deployment of the oxygen masks. Reaching 10,000 feet, the Captain verified aircraft was stabilized, crew was checked for any injuries, and the FO attempted to reach company via AIRINC. With the low altitude prohibiting any contact with ARINC and the aircraft was not equipped with datalink, the discussion began on where to go next. Departure airport ZZZ was approximately 200 NM behind us. ZZZ2 was 190 NM in front of us. And the Destination of ZZZ1 was an additional 300 NM past ZZZ3. The crew discussed the options and in an abundance of safety elected to divert to ZZZ3. The crew notified ATC of the decision to change destination and asked the ATC facility to notify our company of the situation and destination change. The flight continued to ZZZ3 and landed without further incident. Dispatch and Chief Pilot were notified once the aircraft landed.Gaining the ability to contact dispatch Via ACARS when AIRINC is not contactable would have helped in the decision making of this flight.
Synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported executing an uneventful landing after a mechanical diversion due to a pressurization pack failure during climb.

Narrative: Flight ZZZZ - ZZZ1 (all nighter). Runway XXL departure IMC conditions with TS (thunderstorms) in terminal area. Crew briefed to remain seated due to expected turbulence on departure. Passengers briefed in welcome aboard announcement that the Flight Attendants would remain seated due to rain showers and bumps on departure. Performance for A/C weight of 145k, Flaps [set], Runway XXL bleeds on reduced thrust T/O. Normal T/O executed with a climb to cleared altitude FL230 commenced. Passing approximately 11,000 [ft., high elevation airport]. Cabin Alt Red warning light illuminated and horn sounded. Horn silenced - pressurization panel checked - and confirmed correct positioning of switches as terrain noted and communication coordinated with ATC for 'safe' altitude and significant weather avoidance required. Aircraft climbing at normal rate and leveling at 11,000 [ft.] was not an option. O2 masks donned and immediate action items of QRC executed. Remainder of checklist executed as Flying Pilot coordinated deviation with ATC and Captain with regard to safe altitude and course for primarily terrain avoidance and significant weather avoidance as a secondary threat. 17,000 ft. deemed to be safest altitude based on position of aircraft. Requested and set. Executed checklist items concurrently with NO resolution to regaining aircraft pressurization. All indications were normal, but obvious that aircraft was not pressuring at all. Plan determined by flight crew to coordinate safe corridor passage through the 'valley' - again based on terrain primary and weather secondary. Coordination with FAs indicated that passenger O2 had deployed automatically (and of note was deployed manually too during procedure), and that crew and passengers were 'safe'. ACARS NO COMM was illuminated likely due to A/C altitude and mountains blocking signals. Crew coordinated for lower altitudes as safe MORA (Minimum Off-Route Altitude) conditions permitted to account for passenger O2 eventually being depleted. Initially 15,000 [ft.], then 12,000 [ft.] coordinated to attempt to get cabin altitude below 10,000 [ft.]. At 12,000 ft. with the pack switches selected to high - crew was able to get the cabin altitude to below 10,000 ft. On initial communication with the cabin crew - communication with the forward cabin was nearly impossible due to loud noise by door 1L (our apparent source of no pressurization). Crew communication conducted via aft galley inter phone to determine crew and passenger status. Cockpit crew determined return to ZZZZ not best course of action due to terrain, weather, heavy weight of aircraft and passenger O2 depletion. ACARS comm with Dispatch established as determination for diversion and potential diversionary airports weighed. Both ZZZZ1 and ZZZZ2 considered. ZZZZ1 determined to have more threats due to lack of familiarity, time and rising terrain by the airport. ZZZZ2 considered and subsequently determined (in coordination with Dispatch) due to familiarity, the fact that we have been routinely using it as an alternate for ZZZZ flights, safe passage from our current location to airport at 12,000 ft. and relatively easy weather avoidance to get to airport. Aircraft integrity was addressed and deemed not to be an issue to choose the more distant diversionary airport. Coordination with ATC-1 and ATC-2 Control completed to receive priority handling (even though very few aircraft were in the sector). Coordination with Dispatch continued throughout with updated runway data, weather and ZZZZ2 [company] ground operations taken care of. Clearance given to descend for the ILS [Runway] XXR approach to ZZZZ2. Crew understood and briefed overweight landing procedures for ZZZZ2 having previously agreed that the threat of landing at 133,000 lbs outweighed the threat of remaining airborne for another 45 min to burn down below max landing weight. Of note, on descent through 7,000 ft. a loud sound [was] heard in [the] cockpit - aircraft integrity deemed safewith no abnormal engine indications. Aircraft executed a normal approach and landing to Runway XYR in ZZZZ2. Upon arrival maintenance items entered for O2 deployed, aircraft pressurization, and overweight landing. Upon post flight it was determined the aircraft had at least two bird strikes which were also entered in maintenance log book. Maintenance quickly determined that door 1L had failed to seat properly but had given a closed condition indication (never any door indication illumination in the cockpit). Challenges existed in ZZZZ2 for both crew and passengers due to aircraft flight originating in [foreign country] with current COVID restrictions in place and requiring adherence.
Synopsis: B-737 Captain reported executing a challenging mechanical diversion due to pressurization failure during climb. The diversion was concluded with an uneventful overweight landing.

Narrative: Climbing through 34,000 feet we encountered a noise and grinding sound with a significant vibration through the plane. I noticed an odor and told the Captain and at that exact time the flight attendants called up saying that there was smoke in the cabin. We looked at the instruments and noticed both engines were erratic in their readings and a high vibration occurring on the number 2 engine. All of these events were happened at the same time. I flew the aircraft the Captain worked the checklist and requested priority handling. We shutdown the number 2 engine. An airport was right in front of us and we decided to divert there. Captain took care of the passenger PAs and flight attendants while I controlled the aircraft and flew. After completing all the checklists and on downwind Captain took the aircraft and landed the plane. Fire Department was on scene and looked over the plane after we landed. They didn't noticed any leaks or fires so we taxied to the gate with them following us. We had paramedics meet us at the gate to treat any passengers or crew members in case they needed assistance.After we made it to the gate and the passengers deplaned we inspected the number 2 engine. There was damage to the nose cone and fan blades and inner engine cowling. Something happened in flight for the parts to become damaged. We were at FL340 so I doubt there were any birds or anything we hit, not sure why this happened.
Narrative_1: Climbing through 34,000 feet at climb power we encountered a cyclic, significant vibration through the airframe. The First Officer then noticed a toxic odor which I then noticed. This was immediately followed by a call from the flight attendants advising that the cabin was filling with smoke accompanied by a toxic odor. This all happened over a period of about 15 seconds. We then looked at the engine instruments and noticed erratic engine indications along with reduced thrust and high engine vibration on the number 2 engine. The First Officer continued flying the aircraft and I communicated the situation to ATC with a call and a request for lower altitude. I completed the engine severe damage/separation checklist resulting in a precautionary shutdown of the number 2 engine. I then advised ATC we would be diverting for landing.After that I called the flight attendants to check on the status of the cabin. They told me the smoke and smell were dissipating rapidly. I advised them of the situation and that we would be making a precautionary landing and would be landing in about 25 minutes. I then advised Dispatch through the ACARS message of our situation. After checking in with the First Officer on the status of the diversion I made a PA to the passengers advising them that we were having problems with one of our engines and that we were going to make a precautionary landing. I also told them that in an abundance of caution they may see some safety equipment inspecting us after landing. Through the descent I made several more calls to the cabin to check on the status and made another PA to reassure the passengers. I also completed the one engine inoperative checklist along with the non routine landing checklist. I elected to assume control of the aircraft for landing and took the controls after we briefed the approach and after landing considerations. After landing without incident, we cleared the runway on a high speed taxi way and stopped so that the Fire Department could make an inspection of our aircraft. After Fire Department told us they saw no abnormalities I elected to taxi to the gate.The FO and I made a visual inspection of the number 2 engine and saw damage to two compressor blades along with damage to the spinner and the inner engine cowling. I was surprised at the small amount of damage considering the effects to engine performance and the smoke and fumes in the cabin. I'd like to add that the First Officer did a great job in his duties which allowed me to focus on my duties. His calmness, superior airmanship and advice were instrumental in the smooth handling of our situation. I'd also like to commend the flight attendants especially the number 1, on their calmness, communication and professionalism in a very stressful situation.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported engine vibrations along with smoke and odor in the cabin. They shut down the number two engine, diverted, and landed safely.

Narrative: While enroute 1.5 hours into flight, both GPS units began showing intermittent faults. I began coordinating with Dispatch. Eventually, both GPS units failed completely. Dispatch and I agreed that diverting to ZZZ was the best option. It was accomplished uneventfully. No GPS jamming reported by other aircraft or ATC.
Synopsis: An Air Carrier pilot reported both GPS units failed.

Narrative: Just prior to leveling off at FL340, Flight Attendant called and stated there was an electrical burning smell in the forward galley. There was not any smoke nor fire, just an odor. We notified ATC, turned back toward ZZZ, accomplished all checklist items, and landed uneventfully. After clearing the runway, we had the fire department check the airplane for signs of a fire. They saw nothing so we taxied back to the gate. At the gate, the fire department came on board to check the galley. They found nothing. No deviations from FARs.
Narrative_1: Flight Attendant reported faint smell of fumes in forward galley. Verified by [company] deadheading pilot. Ran smoke/fumes checklist. Verified no fire or persistent fumes. Checklist said to land. Captain made the call and we returned to ZZZ. Overweight landing also accomplished and written up in ZZZ.
Synopsis: A320 flight crew reported an 'electrical burning smell' during initial climb resulting in a return to the departure airport.

Narrative: When checking in with SEA Tower, Tower told us 'Cleared to land on [Runway] 34L', and he then asked us which gate we were parking at. We then heard him ask every other aircraft the same thing. Somebody said that's not important right now (which I wholeheartedly agree with), but Tower insisted that it was. I know they want to make their runway exit and taxi plan but asking us which gate we're going to is not necessary, and it's a huge distraction at a critical part of the flight. We're trying to complete our landing check, make sure we're landing on the correct runway, and flying the jet. I don't want my First Officer looking up a gate, or being distracted away from his monitoring duties, and I don't want that for myself when I'm the monitoring pilot. Another thing that SEA Tower is famous for is giving taxi and/or runway hold short instructions while we're slowing through 100 kts. after landing. That also is a critical time, and we're often transferring controls right about then. Tower needs to WAIT until the aircraft is clear or almost clear of the runway and SLOWED down before they start issuing instructions. Nothing further. Educate the tower controllers on critical phases of flight and the their taxi plan is NOT critical. They need to understand that they are there to help the pilots, but instead they're a huge distraction.
Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported SEA Tower Controllers were requesting gate information during a critical phase of flight. The reporter stated SEA Tower routinely transmits instructions during critical phases of flight.

Narrative: Approximately 30 minutes after reaching cruising altitude, the lower display illuminated indicating low oil quantity in #2 engine. It indicated 3. Oil pressure and oil temp matched #1 engine. We opened QRH and learned there is no NNC (Non-Normal Checklist) that covers low oil quantity. Upon a deeper review of our manuals we learned via the 737 FCTM (Flight Crew Training Manual) that the controlling engine indications that could lead to an inflight engine shutdown in regards to engine oil are only pressure and temp. We decided that as long as pressure and temp were good we would continue normal operations. Also based on aircraft logbook and Local Maintenance briefing regarding an earlier flight with a low oil quantity indication we felt it was an indication issue.We monitored pressure and temp and also made contingency plans for an engine shut down just in case. Within 15 minutes the quantity indication dropped to zero, but temp and pressure still matched the #1 engine. After another 15 to 20 minutes we noticed oil pressure was slowly declining with temp still good. Oil pressure continued to decrease until illuminated red. Ran QRH LOW Pressure NNC, which directed us to the inflight engine shutdown NNC.We informed ATC that we were performing a precautionary engine shutdown and will need to divert to ZZZ. ZZZ was chosen based on our cruise altitude and distance at providing the best drift down and descent airport. We completed the inflight engine shutdown NNCWe then completed engine out landing NNC and proceeded to ZZZ and landed without further incident. Upon landing we stopped on runway and were towed to ramp.Low oil quantity.
Synopsis: 737-80 flight crew reported loss of engine oil inflight.

Narrative: I was the Pilot Monitoring on this leg, approximately after 30 min of TOC, the lower display popped up showing Eng 2 low oil qty (3 qts), the Captain asked me to pull the QRH and look if there was a NNC (Non Normal Checklist), and we found out that there is no NNC for low oil quantity, upon searching our manuals we found information regarding this situation, explaining that there is not a min oil qty per se, but that oil temp and oil press are governing, and both indications we normal matching Eng 1. The Captain and I discussed the previous write up that the airplane had regarding low oil qty upon TOD, and how Maintenance personnel had previously drained the oil tank, filled it up again and checked for leaks. Since oil temperature and pressure indications were normal on Eng 2, we assumed it was an oil qty indication issue and decided to continue the flight closely monitoring Eng 2 oil temperature and pressure indications. In the following 10 to 15 mins the oil qty dropped to 0, but all other indications remained normal. Approximately 30 mins after the oil qty indication had shown 0 the Eng 2 oil pressure started to oscillate down and back up in a normal range, gradually getting lower every time, once it remained in the amber range the Captain and I started to anticipate a precautionary engine shutdown. Once the Eng 2 oil pressure indication entered the red range at approximately 14 PSI, the Captain called for the LOW OIL PRESS QRH NNC, we followed the NNC and proceeded to the ENG SHUTDOWN QRH NNC, we informed ATC and Dispatch of our mayday status and proceeded to ZZZ. After completing the ENG SHUTDOWN QRH, we proceeded to the ONE ENG INOPERATIVE NNC, dispatch sent us the landing data for ZZZ RWY XX We landed in ZZZ without further incident, stopping on the RWY and being towed to the ramp.The engine had developed an oil leak that went undetected.I understand the ZZZ1 Maintenance refilled the oil and perform an engine dry run, and then checked for leaks, perhaps the leak would have been discovered if the engine had been started and ran for several minutes.
Synopsis: B737 First Officer reported decreasing oil quantity followed by total loss of oil pressure caused an inflight shut down and a precautionary landing at destination airport.

Narrative: After descending from cruise flight at 360, we leveled off at FL300. We entered the clouds on descent and activated the engine anti ice system. Once level for a few minutes at 300 I noticed a rapid drop of airspeed on my side. I pushed the throttles up and informed the Captain. At that point we realized we had unreliable airspeed on the First Officer side. The Captain assumed control of the aircraft. We had encountered a small amount of rime icing and decided to climb back up. At this point we also realized the Captains altimeter was off. We [advised] through ATC, ran the QRC and QRH checklists. We diverted to ZZZ. We advised Dispatch and the flight attendants of our situation. Passing 15,000 feet our instruments began to return to normal and were equal upon landing. We also accomplished they overweight landing checklist. We landed at ZZZ without incident. I believe the icing conditions could have contributed to the event. Check the pitot static system. Or computers. We had no indication of any heat malfunction.
Narrative_1: After descending from FL360 to FL300 the First Officer, who was the Pilot Flying, noticed his airspeed indication decaying. In the descent we had entered IMC, and the engine heat was selected on due to the OAT. After cross-checking the pilots, standby, and copilots instruments I assumed control of the aircraft and we accomplished all QRC and QRH checklists for unreliable airspeed. We also determined the pilots altimeter was unreliable. [We advised] ATC and we diverted to the nearest suitable airport, which was ZZZ. The flight attendants, passengers and Dispatch were informed of our decision to divert. As we descended and the air became warmer the copilots airspeed and the Captains altimeter started to agree with the correct indications. By approximately 15,000 MSL all instruments were in agreement. Due to our weight we also accomplished the overweight landing checklist. We landed uneventfully at ZZZ and taxied to the gate. An AML entry was made and we entered crew rest at ZZZ.The icing conditions encountered in the descent to FL300 seem to have overwhelmed the pitot-static heating system. There was no indication of anything more than light icing from the pilots perspective. The pitot-static heating system on the 737 needs to be evaluated to ensure this situation doesn't happen to other aircrews.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported icing conditions resulted in unreliable airspeed indications, followed by a descent and diversion to a precautionary landing.

Narrative: While climbing through 9,000 ft. MSL out of ZZZ, we experienced two VERY loud bangs from the #2 engine. We immediately suspected a compressor stall. Scanning the engines, I noticed the #2 engine decreasing in RPM. I immediately pulled the #2 engine to idle and it stabilized there. We coordinated a level-off at 9000 ft. with ZZZ Departure and flew an extended downwind. We ran all appropriate checklists and determined that the engine appeared to be performing normally. Following the checklist, we pushed the power up on the effected engine to approximately 80% with no adverse indications, there was no need to push it up any further. No [priority handling was requested] and we elected to return to ZZZ and fly a flaps 15 approach and landing to Runway 28R. Flight Attendants and Passengers were advised of the situation. After all checklist items were complete, we accomplished an uneventful approach and landing. Weight or brake energy was not a factor.
Narrative_1: Departed [runway] XXR, from ZZZ, radar vectors made a turn to south-southeast, passing through MSL 8,000 ft. deleted thrust reduction at Captain's request, and around MSL 8,500 ft. two loud bangs came from #2 engine followed by vibrations. Contacted ATC, leveled off at MSL 9,000 ft., and ran QRC 'Engine Surge or Stall' followed by the QRH as directed. Engine seemed to run normally after checklist. We returned to ZZZ.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported compressor stalls during climb and elected to return to the departure airport.

Narrative: We were told to expect the RNP approach to 34L from our initial check in. On downwind we were told to expect the visual instead. We had many speed changes. The final speed change was to expedite our slow down to 170. The First Officer called for gear and flaps as necessary. It didn't look like he was going to level at the final approach fix altitude so I was watching that and the plane in front of us. He never called for the landing checklist and I never thought to do it. I completely lost situational awareness. The First Officer ended up getting a sink rate that was quickly corrected. The plane in front of us gave us moderate wake turbulence. We debriefed and decided this was a failure on both of us to maintain situational awareness.
Synopsis: B737NG Captain reported they failed to complete the landing checklist because of distractions and loss of situational awareness.

Narrative: Flight was scheduled to depart ZZZ. We arrived in the flight deck and performed all the normal procedures we have for a normal push back. Captain did the preflight walk around and I loaded the FMC. We agreed the OFP (Operational Flight Plan) looked good and the rest of the flight plan looked sufficient for a potentially bumpy ride to ZZZ1. Captain advised to Flight Attendants to stay seated out of ZZZ until we knew the ride would allow for their safe duties. I was the flying pilot and after Captain did his first flight of the day and PM (Pilot Monitoring) duty brief, I briefed the SID. We planned for a normal pushback with 2 engine start for a quick taxi for departure. We performed the BEFORE TAKEOFF CHECKLIST on taxi out down the ramp for takeoff on runway XX.While we were taxiing down to runway XX, I noticed there was a split between the L and R duct pressure. I made note of it to Captain and we briefly discussed these splits we have seen before in this aircraft and recall it being a known normal occurrence. I cycled the L PACK (Left) switch to OFF and back to AUTO as well as the ISOLATION VALVE switch to OPEN and AUTO and saw the duct pressure needles sync together. We decided it would be a safe action to depart and noted we would keep an eye on the duct pressure and pressurization.We departed runway XX and CLIMBED VIA THE SID. I hand flew the departure to the mid 20s and then turned the autopilot on. I noted Captain mentioned 2 different times that the aircraft was pressurizing normally though the duct pressure still was split. The ride was mostly good and the flight attendants were up but the seat belt was still on. As we approached our level off altitude of FL340 the CABIN ALTITUDE horn and the MASTER WARNING lights illuminated. We verified the CABIN ALTITUDE was high on the pressurization panel and performed the Immediate Action items for CABIN ALTITUDE WARNING OR RAPID DEPRESSURIZATION/EMERGENCY DESCENT. The CABIN ALTITUDE was not controllable, and we continued with the descent. There was a definite issue with immediate communication over the inter-phone with the masks on and all the noise. Getting the mask on and the audio panel correct to be able to speak and hear over the speaker poses a threat in this airplane if not practiced. We were able to communicate with each other and ATC but it was challenging with all the noise and distractions.Captain identified as a priority flight with ZZZ Center and we began the initial descent over the mountains. I initially turned off the AUTOPILOT to pitch over and begin the procedure. Once we were established in a descent, I turned the AUTOPILOT back on and descended to FL190 with the high terrain in mind. We saw an aircraft below us on the TCAS and had to shallow the descent initially before we were cleared lower. Captain proceeded with completing the checklist and communicating with the Flight attendants, passengers, and dispatch. Descending through approximately 16,000 feet I noticed the CABIN ALTITUDE was in a normal range of around 7,000 feet and we took off the oxygen masks. We leveled off at 11000 in the vicinity of ZZZ2. Initially we were planning on diverting to ZZZ2 because we were so close, but Captain's experience and familiarity with ZZZ3. This led to the decision to divert and there was difficulty communicating with dispatch possibly due to our low altitude so we opted to landing in ZZZ3. The flight attendants and passengers were all briefed for the diversion to ZZZ3. I left the AUTOPILOT on and we flew the RNAV (GPS) Runway XY 29 approach and landing. All checklists were completed before ZZZZZ intersection and the landing was normal. CFR ( Aircraft Rescue & Firefighting) was there upon arrival.We were parked at the hard stand in ZZZ3 and the ramp personnel brought over the ramp to allow the passengers to vacate the aircraft. Operations were there to help while we figured out the plan of action for the passengers. Captain discussed the situation with the ChiefPilot, Dispatch, and Maintenance and I aided the flight attendants with passengers. I walked to the OUTFLOW VALVE and noted a mesh substance blocking the OUTFLOW VALVE from fully closing. Captain manually opened and closed the valve and I videoed the movement.
Synopsis: First Officer reported an emergency descent and diversion followed by a precautionary landing caused by Foreign Object Debris blocking the outflow valve from operation.

Narrative: At XA:55Z the master caution light, auto pilot disconnect aural warning and IRS annunciation light activated. The FO was the PF and immediately began to hand fly the aircraft. As PM, I verified the aircraft was stable and performed QRH XX.X IRS fault. After completing the required items and discussing all of the impact items, I sent ATC a CPDLC message as to our loss of navigation equipment and inability to remain in RVSM airspace due to the loss of the auto pilot. ATC instructed to remain at FL370 due to traffic. We called dispatch via SATCOM and relayed our current situation and reiterated our need to use the ILS RWY XX into ZZZ due to the loss of RNAV capabilities. After a conference call with Operations and Maintenance, we continued to ZZZ and landed uneventfully via the ILS RWY XX.We split the flying duties to avoid fatigue (30 minute intervals). ATC was given 2 hours to plan our arrival to the opposite runway, and they did an exemplary job. ZZZ1 was built in route 2 as our primary divert airport.
Synopsis: Captain reported total loss of the autoflight systems required close coordination with ATC for traffic separation and special flight handling due to loss of RVSM and RNAV capabilities.

Narrative: Climbing out of ZZZ in moderate rain and passing through about 18,000 feet, with the FO flying, we got an airspeed disagree and altitude disagree on our displays, a Master Caution for Engine, autopilot (B) kicked off, and VNAV disappeared all within a few seconds. We compared instruments and determined that the Standby and Captain's displays matched with airspeed at 280 and close to the same altitude still climbing. We transferred aircraft control and ran the airspeed unreliable checklist/altitude unreliable checklist. After reporting our difficulties with ATC, we leveled at FL250, to finish checklist and run checklist for EEC alternate mode. At that time the FO instruments showed an airspeed of 130 KIAS and 25,500 feet. It took a while to get through checklist, but we were able to get autopilot-A back. We talked about the bad weather at ZZZ and decided to continue to ZZZ1 due to VMC conditions there. On descent passing through 15,500 feet, FO instrumentation appeared to recover. Approach and landing were uneventful. Priority handling was requested to ensure ATC was aware of our indication problems.
Synopsis: B737-700 Captain reported a loss of reliable airspeed and altitude on the FO's side during climbout. The Captain's instruments were functioning properly, so the crew decided to continue to destination due to it having better weather conditions than their departure airport.

Narrative: The hydraulic reservoirs have a big red caution label. It reads, 'CAUTION DO NOT OVERFILL HYDRAULIC RESERVOIR. FILL TO APPROX. 2/3 BETWEEN REFILL(RFL) AND FULL (COCKPIT PANEL SHOULD READ 92% FULL) REFER AMM 12-12-00.'Below the caution label there is an ATTENTION label. It reads, 'ATTENTION Do Not Overfill the RESERVOIR. Overfill can Cause Hydraulic Fumes To Enter the Flight Deck and Passenger Cabin'Some years ago I had an air return when the cabin filled with acrid mist causing eyes to sting and some to choke. The flight attendants thought we were on fire! The Captain and I used goggles and oxygen to safely return. This event was caused by both hydraulic reservoirs being filled to capacity. I believe the cockpit panel read 107%. If I'm recall correctly this is the most that will register.Although I have not since had visible or detectable odor, I believe crew and passengers are breathing atomized hydraulic fluid whenever the reservoirs are over serviced. The leg noted in this report from ZZZ-ZZZ1, started with both reservoirs reading 100%. At shutdown they were at 92%. Where did the difference go in a three hour operation? The day before, my aircraft had 107% in system A and 92% in system B. I alerted Maintenance of the over service. The Technician proceeded to move System A to B. The result was both reservoirs at 100%.I have dealt with this issue individually before. I find a small portion of our technicians understand the significance. Sometimes I meet with great resistance.[Recommend] a notice for Aircrew to remind them of the placards and similar or more specific training for all our Maintenance Technicians and Maintenance Control.
Synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported loss of Hydraulic Reservoir quantity when reservoir is overfilled. Reporter theorized that hydraulic fluid is being atomized resulting in harmful cabin fumes and physiological symptoms.

Narrative: After intercepting the glideslope it was noted by both pilots the aircraft was not slowing down normally. Despite lowering the gear and deploying speedbrakes we were having a difficult time getting 10 knots below the next flap speed to continue to configure a variable tailwind was noted between 5 & 10 knots which helped explain what we were seeing. Continuing to investigate however both pilots thereafter realized we were abnormally low and the PF disconnected the AP and leveled off. Tower called with a low altitude alert shortly after that and we acknowledged it, configured normally and were stable by 500 feet AGL. Landing and roll out was normal. There were multiple approach NOTAMs that day and we miscalculated the effective times on the one stating the ILS XXL was unusable. We were an hour off and were arriving inside the last 30 minutes of the effective time. It turns out NAVAIDs maintenance was manipulating the glide slope signal at the time, causing the glide slope to appear lower.The ILS to XXL was OTS and NAVAIDs maintenance was transmitting a lower than normal glidepath. It would have been helpful if ILS status had been repeated on the ATIS, as it normally is, but it was not. During the low altitude call from tower they were even quick to add to the call that it 'was in the NOTAMs'. Further investigating with my prior position with FAA Flight Inspection it is still in their guidance that NAVAIDs maintenance is not supposed to transmit a localizer signal if they are going to manipulate the glide slope signal to avoid this hazardous, misleading, information. The localizer and glide slope both were transmitting, with a proper ID, at the time of the incident, we even crossed ZZZZZ at the appropriate altitude of 3,000 and showed on path. It was after that when the aircraft would no longer slow, as it was chasing a depressed glide path. In the end we missed the NOTAM but then multiple holes of the swiss cheese lined up; thankfully it was day VFR and we saw the solution with our own eyes in time. The other layers of protection normally there (ATIS, maintenance procedures) would have helped overcome our oversight.
Synopsis: A320 First Officer reported CFIT event during approach that was due to maintenance before performed on the glide slope equipment but not being announced on ATIS.

Narrative: Climbing through FL180 I engaged CMD (Command) A autopilot. When I pressed the button the airplane instantly had a loud banging noise, jolted very aggressively, nosed down, and started oscillating. It was almost to the point I thought I was going to accomplish upset recovery procedures. I was quickly able to level the airplane off and safely hand fly. We contacted Maintenance and unanimously agreed that the airplane was safe enough to continue to hand fly the plane for the duration of the flight. Maintenance asked if we tried autopilot B. The jolt and aircraft response was significant enough that we did not want to try arming the autopilot again. We safely hand flew the aircraft back to ZZZ1. In our debrief we discussed that for a split second we initially thought it was so severe that we were losing aircraft control. We were greatly startled and hands were shaking for a good 5-10 minutes after the event happened. We were scheduled to fly to ZZZ2 after the flight, arriving the next morning. We hit an emotional lull after the flight and we both determined we were not emotionally, nor physically, fit to continue our pairing. We called in fatigued and were given hotel rooms immediately.
Narrative_1: We were climbing through 180 out of ZZZZ. The CA (Captain) went to engage CMD (Command) A and the aircraft made a loud bang and had a violent nose down control input. It was so severe that we thought the flight attendant could have been injured. It was so bad for a moment I thought that we might have hit something mid-air. I was completely shaken up and so was the Captain. We refused to attempt to re-engage any autopilot. We were just about to divert but we had Dispatch run the numbers for us at non-RVSM altitude. We calculated 6.0 remf on this 700 so we opted to hand fly it. We worked in 30 minute shifts. The arrival was busy with many changes enroute. We were both shaking at the initial event and were completely calmed down enroute but we both started to feel drained after the adrenaline started to wear off. We were both obviously not fit for our next leg which was scheduled to arrive after midnight into ZZZ1. We both got a hotel at ZZZ even though I could have commuted home that evening, I was toast at that point and just went to bed.
Synopsis: B737-700 air carrier flight crew reported autopilot malfunction inflight.

Narrative: The situation happened on leg 1 on the second day of a 4 day sequence. We departed ZZZ for ZZZ1. As the First Officer I completed both the interior checklists and performed the exterior inspection. I noticed during the walk around that one of the red navigation lights was inoperative. When I got back to the flight deck I confirmed that it was previously written up and had been deferred in the AML. No other issues were noted during the preflight. The Captain was the Pilot Flying and I was the Pilot Monitoring. We departed ZZZ on Runway XXL. The takeoff and departure were uneventful. Weather was clear with unrestricted visibility. The climb was continued until we leveled off at FL340. At approximately XA:13Z, I started to smell something. It smelled like burning plastic. At the same time I noticed the smell the Captain asked 'Do you smell that?' Before replying we both saw smoke coming from the 'FL' button on the transponder located on the center console. At this time we both we executed the items for 'Smoke, Fire, or Fumes', donned our oxygen masks and established crew communication. At that point the Captain gave me both aircraft control and the radios so he could focus on the abnormal. While I monitored the autopilot the Captain continued with the 'Smoke, Fire, or Fumes' checklist. I confirmed with him that the proper switches were being turned off in accordance with the checklist. We noticed that the smoke and fumes were decreasing and did not need to run the 'Smoke or Fumes Removal' checklist. While the Captain attempted to locate the transponder circuit breaker to isolate the problem he noticed that the 'ELEC PANEL LIGHTS AFT/CENTER' circuit breaker located at the base of the front of the center pedestal was popped. We were confident the problem had been isolated and the Captain informed me that he was about 90% sure we were going to divert but he wanted to check with company to see if we were missing anything. We quickly realized that a step in the checklist had us turn off the internet and he would be unable to use the crew phone app to communicate with the Dispatcher. The Captain then took the radios back and attempted to get phone patch with the Center Controller. The controller was unable to give us the phone patch but was able to relay information. After communicating through the controller and using ACARS, it was decided that we would divert to ZZZ2. The Captain notified ATC and informed Center we wanted to divert to ZZZ2. The controller asked if we want ARFF (aircraft rescue firefighting) and the Captain said yes. The Captain then gave me back the radios so that he could run more checklists. The Captain continued with the checklists the controller asked what runway we wanted to land on. The Captain and I agreed that we wanted the longest runway due to the fact we would be landing overweight. I then requested Runway XXR. I got the airplane set up for an ILS approach to XXR. I started the descent into ZZZ2 while the Captain finished checklists and briefed the passengers and Flight Attendants. Then the Captain told me that he ran the 'Non Routine Landing Considerations' checklist and that the passengers and flight attendants had been briefed. He talked about the heavy weight landing and did a landing assessment. He asked if I had anything to add or could think of anything else we might need to do before landing. I told him that I think we had covered everything and I had nothing else to add. He then briefed the approach and took aircraft control. We completed both the descent and before landing checklists. After landing we cleared the runway at taxiway. I relayed to ARFF that unless they see anything abnormal from the outside our plan was to continue taxing to gate. They informed us that they did not see any unusual readings on thethermal scan. ARFF followed us to the gate. The Captain had me make a PA to the passengers that we would be taxing to gate and they would be accommodated after deplaning. The taxi and engine shutdown at the gate was uneventful. At the gate we were met by a member of the company Flight Office and he asked if we needed to be checked out at the hospital. We both said we did not require medical attention and that no more than a few seconds went by that we breathed in fumes before getting on oxygen. He then told us that he was pulling us off the remainder of the trip and could positive space home. The Captain completed writing up items in the AML. We then debriefed when it was just the two of us left on the airplane. I told him I thought maybe I could have done more to help. He said I did what he needed by flying the airplane and communicating with ATC while he ran the appropriate checklists and backed him up in his decision making process. We both agreed that we handled the situation in the way we are trained to handle abnormal at the school house. The cause was smoke coming from the 'FL' button on the transponder located on the center console.
Synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported a fumes event in the flight deck during cruise resulting in a diversion.

Narrative: We had been cleared the ILS 25L Approach while on the ANJLL Arrival and assigned 250 knots. At about 12,000 feet, we got a call from the cabin that the passenger we had called STAT-MD for earlier in the flight, was feeling worse. I asked the First Officer to call OPS for medical assistance to meet us at the gate. When he returned back to the ATC frequency, we were approaching 10,000 feet and hit wake turbulence sufficiently strong to cause the airplane to go into control wheel pitch and roll. I redirected the aircraft to KRAIN, re-engaged LNAV and VNAV, and asked ATC what we were following. I was told we were following nothing. This didn't make sense since we had just hit very strong wake turbulence. While established on final, ATC told us to slow to 170 knots. This surprised both of us, because the last speed assignment we recalled being given was 250 knots. 170 knots would be a huge speed reduction and we were still about 25 miles out. ATC then asked us if we were at 210 knots. We told the Controller no, and that we had been assigned 250 knots. He told us we had been instructed to slow to 210 knots back when we complained about the wake turbulence (approaching 10,000 feet). We were now overtaking a B777 ahead, so our approach clearance was canceled. We were given vectors for spacing and vectored back onto the localizer and then re-cleared the ILS 25L. Neither the First Officer no I recall hearing the 210 knot speed assignment. We had only heard 250 knots and read that back. The 210-knot speed assignment probably occurred about the time the Flight Attendant called us about the passenger feeling ill again and just as we hit the wake turbulence.
Narrative_1: A bunch of things happened at once which led to us missing a slower speed assignment. On the arrival to LAX, cleared the approach to 25L and told to maintain 250 knots. The flight attendant called up and said that our previous medical issue in the back (we had earlier talked to STAT-MD and gotten clearance to continue) was not feeling well again, and asked for paramedics. As the Pilot Monitoring, I called OPS at LAX, to arrange for emergency personnel - meaning I was off frequency. At the same time, we encountered wake turbulence, strong enough to knock the aircraft out of both LNAV/VNAV. The Captain, Pilot Flying, reported the wake turbulence to Approach, after getting the aircraft established on profile; apparently ATC told us to slow to 210 knots. Neither of us heard or read back the speed change. A few miles later Approach canceled our approach clearance and said we were too fast. We responded that we were assigned 250. They said no, we were given 210.
Synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported missing an ATC speed assignment on arrival into LAX when they were distracted by a wake turbulence encounter in trail of a heavy B777.

Narrative: Proceeding directly to ZZZZZ intersection on the ZZZZZ 2 RNAV arrival. Was cleared to descend via ZZZZZ 2 RNAV arrival on [Runway] XXR. Prior to ZZZZZ, at approximately FL220 during descent, noticed that the cabin altitude was at 8,300 feet and increasing. I called attention to the First Officer that we might be losing cabin pressurization.
