The Pressurization screen on ECAM was displayed and noticed that both the inlet and extract valve were fully closed but the safety valve had opened.Since we had already been cleared to descend via ZZZZZ arrival and had an altitude of 12,000 set in the MCP I decided to expedite the descent to see if I could control the rate of ascent in the cabin. At approximately FL180 it appeared that we could not control the rate of ascent in the cabin and that at its present rate the cabin would exceed 10,000 feet shortly. I then [advised] with ATC and requested 10,000 feet which was granted. I advised the Lead Flight Attendant that we were experiencing cabin pressurization problems but to expect a normal landing. As we leveled at 10,000 feet I monitored the cabin and noticed that it had climbed to 12,000 feet but stabilized. It took several minutes before the cabin normalized at our cruise altitude of 10,000 feet. I asked the First Officer to see if he could find an applicable checklist to run. During this time I maintained control of the aircraft and communicated with ATC. The First Officer advised that he was able to manually control the outflow valve and that the checklist recommended shallow descents thereafter. I continued to ask for delayed vectors from ATC just north of ZZZ as the First Officer and I reviewed the state of the aircraft and decided it was safe to proceed with the landing. I asked ATC for shallow descents on the arrival to [Runway] XXR into ZZZ. The landing and taxi in were uneventful.
Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported malfunctioning pressurization system on descent.

Narrative: On takeoff from ZZZ we felt a rough bumping at 100 knots. I was distracted by the cause of the roughness and didn't notice the exact speed we initiated the rejected takeoff at but felt it was at least 100 knots, but not above 120 knots. I determined the aircraft was unsafe to fly, called for the aircraft and rejected the takeoff. The First Officer (FO) alerted Tower as we were slowing to a stop. Once we were stopped, I made a Public Address telling the Passengers to remain seated. I was surprised to find that I didn't have a non-normal checklist for the situation and it felt odd as we had so much time to wait for the Fire Trucks to arrive. During that time I communicated with the Flight Attendants FAs to check on them and asked them to look for fire or smoke. They verified no indication of either and also confirmed that there were no injuries. Crew Fire Rescue pulled up and reported the two left main tires were blown and no fire, though they did hose them down briefly. The FO suggested starting the APU, which we did, and I was able to shut down the engine as the Fire Department was tending to the aircraft. We coordinated with Operations by radio and Dispatch by ACARS, and made Public Addresses to keep the Passengers informed and calm. The Passengers were then deplaned by air stairs and bused to the terminal.
Narrative_1: I had done the walk around and hadn't noticed anything unusual about the tires. The brake-wear pins looked fine. Taxi out was normal and even the initial takeoff roll was normal and didn't notice anything. After I heard the Pilot Monitoring call 80 knots, we felt a jolt and then the aircraft started shaking and getting progressively worse. We rejected the takeoff at about 100 knots with the appropriate flows and callouts. As we were slowing (I believe I saw 43 knots), I called Tower to let them know we were rejecting the takeoff. We got the plane stopped. The Captain called the Flight Attendants. The Tower let us know they actually heard the tires blow and that they were sending out the Fire Department and the Airport Operations. They then switched us over to another frequency to coordinate. We started the APU and shutdown the engines and then the Fire Department sprayed something on the aircraft left side. They used the word hot-spot. The people were then deplaned via air stairs and bused to the terminal, and we again confirmed that no one needed medical attention and were uninjured. After thinking about it, I know in training we had been told to wait until below 60 knots to call the Tower, but I'm not sure if that had changed to being at a complete stop or not before calling and could not find guidance in our manuals.
Synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported a rejected take off due to aircraft shuddering.

Narrative: Approximately 80 miles before top of descent MIA Center descended us to FL360 behind a widebody which was left at FL380. There was a quartering left tailwind of approximately 30-35 knots. We were given 280 knots assigned for spacing. The widebody entered the STAR from our left or the east. Our separation grew from less than 10 miles to just at or slightly over 10 miles with our descent and speed. At approximately 60-55 miles from the new top of descent from FL360 we experienced a rapid roll to the left of approximately 30 degrees. I turned off the autopilot and the plane then rolled right rapidly, about 20 seconds later. We [asked] for a speed of 250 [kts]. ATC gave the speed when we reported the wake turbulence. I continued to hand fly for a while until we could assure ourselves the wind dropped a bit and our separation had increased. I had the FO (First Officer) call the FAs (Flight Attendants) everything was secure and everyone was okay. We had them take their seats [and] the seatbelt sign was on at the time of the event. Upon leveling at 8,000 [feet] and turning westbound we had a second event even though the 777 was turning base ahead and we were just entering the downwind and crossing the bay. Approach had kept the 777 high and gave them relief on the restrictions as they descended. The next day, MIA Approach cleared us to 8,000 [feet] behind an aircraft ahead with tight spacing. We did get a slight roll left then right but I immediately slowed to 230 and had the FO tell MIA we were slowing. This time the aircraft ahead was not kept high and so I hand flew slightly above VNAV path to assure at FL230 we would not have wake turbulence. Later [that day] Tower cleared us to takeoff before [another air carrier aircraft] had rotated. After I lined the jet up on the centerline and after takeoff clearance, we waited 8-10 seconds for [the other air carrier aircraft] to rotate. We then took off. We were given heading 105 [on departure, and the other air carrier was given heading 120]. The aircraft behind us was given 090. We encountered wake turbulence behind [the other air carrier aircraft] due to crosswinds. MIA has minimized separation and rushed operations such that it is my experience safety is impacted.First, the next time MIA says keep it rolling and cleared to takeoff, I will ask to exit when an aircraft is still not near rotating. Second, MIA needs to review the operating practices in play. Lack of separation at FL380, being placed below and behind a heavy with a quartering tailwind, 10+ miles separation was not enough with 30+ knot tailwind. Change the practice of [descending] a non-heavy behind and below a heavy to descending the heavy below the following aircraft.
Synopsis: B737 Captain reported encountering wake turbulence on descent into MIA.

Narrative: First Officer flying through FL200 on way to FL270, in IFR conditions. First Officer and Captain's airspeed indicators [were] unreliable. Standby airspeed indicator correct. Captain's airspeed indicator came back, but First Officer's out for 5 minutes and EEC (Electronic Engine Control) Systems went to Standby. QRC and QRH procedures accomplished as well as followup procedures. Anti-icing systems working, Engine and wing heat on. Stayed as much out of weather, ZZZ closed, ZZZ1 still in VFR weather and location of heavy maintenance for the B-737. Briefed flight attendants and passengers. Captain flew to ZZZ1, safety vehicles checked out aircraft.Good crew coordination of verification of the unreliable airspeed indicators.Don't fly into clouds with icing conditions. May have been multiple problems that happened at the same time. EEC Systems went to standby while in heavy thick clouds, on climb out, through the freezing level.
Synopsis: Captain reported diverting after airspeed indications became unreliable in IMC conditions and the destination airport closed.

Narrative: Aircraft was dispatched with an inoperative Pack #2 due to a regulator fault and [the flight] was in full compliance with the MEL at departure. Flight was completely full in the cabin. Due to Pack #2 being inoperative it was difficult to cool the main cabin temp using only Pack #1. Using only Pack #1 at FL370 we were able to maintain 72 degrees in the cabin using max cold and high flow. Approximately 200 nm west of ZZZ at FL370 we received an ECAM AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT. ATC was notified and [priority handling was requested]. Upon checking the pressurization and bleed air page, it appeared that Pack #1 was overheating showing an output temperature in amber yet we never received a Pack 1 OVHT ECAM. The cabin altitude was still under control. A descent to 10,000 ft. was initiated without exceeding the cabin altitude before we complied with the ECAM to turn off Pack #1 leaving us unpressurized. Contact was made with Dispatch and Maintenance Control to discuss the situation resulting in a diversion to ZZZ.
Narrative_1: Approximately 240 nm from ZZZ, at a cruise altitude of FL350 and while in communication with Center, an ECAM aural and Master Caution sounded for AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT. The CA (Captain) said he noted a momentary amber overheat temp in Pack 1, but it did not trigger the PACK 1 OVHT caution. I (Pilot Monitoring) did not see this indication that had subsequently returned to a green inlet temperature. Pack 2 was previously secured and turned off per the MEL deferral on our 2nd release. Pack 1 showed a fault light. The AIR PACK 1+2 FAULT ECAM directed us to secure Pack 1, descend to 10,000 ft. MSL or MEA and then turn on the RAM Air when the pressure differential was less than 1.0. Even though Pack 1 had a fault light in the overhead panel, it appeared to be partially functioning, the cabin pressure holding and the cabin altimeter only increasing at a very slight rate. A flight crew decision was made to begin an immediate normal descent to 10,000 ft. without the use of oxygen while closely monitoring the pressurization page to ascertain the true nature of the Pack 1 malfunction. The CA directed me to assume pilot flying duties and ATC responsibilities while he coordinated with Operations, Dispatch, flight attendants and the passengers. We began a coordinated 1500-2000 fpm rate of descent via two ATC-assigned step down altitudes of FL300 and FL200 before ultimately reaching 10,000 ft. The aircraft was lowered in a steady continual descent with no pauses which I believe helped our situation. Cabin pressure held steady around 8,000 ft. during the normal descent. Upon reaching 10,000 ft., Pack 1 was secured, differential pressure reached less than 1.0, RAM AIR was selected on and the cabin altimeter climbed from approximately 8,000 to 10,000 ft. as expected. We completed all remaining ECAM items until the screens were normal. The rate of fuel burn at 10,000 ft. MSL made reaching our initial destination of ZZZ1 impossible, and it was decided that ZZZ was a suitable diversion while 200nm away and with 11,600 pounds of fuel aboard along with the best Maintenance, aircraft and passenger accommodation options. We informed ATC, Dispatch, Operations, and proceeded accordingly. We switched to the next Center and the Captain [requested priority handling] and returned to the pilot flying role while we coordinated an uneventful arrival via the ZZZZZ to Visual XX approach at ZZZ and ultimately parking at gate XY. We were then met by the ZZZ Chief Pilot at the gate and proceeded to fill out a risk mitigation form following the event. We then accepted a new aircraft and release at gate XZ and ultimately brought the same passengers to ZZZ1 two hours later than originally planned.In totality, I felt the event was handled safely and professionally. The CRM skills taught and utilized allowed both the CA and First Officer to properly divide duties while ensuring sufficient cross checks and communication. At no time did I feel rushed or stressed. I believe the deliberate delay in securing the faulty Pack 1 that appeared to be functioning along with the continual scanning of the pressurization page allowed us to avoid an unnecessary priority descent, use of pilot oxygen, or the deployment of passenger oxygen that might have accompanied a rapid depressurization. All in all, I felt the CA was composed and handled the event in line with Company desires. While I regret the delay the passengers experienced, I believe we handled the event in a safe and caring manner.
Synopsis: Air Carrier Pilot Crew reported departing with one air cycle machine inoperative and during cruise flight the other air cycle machine indicated a fault condition necessitating a diversion.

Narrative: Clean configuration. Airspeed 280 knots. Autopilot on. IMC conditions. Being radar vectored around significant squall line. Anti-ice on. Climbing to cruise altitude and passing altitude about 20,000 feet when my airspeed indicator suddenly went erratic with plus or minus several (at 30 knots greater and less than commanded) indications. Airspeed indicator never reached stick shaker or over-speed warnings limits. Immediately took control of aircraft from autopilot and crosschecked the primary flight display with the Captain and standby indicator. Recommended Captain become pilot flying as his indications were consistent with standby indicator and airspeed indicator was not as erratic as mine (more consistent with turbulent air flying in the 737). After transfer of aircraft control to Captain, I completed the Quick Reference checklist (QRC) and QRH for unreliable airspeed indicator. When double checking the pitot heat was on I notice both Engines Electronic Control (EEC) were in soft alternate mode. During the entire time the aircraft was in IMC the airspeed indicator was erratic and EEC remained in soft alternate. A few minutes later, at level off at cruising altitude (low 20,000s) and out of IMC the airspeed indicator returned to normal along with EEC. Remained clear of clouds and landed uneventfully at ZZZ1. We did not return to ZZZ after [Notifying ATC] because we were more than half way and the squall line was over ZZZ.Unknown as to why airspeed indicator was unreliable and erratic in IMC turbulent air and then returned to normal when clear of clouds. Also did not know why EEC went to soft alternate and then returned to normal.
Synopsis: First Officer reported air data related system failures due to suspected inflight icing conditions which diminished after leaving IMC.

Narrative: We received a request to go direct to ZZZZZ. Dispatch had filed us on a southerly track to avoid significant weather on the H-track. The only options given were to accept or standby. We were not going to accept the re-route so we hit standby. The standby was accepted. We sent a message that we could climb instead of a re-route and ATC gave us a climb.Sometime later, the re-route request showed up again but this time the only option we were given was to accept. We ignored the request but that left the ATC icon up on the Upper DU [Display Unit] (so future ATC alerts may not be noticed).This annoyed me so after crossing ZZZZZ1 we noted that accepting the persistent direct routing request would only bypass our next waypoint by about 10 NM. I accepted the ATC routing but waited for a reply from ATC before proceeding. ATC responded with ROGER. So, we went direct ZZZZZ per the clearance. ATC then sent a message asking us to confirm request. We never sent any request so we followed up with a direct message stating we were accepting the previous direct routing from ATC. Shortly thereafter we asked to call ZZZ Center.I talked with the controller and explained the situation. He closed it out on his end with no action but quality control will still review.With CPDLC, ATC cannot ask a question but only provide one answer (accept). That leaves us with an open request.
Narrative_1: There should be a CPDLC option to accept, reject, or standby. Not just accept or standby. If you don't accept, the message stays open, and the ATC alert never extinguishes. This could cause a future message to be missed.
Synopsis: B737-800 air carrier flight crew reported accepting a reroute clearance on CPDLC that they had initially put on standby.

Narrative: The Captain was flying and after takeoff the white FMC message dealing with the autothrottle appeared and the Pilot Flying noticed an amber EGT exceedance. The autothrottles and VNAV were inoperative at that point after takeoff. The TAT probe was indicating a higher than normal temperature which we determined to be the root cause of all the problems. We consulted with the QRH and Dispatch and all agreed to air return to ZZZ without any further issues.
Narrative_1: Just after takeoff the aircraft experienced a loss of data from the TAT probe (repeat gripe). This initially manifested itself as an autothrottle limit error and a rapid increase in #1 EGT (yellow backfill on gage but no other indications) and loss of VNAV and related FMC functions. We continued to climb to 16,000 feet MSL and informed ATC that we may need to return to ZZZ. I passed aircraft control to the FO and initiated radio contact with Dispatch. After initial contact, radio communications with Dispatch were lost, but Dispatch replied via ACARS that they agreed a return to ZZZ was prudent. Release was amended. ATC, cabin crew and passengers were informed; no emergency was declared. The aircraft returned to ZZZ without incident.TAT failure is a high workload event similar to unreliable airspeed. The number of items that rely on the TAT is huge, and once the event occurs there is (a) no real clue as to what the causal factor is, (b) no QRH guidance for the NN, and (c) a plethora of conflicting data and flight deck indications. Thought should be given to educating our Pilot group to the risks and indications associated with TAT failure.
Synopsis: Flight Crew reported an air turn back after the TAT probe failed, causing the auto throttle to malfunction.

Narrative: Previous flight had reported engine fluctuations on takeoff and climbout. Maintenance took a look at the plane and Ops checked it good. On our takeoff, once takeoff thrust was set we began a normal reduced thrust takeoff with an EPR (Engine Pressure Ratio) setting of about 1.41. Once above 80 knots the Captain called out that the EGT and N1 were fluctuating and took control of the aircraft and performed the Reject. The auto brakes engaged at Max. We made the required callouts, cleared the runway and performed the QRC. We did receive HOT Brakes due to the reject and allowed them to cool before returning to the gate.
Narrative_1: Advancing power was normal with Flex FMA (Flight Mode Annunciator) displayed and EPR (Engine Pressure Ratio) thrust set prior to 80 kts. As the aircraft accelerated EPR indication on eng 1 began to fluctuate. As takoff roll continued EPR EGT and N1 began fluctuations with EPR going above yellow tick mark and almost as low as 1.3 EPR (TO EPR was 1.43). Reject was initiated at approximately 110 kts and we noticed ATC and cabin and cleared the runway to run the rejected to checklist. After allowing the brakes to cool we returned to the terminal.
Synopsis: A320 flight crew reported a rejected takeoff after engine fluctuations reoccurred during takeoff roll and returned to the gate.

Narrative: We were operating our flight ZZZ to ZZZ1. This flight operates at close to if not at its max weight where maximum performance from the aircraft and crew are required due to the short runways. Headwind operations, or more importantly, absence of any tailwinds, should be the main concern of ATC and pilots when utilizing this airport when such performance is required.In the hours prior to this flight ZZZ was running a south operation, departing RWY XX, as one would expect with a reasonable headwind (180/7kts). Approximately 20 minutes before departure, they switched to a north operation, now departing RWY XY. This change seemed illogical as it now was using a runway that had a 7 knot tailwind for takeoff. With this change our flight was unable to depart as we were too heavy due to a tailwind weight penalty of 9,030 lbs from our runway limit.I asked ZZZ Ground/Tower Control why they had changed to a north operation. The answer we received was that arriving aircraft on the XXXXX Visual were encountering a tailwind at altitude and therefore the change. This puzzled me. Is this an official procedure that the FAA ATC has at ZZZ or shouldn't runway selection for takeoff and landing be based on surface winds?We had no choice but to wait for an opening for RWY XX, which caused a significant delay to our companies reliability operation, not to mention putting other aircraft in an awkward position of either compromising safety margins or accepting lengthy delays. Switching runways around based on winds at altitude rather than safety of landing and departing on short runways with tailwinds, puts the pilots in the position as the last line of defense for safety. Just FYI, we also only had one reverser. Although RTO does not include the reversers in its stopping distance calculations, it was still a consideration to us.ATC changing runways from a headwind to a strong tailwind. Putting pilots in a less optimal position to operate their aircraft.The additional work load and max performance requirements when utilizing a short runway with a tailwind should be avoided as much as possible especially at ZZZ. Every foot of runway concrete is paramount to operating safely at this airport. Therefore every knot of tailwind compromises that safety margin.
Synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported ATC changed the departure runway creating a unacceptable tailwind takeoff condition. ATC explained the switch was to accommodate the aircraft on the STAR encountering a tailwind.

Narrative: TCAS RA. On departure from ZZZ on Runway XX, we were given left turn to 149, climb 6,000 feet. In the turn, ATC said maintain 4,000 feet for traffic at 10 o'clock at 4,500 feet. As I went wings level, I could see the helicopter at 10 o'clock within a half mile of our current position. About 3,500 feet, we got a TA. I slowed my vertical speed as I approached 4,000 feet but upon capture, we got a RA telling us to 'monitor vertical speed.' The red line for the RA was on the horizon so I pitched just below the horizon. The First Officer informed ATC of the RA and that we were in a descent. ATC responded saying we were below the MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude) and to get back to 4,000 feet when able. At 3,600 feet, we were clear of conflict and climbed back to 4,000 feet. We continued the departure as normal. There wasn't much room for vectoring because of the mountains surrounding the valley. I believe the helicopter was VFR because of their altitude. ATC could have possibly kept us on the ground longer or given a delayed turn until helicopter was no longer a conflict.
Narrative_1: TCAS RA on departure from ZZZ. Initially received climb via the ZZZZZ4 SID except maintain 5,000 feet. Prior to takeoff received amended clearance of left turn 149 climb 4,000 feet. ATC called traffic in the turn and we were looking. Nearing completion of turn and climb received TA followed by RA target 700 feet to 500 feet above and got the 'monitor vertical speed' we descended and made the standard callouts to ATC. At 3,700 feet ATC warned of low altitude and below MVA (Minimum Vectoring Altitude). We were VMC and received the 'clear conflict' and climbed back to 4000 feet and continued the flight uneventfully.I think ATC knew about this target prior to takeoff and that's why they amended the clearance. I believe their hands were tied with a vector because of rising terrain and altitude separation due to Minimum Vectoring Altitude. We followed our training and everything worked out, would have been worse in IMC. Captain (Pilot Flying) says he saw helicopter but I couldn't see from First Officer seat in left turn.
Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported they responded to a TCAS/RA for a VFR helicopter by descending then were advised by ATC they were flying below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.

Narrative: We were flying ZZZ1 to ZZZ, a XA00 report in ZZZ1. It was the First Officer's (FO) initial trip back from a 10-month furlough. We were on the ZZZZZ RNAV arrival from the northeast. I was the PF. ZZZ was landing north. ZZZ airport had an overcast layer obscuring the airport. At the appropriate time, I briefed the ILS XXR approach. We set up the FMS and tuned/identified the NAV radios for XXR, the normal approach for this arrival. When we checked in with ZZZ Approach, we were advised to expect the ILS XXL. I briefed the approach and we tuned/identified the NAV radios. We were being vectored to intercept the localizer. It looked like we overshot the localizer on the NAV display, so I turned to intercept. ATC advised us, 'It looks like you are lining up for the wrong runway,' and turned us off of the approach. There were no conflicts with any other aircraft. They then told us to expect the ILS XXR. We flew that approach successfully to a landing. While we were setting up for the XXR approach, we discovered we never set up the FMS for the ILS to XXL. [I believe the cause was] early sign-in. Overcast skies obscuring airport. [It was also the] FO's first trip after furlough. [I suggest] verification that both the NAV radios are tuned and identified and the FMS is set for the proper runway/approach.
Narrative_1: Planned and briefed approach for ILS Runway XXR and was given ILS Runway XXL. The CA (Captain) set up and briefed new approach. I verified the frequencies and inbound course but neither of us set the new approach into the FMS. Was getting vectors to the ILS XXL [and] we had the correct ID for the ILS. When the CA looked at the ND and saw himself flying through the course for what was ILS XXR, the wrong approach, he corrected the heading to go back to intercept the course on the ND. The Controller said you are turning to line up for wrong approach and told us to go around.I have not flown since [last year]. I also do not have much experience in the aircraft. Was first flight since furlough. [I plan on] getting more flying in and becoming more comfortable in the aircraft, getting back into the rhythm of the flights.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported a clearance deviation due to automation mismanagement and CRM issues.

Narrative: During the takeoff roll, the FA's (Flight Attendant's) dinged us twice. We continued the takeoff. Upon rotation they dinged us four times, twice before clean-up altitude. After reaching clean-up altitude I called the cabin and the FA's reported passengers seeing flames and sparks coming from the right engine, as well as hearing popping noises. The FA's reported the entire cabin lit up brightly, but that there was no smoke in the cabin. We informed ATC that we had a #2 engine fire, were returning for landing, and requested fire truck assistance. We had no cockpit indications of a fire or malfunction. Both engines were producing symmetric power and operating normally, according to our gauges. Upon landing and shutting down the engines on Taxiway XX, Fire Rescue took temperature readings and reported them in the normal range. We were towed to the gate.
Narrative_1: Incident for [the] flight [from] ZZZ to ZZZ1. I was the pilot flying. During the takeoff roll with takeoff power set, the flight attendants called the flight deck with two dings. We elected to continue to takeoff. Right at rotation speed, the flight attendants called the flight deck again, but this time with four dings. We continued the takeoff and climbing through 1000 ft., the Captain transferred the radios over to me and she started coordinating with a Flight Attendant.Flight attendants were reporting that the passengers on the right side were saying that the engine was on fire and they heard a popping noise and at the same time the flight attendants said they noticed that the cabin lit up momentarily. However, there was no smoke in the cabin, all engine indications were normal, and none of the Fire Handle Warning lights were lit. The Captain [requested priority handling] and told Tower that our #2 engine was on fire and that we needed to return for an immediate landing and requested the fire trucks. Tower cleared us for Runway XXR, I continued to climb to 3000 ft. at 210 kt. and started my turn for a left downwind for Runway XXR. On downwind, Tower cleared us for the visual and cleared to land XXR. A flaps 30 landing was conducted and we taxied off the runway on Taxiway XX where we shut the engines down. The Fire Crew inspected the engine and stated that everything seemed normal and that their heat sensors also indicated normal readings. After a short time, we were towed back to the gate.
Synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported an engine fire that was noticed by the passengers during takeoff and performed an air turnback.

Narrative: Enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1. Aircraft had MEL for #2 engine generator. Dispatched with APU powering #2 transfer bus. At 35,000 ft. over ZZZ2, APU failed and did automatic shutdown. We diverted to ZZZ2 due to only one AC power source remaining. Uneventful approach and landing. Multiple, unforeseen failures caused the event.
Narrative_1: Right generator was MEL'd after gate return at ZZZ. MEL required APU to be operated continuously on the ZZZ - ZZZ1 leg. During cruise FL350 the APU failed, leaving us with a single generator. Accomplished QRH items for 'APU low oil pressure' and decided to divert to ZZZ2 due to the requirement to land at [the] 'nearest suitable airport' from MEL and QRH. [Requested priority handling] in the descent due to [the] nature of [the] malfunction and overweight landing. Landed uneventfully in ZZZ2 6,000 lb. overweight. At ZZZ2 we deplaned passengers, and after a six-hour delay, the APU was repaired and overweight inspection [was] completed. Completed flight to ZZZ1 uneventfully.
Synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported an APU failure inflight combined with an MEL'd engine generator resulted in single-generator operations, which led to a diversion to the nearest suitable airport.

Narrative: During our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, Aircraft X, a flight attendant seated near the 4L lavatory reported that about 3 minutes after take off he began to notice a urine smell coming from the 4L lav. The smell began to dissipate about 15 minutes later. We suspected a contributing factor could be the high deck angle associated with the take off. This has been a continuing write up for a few weeks. Unfortunately maintenance personnel have been unable to identify and fix the exact cause. Hopefully this report will help bring together the appropriate resources to fix this problem. Our passengers and flight attendants will appreciate it.
Synopsis: B777 Captain reported urine odor emanating from the aft lavatory during initial climb which lasted for approximately 15 minutes.

Narrative: Eighty miles southeast of ZZZ, while we we're deviating around thunderstorms, we received a call from the B Flight Attendant that we had a strong electrical smell in the aft galley. A few seconds later another call from the flight attendant said the cabin now has the strong odor and a passenger said there is a haze. We notified ATC and were cleared direct to ZZZ. We had a thunderstorm between us and the field, so this required some deviations. We elected not to don the mask because we didn't have smoke or odor in the cockpit. We briefly talked about it and didn't want the added condition. We also decided that we would don the mask at first sign of smell or smoke. Things obviously were very busy because we made it from 36,000 [feet] to the Runway in 18 minutes. By the time we were pointed in the right direction we started to run the Smoke Fire Fumes Checklist but never finished it. We were very tired from the multiple reroutes, PM trip to an AM, back to a PM. I elected not to finish the checklist because I wanted all eyes up so we could get the aircraft on the ground safely. On approach we also had a bird strike, which was a non-event and we landed 10,500 pounds overweight, also a non-event. After we cleared the runway we had the fire trucks shoot the brakes, and after we ran the brake cooling numbers found that we could taxi to the gate.
Narrative_1: At roughly XX:20 CT and at FL 360, while diverting around thunderstorms and turbulence approximately 80 miles southeast of ZZZ, we were alerted by the B-Flight Attendant of a strong electrical odor in the aft galley. Moments later we were notified that it had spread through the cabin with haze reported by a Passenger. Considering the seriousness of the issue and our #1 priority of Safety, we immediately [requested priority handling] with ATC and received direct ZZZ. The Captain turned off the galley power and advised me to alert Dispatch while he flew and communicated with ATC. We continued to get updates from the Flight Attendants/Dispatch/ATC and kept them in the loop of our emergency diversion into ZZZ. The Captain continued to deviate around thunderstorms and turbulence while I adjusted the route in the FMC, loaded the approach and got weather and landing information. We quickly discussed our arrival with overweight landing, minimum braking, and plan for fire trucks to meet us. We ran the Descent/Arrival Checklists and just started the Smoke/Fire/Fumes Checklist when, as we were now very near the airport, the Captain requested we stop the checklist as he needed me heads up with him and our focus to get the aircraft quickly on the ground. We got the airport in sight, configured, completed the Before Landing Checklist and had a bird strike on approach with a very smooth touchdown and roll out to the end of [runway] XXR. We cleared the runway, advised the Passengers to remain seated and the fire trucks evaluated us with an all clear. We ran a brake cooling with no limitations, so we taxied to the gate with the fire trucks following us. There were no damages to the aircraft or injuries to the Crew or Passengers.The short 15 minutes from first notification to landing in ZZZ was filled with the threats of task loading, additive conditions and Crew factors. It was the last leg of a four-day trip and we were both fatigued from many trip changes/delays, and I was on an FDP extension leaving ZZZ1 and two prior trip extensions. We had additive conditions of thunderstorms and turbulence to deviate around, both en route and on descent while dealing with the emergency. We had task loading with the very short period of time to assess/handle the situation/navigate/communicate/run checklists etc., and get the aircraft on the ground in minimum time.
Synopsis: B737-700 Captain reported a fume event during cruise resulted in a diversion.

Narrative: Complete right side brake failure upon landing in ZZZ. Brake line became detached. Failure of some sort after brakes had just been replaced on #3 and #4. Surprised that entire right side brakes failed. One brake line detaching should not have resulted in complete right side failure.
Synopsis: Air Carrier Flight Crew reported brake failure on landing.

Narrative: On climb out from ZZZ, we noticed engine oil quantity on engine #2 had gone to 0. We notified ATC and returned to ZZZ. All other indications were normal. The landing was uneventful and we taxied to the gate.
Synopsis: First Officer reported loss of #2 engine oil quantity caused them to make an air turn back to a precautionary landing.

Narrative: After a 5 hour maintenance delay to change a flat tire, we departed for ZZZ1. We executed a normal, flex, CONF1 takeoff from [Runway] XXL in VFR weather with light winds and a light aircraft. I was PF (Pilot Flying) and was hand-flying the departure. At approximately 1,000 AGL I heard several loud bangs from the right side of the aircraft. My first thought was bird strike but the CA (Captain) called out 'engine failure.' I called out 'my aircraft' and we determined there was a problem with the #2 engine. I don't recall any ECAMs but I do recall seeing the #2 EGT was high. I was continuing to hand-fly and CA suggested we reduce thrust to idle on the #2 engine. I agreed and we reduced the thrust and the surging and vibration ceased and the engine parameters went into the green. CA suggested an immediate return to the departure field and [advised] ATC and coordinated a downwind turn and level-off. I engaged the autopilot and prepared for a return to runway XXL with an ILS approach. CA set the FMGC up for the approach and I flew the downwind and base. CA advised the FAs (Flight Attendants) to prepare for a precautionary landing and gave a short PA as well. ATC vectored us to the ILS and cleared us for a visual approach once I had the field in sight. I executed a normal landing on XXL and we taxied clear on taxiway 1 and had the fire department inspect the aircraft. CA made several PAs instructing the passengers to remain seated and that the situation was under control. I noticed the #2 EGT was increasing and approaching the upper limit and we shut the engine down as the fire department was inspecting the engine. CA coordinated with operations a return gate and once the fire department was done and deemed the aircraft safe to taxi we returned to gate. The passengers deplaned normally. CA then called Dispatch to advise them of our return.We both determined the safest course of action was to get the aircraft back on the ground as soon as possible. This was made easier with good weather, no air traffic, and being below max. landing weight. We were only in the air ten minutes and this didn't give us time to do much troubleshooting or communication with anyone except ATC and the flight attendants. I was 100% busy flying the aircraft the entire time, but due to excellent ATC and constant communication with the Captain/PM, I felt in the yellow most of the time and in the green for the final approach and landing. I only felt I was 'in the red' for the few seconds between when the engine began surging until the CA said 'engine failure.' That statement immediately told me what was happening and I snapped into our trained procedures. We continued to discuss the plan and agreed that a quick return to the field was best throughout the short flight. Since the engine seemed stable at idle and we had no ECAMs we decided not to complicate things by troubleshooting but rather execute a quick precautionary landing. I feel our combined experience in the Airbus as well as constant precise communication and exchange of ideas led to the successful outcome. We backed each other up, trapped errors, and executed our plan efficiently and effectively. I don't see this event being preventable, but I think our training and emphasis on SOP and communication made for a good outcome.
Narrative_1: On takeoff, at approximately 1,000 feet AGL #2 engine compressor stalling with high EGT. We brought the thrust lever to idle and stalling stopped. We [notified] ATC and returned to field. Firefighters inspected the airplane and it appeared normal. Taxied to the gate.
Synopsis: Flight Crew reported compressor stall required an air turn back and a precautionary landing.

Narrative: On the RNAV Stadium Visual to runway 29 we were vectored behind an Airbus 321 on the ILS to 22R. We joined the visual at GIMEE with the airport and the [A321] in sight. We had been cleared to land prior to crossing GIMEE. Tower reported winds calm, ATIS had winds 200/6. Prior to SLIMR we were configured and slowing to approach speed. At approximately 1,500 ft AGL I called for the landing check and called to the FO that [the A321] appeared to be crossing the numbers and spacing looked good. Continued in LVAV/VNAV till the autopilot rolled us out on final at about 1,000 ft AGL. At this point PAPI showed slightly high and corrected to visual glide path. A rapid right roll was encountered just prior to touchdown causing contact of the right main. This slowed the roll but aircraft was still rolling right. Immediate left aileron was applied along with deployment of the auto speed brakes quickly caused the left main to touch down. Roll out was normal from this point. Wing drop was so rapid that I thought the right gear leg had collapsed. The event occurred so quickly that there was not even time to consider a go-around. The application of power and lifting off again would likely only have exacerbated this situation placing us at a bank angle at low speed with an at the time unknown problem. During debrief we determined that the event occurred just prior to the intersection with Runway 22R and was likely a wake turbulence event. An ACARS generated report showed a max bank angle of 6.9 degrees with a predicted wing tip strike at a bank angle of 7.5 degrees. The FO inspected the aircraft for possible damage, none was found. The event was reported to Tower, but they did not seem concerned. I contacted Clearance Delivery to get more information on the preceding aircraft. CD took more interest and sounded like it would be reported.
Synopsis: B737NG Captain reported encountering wake turbulence shortly before touchdown on Runway 29 at EWR from an A321 on short final to Runway 22R.

Narrative: Suspected GPS jamming between LOGMU and ROKUB on T561 XA:17Z-XB:03Z. EICAS alert for NAV UNABLE RNP. Followed checklist and used radio/IRS updating during the event. Was able to resume normal GPS ops for remainder of flight. Most likely some crazy militants in the area. Perhaps pay the big bucks and fly over Siberia on this route. Most likely less GPS jamming and probably more efficient for flight planning. Although I appreciate the longer rest opportunities on these double crewed flights.
Synopsis: An air carrier Captain reported GPS jamming.

Narrative: On approach in to ZZZ, we were cleared direct ZZZZZ intersection and to descend to 3,000 feet There was a thunderstorm cell between ZZZZZ and ZZZZZ1 (Final Approach Fix) on the approach to Runway XXR to ZZZ. We asked ZZZ TRACON (Approach Control) for direct ZZZZZ1 to avoid the thunderstorm cell. We were anticipating a visual approach to Runway XXR because the most recent ATIS (weather report) was reporting only Few and Scattered clouds at the airport with adequate visibility for a visual approach. The TRACON Controller asked if we would be able to 'get the airport?'My First Officer and I were slightly confused by his phraseology and tried to discuss what the Controller meant. At that time, we were within a few miles from ZZZZZ and just about to level off at 3,000 feet. The Autopilot Mode Control panel was in Vertical Speed (Altitude Acquire) and LNAV to ZZZZZ. I was anticipating going to ZZZZZ1 and was ready to change the altitude to 2,800 feet in MCP for the autopilot. We were then cleared on a 160 degree heading to join the final approach course of 128, and cleared for the approach. I didn't hear the Controller say 'maintain 3,000 feet until established.' I selected VOR/LOC and dialed 2,800 feet into the autopilot Mode Control Panel. Because we were in a descent and in Altitude Acquire, the autopilot continued to descend towards 2,800 feet.My First Officer said we were supposed to maintain 3,000 feet. I had missed that part of the clearance so I dialed 3,000 feet into the Mode Control Panel, but by that point the aircraft had descended below 3,000 feet and was continuing to descend and would not ever capture 3,000 feet. I was also trying to slow the aircraft and get it to capture the localizer. Seeing that we weren't going to level off, I tried to use Vertical Speed to make the aircraft climb back to 3,000 feet, but it was continuing to descend. Our descent was exacerbated by the fact that I still had the speedbrakes deployed almost to the flight [descent]. ZZZ TRACON (Approach Control) said he he had a low altitude alert and his MVA [Min Vector Altitude] was 2,800 feet. We were now at about 2,300 feet. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles, started a climb and we decided to go missed approach. I finally stowed the speedbrakes, climbed to our clearance altitude and we then got re-vectored by ZZZ TRACON for another approach to Runway XXR and landed safely.
Narrative_1: We were being vectored around some weather coming into ZZZ and were given a descent to 3,000 feet and direct ZZZZZ outside of ZZZZZ1 on the ILS XXX. There was some confusion as ATC asked if we would be able to get the airport. I wasn't sure if he meant visually or altitude wise. After a pause, as I pondered his meaning, I responded that we were IMC. At the time, I didn't think we were high, so I assumed he meant visually. Just a couple miles outside of ZZZZZ, Captain asked for a turn to ZZZZZ1. I paused because I was anticipating a vector shortly to intercept the final approach course. I then asked ATC for the turn inbound, and ATC responded that he was just about to give us a vector and then provided the clearance. We were given a 160 heading to join and maintain 3,000 feet until established and cleared for the ILS to [Runway] XXR. This extra communication ultimately caused a delay in getting turned in. Because it all got really busy, I didn't see that Captain dialed in 2,800 feet. So, I don't think it acquired 3,000 feet and was now descending below it. Then I think 3,000 feet was reset into the MCP and yet the aircraft was still descending. All of this was happening while I was replying to ATC and I didn't realize what happened until after we talked about it later. We triggered a low altitude alert, and ATC informed us that we were to maintain 3,000 feet until established. I responded that we were correcting. Captain was climbing back up to 3,000 feet and we were slightly south of the localizer. I figured by the time we got back to 3,000 feet, we would then be high for the approach and not being established on the localizer, I said we should go-around. Captain agreed, and we did. This whole thing took me out of the Green, made me feel rushed and got behind in my responsibilities. A go-around was the best decision.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported a CFIT event during approach resulting in a go-around. A communications breakdown between flight crew and ATC was cited as a contributing factor.

Narrative: Primarily, en route ATC was task saturated the entire day working multiple frequencies while providing speed and vector control, versus sequencing traffic on the arrivals. On the leg from ZZZ to ZZZ1, we were handed off to ZZZ near the waypoint ZZZZZ. After multiple failed attempts to reach ATC, we returned to the previous frequency to try an alternate frequency. This frequency was very busy as ATC was working multiple frequencies and also providing multiple aircraft with vectors and speed control. We were given 10 degrees left. ATC told us to expect direct ZZZZZ1. As we approached ZZZZZ2, we tried multiple times to reach ATC on the frequency assigned. Unable to reach them we tried the alternate frequency multiple times with no success. Shortly after those attempts, ATC transmitted on Guard frequency for us to turn south immediately. We replied that we are turning south and had attempted to reach them multiple times on two separate frequencies. Their reply was, 'Yeah, right!'
Narrative_1: On (date) at approximately (time), we lost communication with Center, while on a vector and ended up in Special Use Airspace. About 10 minutes prior, we were switched to a frequency from previous Controller. We were unable to get contact on this frequency, so we went back to our previous assigned frequency and were given a new frequency. We were able to contact Center on this frequency. While with Center on this frequency, we were given a vector for spacing with an expectation to rejoin our arrival. After a few minutes, without hearing anything we began to query the Controller. We had no contact. We tried a few times, when the Captain said we should try the other frequency we were given earlier. As we switched over, we hear Center simulcasting on Guard, to come up. As we contacted Center, the Controller asked us where we had been and we explain that we were up on the frequency where they were talking to us earlier. The Controller then proceeds to give us a vector and tells us that we are in Special Use Airspace. Once we cleared the Airspace we continued with the arrival uneventfully.
Synopsis: A flight crew reported they flew into military Restricted Airspace when were assigned a vector off course and issued a frequency change. They could not establish communications on the new frequency in a timely manner due to frequency congestion and saturation on the new frequency.

Narrative: After takeoff, in our climb, smoke was detected in the cockpit. The smoke was coming from the First Officer's yoke. We also started to have BAT DISCHARGE caution light come on multiple times. Followed appropriate check list and QRH procedures. Decided to go back to the airport. We got clearance to go directly to the airport and got vectors for ILS. All the appropriate procedures and check list were completed before landing, with verification of speeds and weight. After an uneventful landing, we did not need any further assistance, and went to our parking spot.
Narrative_1: Advised ATC due to smoke in cockpit. Returned to [departure airport]. QRH was read, approach was briefed and setup. Checklists were followed. Uneventful landing was made under maximum weight. Battery discharge light annunciated several times during the event. First Officer smelled electric burning, then noticed smoke. Caution light annunciation and battery discharge light noticed during normal scan. I should have waited and asked ATC to standby before announcing the aircraft condition. This would have given time for the crew to evaluate all resources and outcomes before making a decision.
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported returning to departure airport after experiencing smoke from the First Officer yoke and a battery discharge annunciation.

Narrative: I was the Pilot Flying on the ZZZZZ 1 Arrival into ZZZ. ZZZ TRACON asked us what approach we wanted to [Runway] XXR into ZZZ. We requested the RNAV visual to [Runway] XXR. We were cleared to 7,000 feet and cleared to intercept the final approach course for [Runway] XXR after ZZZZZ. We thought we were cleared for the approach so we set the next altitude of 4,000 feet in past ZZZZZ. After crossing ZZZZZ the aircraft started descending to 4,000 feet. ZZZ TRACON informed us of a Low Altitude Alert and had us climb to 7,000 feet, then he Immediately cleared us for the visual. Told us to take down the phone number for possible pilot deviation.
Narrative_1: Both our first time to ZZZ. We were cleared to intercept final segment. We said to each other, 'ZZZZZ is IAF,' and then we determined it was the final course we were supposed to intercept. We should have asked ATC to repeat, but we put 4,000 feet in the autopilot, as in VNAV, to continue published approach, but 7,000 feet was still our clearance limit. On the published segment it continued down, inside ZZZZZ, below 7,000 feet. ATC queried us at 6,000 feet and told us to climb. We had the field in sight and ATC then cleared us immediately for the visual.I was so focused on terrain and being in VNAV. As Pilot Monitoring, I should have questioned the clearance and any confusion we had. I am sure what we heard, thought we heard and what ATC said were all different.
Synopsis: B737-700 flight cew reported a low altitude alert and initiated a Go Around at an airport that both crew members were flying into for the first time.

Narrative: On final approach, we lost the green hydraulic system. We entered holding to complete the non-normal procedure and get fully configured. We also requested a longer runway and emergency equipment. The landing was made to a full stop because of loss of normal brakes and nose wheel steering. We were then towed to the gate.
Narrative_1: We experienced a mechanical failure (HYD G SYS LO PRESS) upon our descent into ZZZ on the ZZZZZ1 Arrival beginning approximately outside ZZZ waypoint. I was Pilot Flying, the Captain followed appropriate ECAM actions and checklists following company procedures. We advised ATC based on this ECAM considering our location and situational aspects. We elected to hold over the final approach fix for GPS approach to Runway XX while we completed all of our necessary actions in the interest of safety. Upon completion of these duties, we exited the hold, completed approach and landed successfully coming to full stop on the runway. Based on the mechanical condition of the aircraft as result of systems lost from hydraulic system, we coordinated with company operations to tow us in due to loss of nose wheel steering and deplaned normally. Mechanical malfunction (HYD G low pressure) ECAM.
Synopsis: A320 flight crew reported the loss of the green hydraulic system resulted in a precautionary landing and a tow to the gate.

Narrative: Inadvertent switching off of IR1 mode selector which deactivated that associated ADIRU. ADR and IR data not available. This occurred during flight one of day two of an initial Captain upgrade. The trainee came off the B777. He has been with our company for many years. The three legs of day one was extraordinarily busy. It was immediately clear to me during those three legs he had studied hard during training and had mastered much of the material. On the first two legs of day one I had a LCA (Line Check Airman) in-training watching me conduct the line check as part of that LCA's upgrade training. I commented to the new LCA not all trainees will be so well prepared as this one.This flight was leg four of the IOE and the first flight of day two. Our transportation to the airport was 15 minutes late and there was a detour so we arrived at the aircraft about 30 minutes prior to departure. Normally, I introduce myself to all the FAs (Flight Attendant). However, because we were on IOE, [we] were somewhat late to the aircraft and on Release 6. I only introduced myself to the FM. I felt I did not have time go to the back to introduce myself to the FAs assigned to the rear of the aircraft.We had been in the seat for approximately 3 hours. The upgrade Captain requested I ask the FM to prepare the meals and that we would then take a restroom break when the meals were ready. I did so. The FM called us about 25 minutes later to state the meals were ready. The upgrade Captain offered me the opportunity to use the Lav first. I declined and said he should go first and I would then go. The door chime rang and then I heard a knock. That knock is not standard. However, it occurs occasionally with legacy Company 2 flight attendants. We put on our masks. I saw the upgrade Captain move to get out of his seat, stand up, and let the FA in while he then left the cockpit. I noticed nothing odd about his movement out of the seat and to the rear of the cockpit. I saw out of the corner of my eye the FA was standing near the rear of the cockpit just behind and to the right of the Captain's seat, a normal position for a relief FA.My concentration then focused on something else. I think it was because we were getting ready to enter a large area of convective activity. I might have been looking at WSI and comparing that to what I was seeing on the weather radar. Why my gaze was generally focused forward and right I am not sure, but it was. I planned to brief the relief FA about this weather and its possible effect on their service in a few minutes. It was at that point, maybe 30-45 seconds after the upgrade Captain had left the cockpit, that for lack of a better description, 'all hell broke loose.' The cockpit went from a completely benign environment to one of confusion. The startle effect was in full force. The first warning was a continuous repetitive chime and the warning lights flashing. I immediately looked at the E/WD (Engine/Warning Display) and noted about 4-5 ECAMs listed, primary secondary and independent failures in both red and amber. I silenced the CRC (Continuous Repetitive Chime) by pushing [the] master warning light. That silenced the CRC. However, there still was an aural alert going off that I could not silence, which created a fair bit of consternation on my part. I look at my PFD and saw the FMAs were wrong. I then saw the AP (Autopilot) was off and that there was nothing where I expected to see the AT (Autothrottle) condition. I noted the aircraft climbing slightly and corrected that. I knew the AP disengaged for some reason but didn't know why. I thought about engaging AP 2 but then thought that may create new problems, so I elected to hand-fly until the ECAMs were sorted out. I saw we were no longer in NAV but again, wasn't sure why. I did see that the aircraft didn't diverge much from the 'green line' so lateral stick inputs weren't necessary. At this point ATC called to ask us something about recycling the transponder. We wereon speaker at that time; I responded we had a problem and to standby.I then noted the airspeed increasing and pulled the TLs (Thrust Lever) back; I didn't want to add an over-speed to our problems. This silenced another aural sound. I do not recall seeing a Thrust Locked ECAM or FMA which I thought would have been the source of the alert I couldn't silence. I glanced at the Captain PFD (Primary Flight Display) and ND (Navigation Display) and saw they didn't look right.The aircraft was reasonably stabilized now but, in my mind, because the ECAMs were displayed, the situation wasn't. I then told the FA to recall the trainee Captain to the cockpit. He opened the door, looked and then closed it, and said he was in the bathroom. I told the FA I knew that and I wanted him back in the cockpit now. He then had the FM knock on the Lav door. The trainee Captain returned to the cockpit and the relief FA left. The trainee Captain was incredulous when he looked at the E/WD. I told him I was hand-flying, had the aircraft and radios, and that he was to handle the ECAMs. It was at this point I noted we were about 20 knot slow, well within flying speed but slow for planned speed. I had overcompensated for my worry of overspending the aircraft. I pushed the power back up. Airspeed had fallen out of my cross-check. The trainee Captain methodically and correctly went through the ECAMs. As I recall the first several ECAMs had no action items, one ECAM had us switch the air data switch to three. At some point during this, ATC stated they now had data on us and asked if we needed assistance. We told him we were completing a procedure and to standby. Once the status messages were read and the ECAM procedure completed, I reached up to engage AP two. It did so. I armed the AT and then moved the TLs to the climb detent to engage it. Our ATC clearance was to proceed direct to a fix so we reinserted that. I don't recall having to pull or push to capture our assigned altitude but I can't be sure.It was now maybe 4-5 minutes after the initial event where I could take a breath. I recalled the ECAM and saw the ADR 1 fault. I then looked over to the ADIRS panel and saw IR mode selector one was in the OFF position. It, of course, was on for the flight up until some point in [the] last few minutes. I asked the trainee Captain if he recalls hitting the switch with his head or back as he left his seat. He said no. I then thought perhaps the switch was defective. This aircraft came to us as a through flight. We did not have to turn them on so we had no knowledge of how that switch felt by turning it on. We again discussed it and he stated he didn't recall even touching the overhead panel while leaving the seat.Because I didn't introduce myself to the FAs at the rear of the aircraft prior to the flight, I wasn't sure which FA came to the cockpit during our break. I asked the FM to ask the FA who came to the cockpit to call us on the interphone. That FA did and I asked him if he recalled touching anything on the overhead panel; he stated he did not. What I found unusual was that during the event, the FA seemed very nonplussed by the cacophony of sounds in the cockpit. I would have expected a FA to at least ask what was going on, but maybe he was somewhat shocked by what he saw and heard during his short time in the cockpit.The trainee Captain and I discussed that I would write up the ECAM and then conference Dispatch and Technical Support Maintenance Control to provide further details of what we thought may have occurred. I wanted the switch looked at but also didn't want Maintenance to search for a problem which might not exist. I ACARS'd Dispatch with the request and he set up the conference call. The communications with Technical Support Maintenance Control were reasonably good and he captured exactly what I wanted him to know and he appended it to our write-up. Since the Captain's displays were significantly degraded, we switched PF/PM roles. Fromthat point we continually deviated for weather, were put in holding, and changed our alternate three times. We over-burned by almost 5500 lb on this flight, more than on any flight I have been on in [an] Airbus. It was an understatement to say this was a busy flight. I don't know how this happened. The final flight of the day was a termination. As the trainee ran that checklist and turned off the IRUs, he stated he couldn't believe how he accidentally managed to switch that style of switch - pull and turn - off by getting out of the cockpit.I am disappointed in myself for not more thoroughly reviewing the flight manual for ADR 1 fault after things had settled down. We did not have a GPWS TERR FAULT light and no ECAM direction to switch it off so it remained on. We discussed that threat in that we were now the aircraft's GPWS system and to be cognizant of the terrain. We also discussed changing the transponder to position 2 but did not do so because there was no ECAM direction to [do] so and ATC noted no anomalies in our reporting. Also, once I saw the IR mode selector switch in the off position, I should have considered reviewing the NAV IR fault non-normal even though we didn't have that ECAM. I did not do a word search in the flight manual for ADR. Had I done so, I would have seen that there may be RVSM limitations associated with its failure and should have gone to the FOM for further information. I recall many years ago, our Line Manager at the time, wrote up in his weekly update a similar event. As I recall he wrote the trainee somehow managed to hook the window shade into that same switch and turned it off. That of course didn't happen here.
Synopsis: A320 Captain reported that a component was inadvertently switched off after the other pilot left the cockpit for a lavatory break and a multitude of warnings and ECAM messages went off as a result.

Narrative: We took off out of ZZZ to ZZZ1 for a night ETOPS flight. Everything was normal. Although the crew was current, all hadn't flown much in the past XX months due to COVID. We briefed this fact and were aware that we would all have to be on our toes due to the fact that our flying skills were rusty.The flight was normal. We operated the flight very close to the flight plan.After a normal approach and smooth landing, we taxied to the gate. After shutting down the engines and performing the Parking Checklist, we were surprised to see an overweight landing message being printed. We had landed approximately 700 pounds overweight.We sent the appropriate overweight landing code and I called local maintenance to report the issue.
Synopsis: Air carrier Captain reported an overweight landing at destination airport caused by failure to monitor fuel burn during flight. Captain cited rusty pilot skills caused by COVID inactivity as a contributing factor.

Narrative: I, the CA (Captain), was PM (Pilot Monitoring); the FO (First Officer) was PF (Pilot Flying). During the climb-out phase in level flight in mildly hazy VMC at 17,000 MSL at 290 KIAS with Autopilot B engaged the Master Caution, the 'FLT CONT' item on the CA-side SAP ('6-pack'), and the right half only of the 'STAB OUT OF TRIM' light illuminated. Press-to-test of the 'Stab out of trim' light showed both bulbs operable. After establishing that FO was actively remaining the PF, I performed 'Stabilizer Out of Trim' QRH procedure with the result that the autopilot electric trim and both pilot yokes trim switches were inoperative in both directions. I notified ATC that we had a mechanical problem that would eventually result in [requesting priority] and landing at a nearby airport, probably ZZZ, but for now we were content to remain at 17,000 slowly outbound from ZZZ while we worked the problem. Knowing we were also over landing weight, nicely under control, and still had a lot of checklists to run, I had no desire to rush into diving towards some final approach fix before we were ready to land. I performed the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' QRH procedure with the result that manual hand-cranked trimming was possible in either direction, albeit against unusually high resistance and with a 'cogging' feel as if pushing against a powered but stalled electric motor. This was true even when the aircraft was in-trim. One pilot could move the trim using one arm, but two pilots using one arm each worked much better for anything more than a couple turns of the trim wheel. We found that one pilot could both hand-fly and crank the trim, but tended to make unwanted aileron inputs while doing so. So it was doable in a pinch but not smooth. The forces required to turn the trim wheel did not appreciably reduce as we later slowed & configured. In the course of reading & discussing or doing the 'deferred items' section of the 'Stabilizer Trim Inoperative' QRH I started to activate the GPWS Flap inhibit switch. The FO stopped me saying we were above the 250 KIAS speed limit at that time. That sounded familiar to me, but no such limitation is stated at that point in the QRH. Nevertheless, we chose to delay activating the GPWS flap inhibit until we had slowed to first configuration speed around 220KIAS. Discussed with [the] FO whether ZZZ was the best divert option and which runway to use. ZZZ & longer Runway XXL was the unanimous choice. By that time we were a few miles south of [the] VOR on a south-southwesterly course for ZZZZZ, roughly 100nm from ZZZ.I then performed the 'Non-routine Landing' QRH procedure, alerting ATC for a return to ZZZ XXL with ARFF (Airport Rescue Firefighting) standing by. Coordinated with ATC for return via direct arrival for ILS XXL. Asked Company explicitly to alert ZZZ Approach & Tower of the intended non-standard XXL landing. Notified Dispatch via ACARS report. Briefed FAs via intercom, and passengers via PA on the situation, my expectations, and their roles. We selected the non-standard landing Runway XXL based on that runway being much longer than the more typical landing Runway XXR. That was a minor miscue, because I/we had not considered the effect of the large displaced threshold. Which I now consider insignificant. For landings eastbound the difference is 2500 feet and would be significant. Lesson learned: the big runway length number on the 10-9 page can be significantly misleading; take the time to dig into the 10-9A details page. The fact that was our takeoff runway and within Jepp FDPro I'd used the green highlighter to extend the highlighting all the way to the takeoff threshold didn't help. What had been useful to help direct my taxi to the correct threshold for takeoff became mildly misleading when evaluating which runway to land on. Which was not a side effect I noticed at the time or had considered previously. Still working as PM I performed normal divert preparations and top-of-descentprocedures: Reconfigured FMS & ACARS for ZZZ arrival, obtained ATIS, set up radios and performed approach brief, landing assessment, etc. Notified ZZZ Ops of our return by direct radio call to obtain a gate assignment.We discussed that we'd be a little above the normal max landing weight, but the already requested priority covers for that administrative requirement, and the runway available was nearly double what the QRH procedure's performance chart said was required. Performed descent checklist and before landing checklists and flows as normal. Throughout the evolution the FO kept us neatly in control, tight on the FD despite sometimes having to hand-crank the trim himself, caught a few radio calls I missed, and demonstrated overall high situational awareness and excellent systems knowledge. This is especially impressive for someone fairly new to the airplane who is just back from 6 months of furlough. During descent below 10,000 ft approaching downwind we changed control to CA as PF w FO as PM. We sighted the field while on base. During the turn-on to final I was using visual lookout primary, backed up by the LNAV purple line and the ILS. There was a moment of confusion as the ILS and LNAV came together before I was aligned with what I had thought was the landing runway. Having landed on XXR dozens (hundreds?) of times over the decades, that habit was unhelpful for a few seconds before we got fully established pointing at the correct runway. We then realized that Runway XXR is concrete and very easy to see in mildly hazy conditions while Runway XXL is asphalt and much harder to see. In fact XXL was invisible until we got closer in following the LNAV & LOC. My general habit on any landing involving parallel runways is to verbalize seeing all the relevant runways by name and explicitly saying which one I'm aligning / aligned with. E.g. 'I see XXL and XXR. I'm aligning with XXL.' For whatever reason that verbalization didn't occur; with sorta predictable results.Intercepted final outside intermediate fix in level flight at 3,000 ft. Configured to flaps 15 early and slowed gradually to Vapp of approximately 160KIAS before glideslope intercept at final approach fix. FO kept the airplane nicely in trim on my requests.Made a flaps 15 slightly overweight (approx. 148K#) approach and landing to a smooth touchdown on ZZZ Runway XXL just shy of the 2000ft marker. Upon stopping made a PA to reassure the passengers & remind them the safety vehicles would be seen around the airplane. ATC gave us an alternate frequency to contact ARFF on. Which surprised both of us a bit. Once we were communicating with ARFF I requested they inspect us for hot brakes or damaged tires. ARFF found normal brake temps and no tire damage. At ARFF's request I released them at that point and we taxied normally to [the] gate.Following shutdown the FO attempted to manually crank the trim to the usual post-shutdown 5 units from the 8-9 units we'd used at touchdown. At zero airspeed the trim was still 'cogging' and almost as difficult to move as it had been in flight. So we left the trim at the landing setting for Maintenance's edification. Which point we discussed with the Chief Pilot who met the flight and again later with the maintenance folks who also met the flight. I made appropriate aircraft maintenance log book entries for the stab trim failure and for the overweight landing. Spoke with Dispatch by phone before leaving aircraft per FOM. The next morning I filed the required report. In all I think this event worked out pretty close to textbook, minus the small glitches identified above.The main electric trim failing was the causal factor. Everything else is just details.1.
Narrative_1: We were both surprised to see that only half of the 'Stab out of trim' annunciator illuminated. Which left us wondering at first if we had a warning system malfunction or a trim malfunction. I surmise now that the right bulb is connected to FCC (Flight Control Computer) B and the left is connected to FCC A. And that had the Captain been PF, we'd have seen the left half illuminate instead.However it works, the details of left & right are not documented in [manual] where the annunciator is described. At a minimum there should be a statement like 'Only half of the annunciator may illuminate. That is still a valid indication of an out-of-trim condition.'3.

Narrative: While cruising at FL370, approximately 40 miles south of SAV, we experienced a severe updraft, causing the aircraft to rapidly climb to approximately 37,300 ft and then rapidly descend to approximately 36,500 ft. There was no weather displayed on our weather radar in our area of flight. The fluctuations lasted for about one minute. The rest of the flight continued as normal.
Narrative_1: In cruise at FL370, encountered clear air turbulence. No radar echoes, must have been convective activity building below our altitude. Updraft produced rain from below, lifted aircraft 300 ft above our cruise altitude. First Officer applied upset recovery controls which required descent 600 ft below our cruise altitude. Reported the event to Jacksonville Center. No other traffic in the area, no evasive action required. Flight continued normally without further incident.
Synopsis: Flight crew reported encountering severe updrafts and downdrafts resulting in deviations from their assigned altitude. The flight crew recovered from the upset condition and continued the flight without issue.

Narrative: Dirty sock odor descending into ZZZ. [Suggest] aircraft filtered bleed air.
Synopsis: Air Carrier Captain reported a fume event of 'dirty socks odor' during descent to destination.

Narrative: We commenced our takeoff normally. At around 95 kts, we got an ECAM for Y RSVR Lo Lvl and Y RSVR Lo Air Pr. The Captain initiated the abort with a max speed of approximately 100 kts. All callouts and notifications were made and we were able to taxi clear of the runway and stop. ATC notified us that we had trailed smoke so we asked him to roll the ARFF (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting) equipment. We ran the rejected takeoff checklist and then ran the ECAMs of which there were several all relating to the hydraulic issue. ARFF indicated that we had dumped a lot of hydraulic fluid. We were towed to the gate for repairs and offloaded the passengers and bags.
Narrative_1: Received a Master Caution light and ECAM during takeoff roll on Runway XXR at ZZZ and accomplished a rejected takeoff. The Master Caution and ECAM occurred at approximately 95 kts and Reject initiated between 95-105 kts. During the reject, several ECAMS displayed indicating loss of the Yellow Hydraulic system reservoir and Yellow system air pressure. At slow speed and with normal brakes and nosewheel steering available, I opted to take high speed Taxiway XX to safely clear the runway and bring aircraft to a full stop while the First Officer coordinated with Tower controller to roll the AARF (Aircraft Rescue and Firefighting) equipment as Tower stated they saw what appeared to be smoke trailing from the number two engine. While awaiting AARF response, we ran the Rejected Takeoff QRC and handled the ECAMS, started the APU and communicated with the passengers [and] inflight crew. After AARF arrival and initial inspection, we shutdown the number 2 engine with AARF on scene, then chocked the gear and shutdown the number 1 engine which had been used to keep normal brakes available. We coordinated with Operations and Ground Control for uneventful tow back to the gate for repair.
Synopsis: A320 Flight Crew reported a Rejected Take Off when the Yellow Hydraulic system showed low quantity and had to be towed back to the gate.

Narrative: During initial climbout from Runway XXR, the Trailing Edge (TE) flaps failed to retract from the takeoff position, flaps 1. I noticed this, as I prepared to place the Landing Gear lever to OFF and autobrakes to OFF. I directed to the FO (First Officer), who was PF (Pilot Flying), to slow to 210 KIAS while I coordinated with ATC to level off at 6,000 ft. MSL and Hold PPOS, approximately 15 miles southeast of the airport. I pulled out the QRH as we assessed our indications. The TE Flap gauge showed a slight split in the needles, with the R needle slightly retracted from flaps 1 and the L needle at flaps 1. I considered both Flap Asymmetry and Flap Disagree Checklists, and we decided the Asymmetry Checklist was more correct, despite the flap lever being UP. The PF did indicate very slight anomalous roll indications, prior to engaging the AP (Autopilot). I then informed the Passengers of our issue, briefed the FAs (Flight Attendants) that we would hold and work the problem and that we would be diverting to either ZZZ1 or ZZZ. Dispatch was very helpful in getting the Company Operations Center involved and suggesting ZZZ, editing the Release and giving us fuel and weight and balance data for worst case scenario. We began the QRH, holding at the deferred items for descent and landing. I then coordinated for the RNAV Z XXR Approach, briefed the Passengers of our decision to return to ZZZ, and briefed the FAs on the ETA and after landing plans. We briefed and commenced the approach, completed the QRH, ran brake cooling and reviewed the plan one last time. The PF flew a very nice approach at Vref 40 + 30 to a smooth flaps 1 landing with AB3 required and selected. On rollout I suggested he quickly disarm the AB and let the aircraft roll out at max reverse thrust to allow for more brake cooling. The data indicated 18 minutes of cooling at the gate so we taxied to the gate, shut the aircraft down and coordinated with Operations and [Maintenance Control]. Training and Company operational priorities had us well-prepared and allowed us to handle the issue safely and with ease.
Synopsis: B737 Captain reported trailing edge flaps did not retract after takeoff and was diagnosed as a flap asymmetry problem, resulting in an air turn back.

Narrative: The Captain was hand flying the aircraft on the ZZZZZ RNAV Departure off of Runway XXR from ZZZ, climbing to FL 190. ATC issued our flight an intermediate level off altitude of 10,000 ft. Approaching 10,000 ft. and about to level off, our flight received a TCAS RA to 'Maintain Vertical Speed,' due to an aircraft that appeared to be descending towards our aircraft and crossing our flight path. The Captain complied with and performed the TCAS RA maneuver. Then, the ATC Controller and what sounded like an ATC Supervisor intervening, issued instructions to the other aircraft to turn and climb immediately. At this point, our flight's TCAS RA changed from a 'Maintain Vertical Speed' to a 'Descend Now.' The Captain complied with the changing 'Descend Now' TCAS RA maneuver. Once the radio communications cleared, the First Officer was able to inform ATC of our TCAS RA. As a result of our TCAS RA maneuvering and the ATC issued turn and climb instructions to the other aircraft, the other aircraft appeared to pass our aircraft forward, above and to the right at less than 500 ft. Our flight then continued to ZZZ1 without further incidence.
Narrative_1: Departing ZZZ on the ZZZZZ ZZZZZ1 transition, we were initially cleared to FL190. Passing 8,800 ft., we were told to stop our climb at 10000 ft. The Captain was hand flying. At 9,800 ft., we received a 'maintain vertical speed' in a climb RA. ATC gave the conflicting aircraft, a light twin, an immediate climb and turn to the east. The traffic was pointed out to us and I responded, 'Roger. Aircraft X TCAS climb.' I then spotted the aircraft (conditions were VMC) but was unable to tell ATC due to radio congestion.
