As the conflicting aircraft began to climb away from us, we received a course reversal to 'DESCEND. DESCEND NOW' RA. The Captain followed the guidance. ATC gave us a frequency change and I read back the clearance and added 'TCAS descent' and changed frequencies. I estimate we passed within 500 ft. as the aircraft passed above us and to the right, turning away from us. The flight continued without incident to ZZZ1.
Synopsis: B777 flight crew reported an NMAC during the departure climb

Narrative: [There was a] nose gear tire issue followed by a loss of System A Hydraulics. We were flying Flight XXXX from ZZZ to ZZZ1 on (date). As we were rolling down the runway, we heard a loud bang from the nose gear area. It went away as quickly as it arrived, engine parameters were normal as well as directional control. After the takeoff, we talked about what it could have been. During the climb to our cruising altitude, we decided to call ZZZ Tower back and ask them to inspect Runway XR for any clues to what had happened during our takeoff roll. It took a while before we got an update from ZZZ Tower. They had found a two feet by two piece of rubber. We immediately contacted Dispatch and Maintenance, and we discussed various options. We were now in cruise and still bound for ZZZ1, when all of sudden the Number 1 Eng Hyd A LOW PRESSURE light started to come on and off a few times. We got the QRH Checklist and ran the HYDRAULIC PUMP LOW PRESSURE.I looked down on the instrument panel and noticed the System A Hydraulics quantity was down in the low 20's percent. We could watch that number was dropping fast. We now went quickly over to another chapter in the QRH, to LOSS OF SYSTEM A. We also [requested priority landing] with Center, and they immediately gave us direct to ZZZ1 airport. We determined that it was likely that a possibly piece of rubber had hit some of the Hydraulic lines. We quickly updated Dispatch about our loss of Hydraulic A quantity, and that we had [requested priority landing]. Dispatch gave us the Landing Distance information data, and we compared it to our own. We were all in agreement to continue and land in ZZZ1. We informed our Flight Attendants about our situation and what they could expect from our landing. We flew overhead ZZZ1 airport, and manually extended our landing gear per QRH. After completing all the steps in the QRH, we lined up with Runway XXL and landed. I immediately noticed the tiller was Â«lockedÂ» and unusable upon landing, and had to use rudder and differential braking to get back on center line. Both NORM and ALT nose wheel steering where both unavailable. We elected to stop the aircraft on the runway, and asked the Fire Trucks to visually inspect the aircraft from the outside. After getting the OK from them, we had Company Maintenance meet us on the runway with a tug, and to tow us clear of the runway. We had just cleared [Runway] XXL when the tow bar snapped, and they had to get another one. Once we got the second one, we were towed over to Gate X where our passengers were able to deplane.
Narrative_1: Departed ZZZ Runway XR. On takeoff roll, prior to rotation, a noise was heard similar to a hand slap on the front of the aircraft. Takeoff was continued with no adverse indications. As we continued to climb, the Captain and I assessed the probable cause of the noise. ZZZ Tower was advised of possible FOD on the runway. Before we were out of range of ZZZ Tower, we inquired for any findings of the FOD. Tower advised a piece of tire rubber was found on the runway. Still unsure whether the rubber was from our aircraft or a piece we hit on takeoff roll, we continued the assessment. Dispatch was brought into the loop and we all agreed to continue. As we continued to discuss the current situation, the #1 HYD LOW PRESSURE light illuminated and we ran the HYDRAULIC PUMP LOW PRESSURE QRH Checklist. SYSTEM A HYDRAULIC quantity was noted to be around 20 percent. SYSTEM A HYDRAULIC quantity continued to drop. LOSS OF SYSTEM A QRH Checklist was started. [After] reassessment of the loss of HYDRAULIC SYSTEM A and the noise heard at takeoff, [they] led us to believe that we had blown a tire which had damaged the hydraulics. A [priority landing was requested] with Center and direct ZZZ1 was issued. We continued discussions with Dispatch, as well as informed the Flight Attendants of our current conditions, plans and what to expect on arrival in ZZZ1. All went as planned with the completion of the LOSS OF SYSTEM A Checklist and landing on Runway XXL in ZZZ1. The only unexpected item on landing was no nose wheel steering on landing. Both NORM and ALT nose wheel steering was inoperative upon landing so we were unable to exit runway. CFR (Crash Fire Rescue) met the aircraft on the runway to assist. Aircraft was towed to the gate from the runway.
Synopsis: B737-700 flight crew reported hearing a loud bang from the nose gear area during the takeoff roll. In flight, the hydraulic system malfunctioned and the crew performed a manual gear extension prior to landing.

Narrative: On the final phase of the Visual Approach, backed up by the ILS Runway XY to ZZZ, with the intention to capture the glide path from above, the Auto Pilot (AP) and Auto Throttles were disengaged. Prevailing conditions were Good Visibility and varying Tail Winds of up to nine (9) Knots. During the final portion of the descent to touchdown, with a visual transition to the PAPI reference already established (PAPI were showing 3 RED-1 WHITE), the Aircraft descended below the referenced visual glide path, with the tendency to fly over the Runway XY overrun area at an altitude (AGL) of less than 50 ft. The moment the Captain, having the Pilot Monitoring (PM) duties, mentioned his estimation for being low on the glide path, the aircraft was overflying a point short of the RWY by about 500 feet. He consecutively called for a Go Around, which was immediately executed by the PF (Pilot Flying). The Flight landed after a RADAR pattern on the same runway uneventfully.[The cause was] Human Factors / Pilot Flying error on visually estimating the projected Glide Slope to Runway XY, with the current Tail Wind conditions. Root cause is the initially higher angle of descent / rate of descent to capture the glide slope from above, that ended up to an over correction - reverse situation of flying finally lower than the projected/correct slope. [I suggest] earlier Aircraft configuration for the Final Approach Phase and timely request from the ATC for lower altitudes / earlier descent to the recommended altitudes that lead to a better projected sequence of flying tasks.
Narrative_1: FO was flying pilot. Performed visual approach and FO had a hard time trying to catch the glide slope from above because he was trying to slow down and put flaps down while on OPEN DESC. FO called for 'the bird', which caught me off guard because it is the first time anyone has asked for the flight path vector while trying to intercept the ILS and while disconnecting the AP. He not only disconnected AP but also eventually the auto thrust without previously briefing it. I told him to never disconnect the auto thrust again while trying to save a visual approach. Finally he was established on the ILS. Below 500 feet he said he was going to follow the PAPI. I glanced down at the VSI to make sure we were stable and when I looked backed up we had 4 red on the PAPIs and at the same time we received a GS GPWS warning. Became unstable. I loudly and sternly called 'unstable, go-around.' Performed go-around as RA called 50 feet. FO performed a soft go-around. I overrode his decision after he brought back TL (Thrust Lever) to CLB and I pushed TL to TOGA since we were in ZZZ (high airport elevation) with high OAT. I honestly could not tell you the altitude when the FO brought back the TL to CLB. I wanted to make sure we were safe since the go-around was performed at 50 feet from an unsafe position. At 50 feet RA, aircraft was not anywhere near the approach end of the runway. Came back for an uneventful landing.FO descended below glide slope and PAPI showed 4 red.Soft Go-around procedure should be changed or at least highlight the need to take into account airport elevation and OAT when deciding to make a soft go-around from a low altitude with an obvious performance deterioration.Soft Go-around procedure should be changed or at least highlight the need to take into account airport elevation and OAT when deciding to make a soft go-around from a low altitude with an obvious performance deterioration.
Synopsis: Flight crew reported that the First Officer made errors during final approach to landing and the Captain elected to call for a go around.

Narrative: Arriving SEA, ATC cleared us to follow aircraft ahead to visual approach 34L. We were given 170kts to final fix due to ATC spacing us just over 3 miles behind a B737. I was Pilot Monitoring, the First Officer the Pilot Flying had our plane on autopilot using heading select and vertical speed to navigate onto the localizer and glideslope.Just as the plane was joining the localizer, a mild buffeting was felt followed by a rapid roll in direction of the turn. Aural warning 'Bank Angle' annunciated. The First Officer immediately disconnected the autopilot and reduced the bank angle to normal parameters. The rest of the approach was uneventful.On visual approaches, especially with close spacing, fly above the path of the preceding aircraft.
Narrative_1: While on dogleg to final for RWY 34L, descending to 2,400 feet MSL following preceding B737 by 3.5 NM encountered wake turbulence while on autopilot. As autopilot initiated turn to join the localizer the aircraft encountered the wake turbulence causing a rapid roll to the right (in the direction of the turn). The aircraft rolled past 30 degrees of bank and an aural warning 'bank angle' sounded. The Pilot Flying recognized the excursion and disengaged the autopilot and reduced the bank angle to normal range. Pilot Flying continued the approach and landed uneventfully.Consider staying above preceding aircraft's altitude/flight path to avoid wake turbulence or increase range between aircraft.
Synopsis: B737-900 flight crew reported encountering wake turbulence on final approach to SEA in trail of a B737.

Narrative: Thunderstorms were quickly approaching XXL final approach course upon our arrival at ZZZ. ATC provided significant vectoring and cleared us for visual XXL during base leg of approach. Base leg was squared off toward final approach fix due to approaching weather. During turn to final approach course, pilot flying went below GS (Glide Slope). Tower issued low altitude warning. Pilot initiated corrective action. Aircraft Landed uneventfully.
Synopsis: First Officer reported descending below altitude on approach and climbed back to correct altitude to continue the approach to landing.

Narrative: Upon configuring flaps from 25 to 30, Trailing Edge Flaps indicated a split and stopped tracking at 27 degrees. LE FLAPS TRANSIT light was also illuminated (amber light). A go-around was accomplished to enable time for non normal checklists to be run. LEADING EDGE FLAPS TRANSIT checklist was run which led us into TRAILING EDGE FLAPS DISAGREE checklist. Flaps were left at 27 degrees with flap handle at 25 setting. Vref15 +5 was the approach speed selected and an uneventful landing and taxi to the gate was accomplished.
Narrative_1: On Final Approach to XXL in ZZZ and configuring from flaps 25 to flaps 30 at about 1,500 feet the trailing edge flap needle indicators displayed a split and the flaps stopped at approximately 27 degrees. The LE FLAP TRANSIT light was also illuminated. After taking a few seconds to realize what was happening and coming through approximately 1,000 ft the Captain called for a go around. I executed the go around, however upon attempting to retract the flaps we realized they were stuck at 27 degrees and would not retract at all. I continued to fly the plane and the Captain advised ATC and then ran the non-normal LEADING EDGE FLAP TRANSIT QRH followed by the TRAILING EDGE FLAP DISAGREE QRH. We received vectors from ATC and took our time setting up for a flaps 27 landing using the VREF15+5 knot wind additive. While being vectored back to the final approach course the Captain TEST and the FA's and made an announcement to the PAX. We landed and taxied to the gate uneventfully.
Synopsis: Flight Crew reported receiving a trailing edge flap asymmetry indication with a leading edge devices in transit light while on approach and elected to perform a go around in order to accomplish checklists and subsequently landed at destination airport.

Narrative: Flight planning, preflight, ground operations, and takeoff were accomplished per SOP and were uneventful. Captain was pilot flying. Passing 18000 STD, altimeter was selected and AP 1 was selected. At XA:17, we got a master caution light, with HYD G RSVR LO LVL, HYD G ENG 1 PUMP LO PR, and HYD G SYS LO PR displayed on the upper ECAM. After confirming no Green Hydraulic QTY, I asked the FO (First Officer) to request to stop climb and return to field. Captain continued to fly and handle radios. FO accomplished the ECAM procedures, turning off the PTU and Green Eng 1 Pump. QRH was referenced after ECAMs completed, screens normal.We requested priority handling with ATC. Advised Dispatch through ACARS that we had lost all Green Hydraulic QTY, were returning to ZZZ, and would require a tow off runway due to loss of nosewheel steering. Purser was advised of the malfunction, that we were returning to field in 20 minutes, and a cabin prep was not required. A visual approach to XXL was briefed after runway assignment and the descent checklist was accomplished. Aircraft was configured early due to slow flaps/slats and alternate gravity gear extension. Approach and landing were accomplished per SOP and were uneventful. Aircraft was stopped straight ahead on centerline. Engines shut down with timing after starting APU. Aircraft was inspected by Fire Response Team, confirming gear doors down and fluid [was] leaking from under plane behind gear. Super tug arrived and towed us clear of runway to Gate XXX.
Narrative_1: On climbout passing approximately 21,000 feet, we got an ECAM indicating loss of the green system, LO G Press, and another green system ECAM but I cannot recall it now. We ran the ECAM action items which had us turn off the PTU and Eng 1 G pump. As soon as the ECAM action items were complete, we communicated with ATC, advising them we needed to stop our climb, and requested priority handling and requested a return to ZZZ. The CA (Captain) and I split up the flying and comm duties, he advised the FA's (Flight Attendant) of our situation, and sent a message to Dispatch. I talked to ATC and flew the aircraft for a brief time while he handled the message to Dispatch.We got the expanded checklist and discussed the effects of [a] loss of the green system in terms of manual cranking of the gear and needing to stop on the runway due to loss of steering, which the CA sent an ACARs to the station to start working on a tow for us to minimize us sitting on the runway. I also advised ATC to let ZZZ know we would be a full-stop on the runway and would need to be towed. We were given priority handling back to ZZZ and we briefed the approach and threats of a go-around since the gear could not be retracted once it was hand-cranked down. The CA flew the approach XXL and the landing and stopping at the end of the runway was uneventful. We dropped the landing gear pins to the tug team and got towed back to the gate. We debriefed once we were off the aircraft and the passengers disembarked. The CA was cool, calm, and collected and flew a textbook approach. We worked well together as a team; I can't think of much that we could have done to improve on how the situation was handled.
Synopsis: First Officer reported loss of all green hydraulic system fluid caused an Air Turn Back and precautionary landing.

Narrative: Immediately after takeoff from ZZZ all communication was disrupted by extreme static which inhibited the ability to transmit or receive any communication by either VHF 1 or VHF 2 radio through headsets, hand mics, or speakers. The static continued throughout the entire flight with brief periods of communication possible for 1-5 minutes. Crew elected to continue normal departure and climb and adhere to our filed route clearance while squawking 7600. Dispatch was notified via ACARS and was requested to coordinate down link ATC communications. During brief periods of open communication we informed ATC of our intentions to fly our filed route, arrival STAR and land on runway XXC at destination ZZZ1. Captain and FO discussed and agreed that the safest course of action was to fly our filed and comply with lost communication procedures and not complicate the current flight plan by returning to departure field or an unplanned alternate. FO flew the aircraft from takeoff to landing and captain handled the communication and ATC coordination issues. Arrival landing, taxi and parking at ZZZ1 were uneventful and flight was completed safely.
Synopsis: Captain reported loss of all VHF communications and elected to continue the flight to destination airport.

Narrative: During cruise at FL370 while deviating for thunderstorms in IMC conditions we encountered an airspeed unreliable condition. After performing memory items we ran the Airspeed Unreliable checklist. While going through the checklist we may have deviated from our assigned FL370 however we don't think we did. While running the checklist the event seemed to end. We continued through the entire checklist to make sure we were aware of all of the possible actions required if the event returned. This event occurred on the same aircraft about 3 weeks prior and maintenance addressed it at that time.I don't have any suggestions as we followed SOP and checklist usage. We don't think we had an altitude deviation but we aren't sure.
Narrative_1: During Airspeed Unreliable event at FL370 and IMC, CA (Captain) was pilot flying. Both CA and FO (First Officer) airspeed and altitude were unreliable for at least a minute or more, Airspeed Low and IAS Disagree alerts. Accomplished procedures, and hand flew based on Standby Flight Display. As best we could tell, stayed within +- 200 ft of FL370. Exiting IMC, indications returned to normal. ATC made no comment about altitude.Factors include equipment malfunction and icing. Equipment malfunctions unavoidable
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported unreliable airspeed and altimeter in IMC conditions. Systems returned to normal after exiting IMC.

Narrative: While at en route cruise FL370 Flight Crew noticed a decrease in left engine oil quantity. The white exceedance box illuminated around the secondary engine parameters and the left oil quantity soon went to reverse video. At this time, oil pressure showed normal at 69%. As we watched the oil quantity continue its slow drop, the decision was made to divert to [a suitable airport] out of precaution. Knowing we were above MLGW (Maximum Landing Gear Weight), we requested to hold and burn down. ATC directed us to hold as published. I believe we were at 11,000 ft. We lowered the gear, extended the speedbrake and dropped flaps to expedite the fuel burn. Once the oil quantity dropped below 10% and anticipating a loss of oil pressure, [we requested special handling from] ATC. Eventually with oil quantity reaching zero, oil pressure started to fluctuate between 37 and 53%. At this point feeling the engine oil pump was beginning to cavitate, the Captain took controls and ordered the QRH ENG Low Oil Press checklist and subsequent Engine Shutdown Checklist based on the abnormal indications. We did not wait for the Low Oil Press light to illuminate because we knew it was soon to come. The left engine was secured. Once MLGW was ensured, Captain landed [using] flaps 15. Aircraft cleared the runway at the end where fire trucks were waiting. Airport personnel inspected the left engine and gave the go-ahead for taxi to the gate. During this event, the passengers were well informed of the situation and the diversion. Dispatch was notified and offered assistance as needed. Post flight inspection revealed the bolts holding the left engine Air Turbine Starter had sheared. With the ATS (Air Turbine Starter) detached, engine oil which normally lubricates the seals was leaking from the breach.
Synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported diverting to an alternate airport after inflight shutdown following loss of left engine oil quantity.

Narrative: We were flying RNAV Stadium Visual to Runway 29. We were on speed and fully configured by the approach gates. I was hand flying. As we were rolling out on final, [a] B777 was holding in position on Runway 22R at intersection Y. As our aircraft was approaching Runway 29, [the] B777 was cleared for takeoff on Runway 22R. Flight conditions were VFR, there was about a 9-knot tailwind on final. Up to the point of the incident, approach was normal. As I started to bring the airplane into a flare, we experienced a pretty significant upset. To the best of my recollection, we first experienced a significant yawing to the left, followed by a wing drop. I cannot say with any certainty whether the left or right wing dropped. I applied multiple aileron corrections to recover and the touchdown was normal. As we rolled out, it became very obvious that the upset was caused by the B777 applying takeoff thrust as we crossed 22R behind that aircraft. As we rolled to a taxi speed, the Captain advised the Tower of the incident. Also, one of the aircraft awaiting departure on 22R made a comment about what they observed, making us believe that the upset was quite significant to be noticed by another aircrew. Upon arrival at the gate, both Captain and I made a post flight aircraft walk around. We did not observe any type of damage or scratches on either wings, nor the engines nor the tail.
Narrative_1: On short final to Runway 29 at EWR. At approximately 100 ft noticed a 777 was cleared to Takeoff from 22R at Y. I noticed we had a crosswind of about 8-9 kts from the left. While in our flare, approximately behind the 777 we experienced a large jet blast of 50 to 60 kts from left. Aircraft got displaced to right. Due to large wind addition, left wing briskly rose due to added lift. Once jet blast hit vertical stabilizer aircraft yawed strongly to the left as well. The aircraft also ballooned up about 50 ft due to all the added wind/lift. I considered a go around but reasoned that any asymmetric thrust application to go-around thrust from a slow spooling engine in an older -800 would prove disastrous in such a low energy state and may possibly have resulted in a cartwheel as we had minimal controllability. This was evidenced to me by the large control wheel applications by the First Officer resulting in only minor flight path modifications. To be frank, if I were to apply full go-around thrust and one engine spooled right up and the other lagged, I did not feel that I would have adequate aileron and/or rudder to control the airplane from it's present state. The First Officer did a masterful job (15 years in present seat) of adding just enough power and slowly bringing aircraft back to centerline. We had a firm but safe landing and stopped with about 1000 ft of runway left. Again, the First Officer showed his experience and did a masterful job recovering. I never even for a second doubted the outcome.
Synopsis: B737 NG FO reported his aircraft was 'significantly upset' just before touchdown at EWR by jet blast from a taxiing B777.

Narrative: During IRNMN arrival descent into LAX we encountered a small amount of turbulence I would classify as light above FL190 that felt like wake turbulence so we asked ATC who we were following. Oakland Center responded that it was a B767. We were surprised that we got the wake off them with 10 miles separation but it was minor. Winds were light aloft. After we got on to Approach Control frequency and were still descending via the arrival we received a little more that was stronger and I had the First Officer seat the flight attendants over the PA.Just as we were in the LNAV turn over BAYST to JUUSE at approximately 10,000 feet we encountered moderate wake turbulence from the B767 that was still 9 miles ahead of us and we encountered significant roll rates with the wake turbulence and banked about 25 degrees Left. I was holding the controls to stabilize the aircraft and the autopilot kicked into Control Wheel Steering Pitch and Roll because I was countering the significant left roll. The First Officer was still off seating the flight attendants so I told Approach Control we were encountering wake turbulence and we needed an immediate turn away from the B767.When countering the wake roll we ended up slightly south of the magenta line, maybe .1 or .2 Actual Navigation Performance due to arrival turn when the wake was encountered so I manually flew the aircraft back on the LNAV track. ATC then gave us a 070 heading and to maintain 9,000 feet while in the process of flying the magenta line. We were vectored north of the B767 and then we preformed the RNAV Y 24R and the B767 was sent to the south Runway 25L. We encountered no further wake turbulence. We checked on the status of the flight attendants and they were OK and they did their final checks from their jumpseats. Upon arrival at the gate, I personally checked with all the flight attendants to explain what happened and to verify one more time that they were OK, which they were.
Synopsis: B737NG Captain reported encountering wake turbulence on descent into LAX in trail of a B767.

Narrative: During initial takeoff roll, at takeoff thrust setting and less than 30 kts, aircraft began uncommanded hard left turn. Initiated slow speed reject, tried to counter with full right rudder and full right nose wheel steering. Tiller was binding, only 10 degrees of travel available as if fighting left tiller inputs. Continued manual braking to a full stop with the aircraft nose close to 45 degrees left of centerline with the aircraft fully blocking taxiway. We informed Tower of the rejected takeoff and that we required a tow back to the ramp. Suspected nose wheel steering malfunction
Synopsis: B777 Captain reported rejecting the takeoff and returning to the gate when the aircraft initiated a hard left turn early in the takeoff roll.

Narrative: Halfway through our flight, our B-Flight Attendant asked to come into the flight deck and talk with us. When she got to the flight deck she indicated that there was a very strong cleaning/bug spray smell in the aft galley. And, our C-Flight Attendant was complaining of coughing and a hard time taking a deep breath because of the strong cleaning smell. Our A-Flight Attendant didn't smell anything. No passengers were indicating concern and, we didn't smell anything. I informed the Flight Attendant (FA) if she was medically concerned we would patch through to medic so she could communicate her concern. All the FAs indicated they were feeling OK and did not want to contact medic. They just wanted someone to look at the aircraft in ZZZ2. At that point I told her we would put the packs to high to help eliminate the strong cleaning odor. We contacted Dispatch through ACARS to discuss the situation and see if there was an anti-microbial spray completed the night before. Also, to inform Dispatch that they were not comfortable taking the aircraft on our next leg. Dispatch wanted a patch through ARINC. We agreed on a patch to medic. During their discussion, Dispatch sent us an ACARS to divert to ZZZ1. The First Officer (FO) notified ATC of our intention to divert. I notified the FAs and passengers of our intent, as well. As a precaution we accomplished the Smoke, Fire, or Fumes QRC and referenced QRH Smoke, Fire or Fumes Checklist in case the situation escalated. Dispatch notified us the aircraft had been sprayed the night before. We communicated with our A-Flight Attendant on what to expect on landing, taxi, and at the gate.We kept in constant communication with the A-FA to constantly reassess our situation. On our descent into ZZZ1, medic recommended the two Flight Attendants in question use the portable oxygen. With that information I notified ATC. We then accomplished all appropriate checklists and landed uneventfully.
Synopsis: B737 Captain reported a fumes event during cruise resulting in health issues for some flight attendants and an eventual diversion.

Narrative: Upset/wake turbulence event. Approximately five minutes prior to this event First Officer and I had completed our arrival brief and I had given a PA to the passengers that the seat belt sign would be coming on in the next 10 minutes. Ahead of us was a B787 at [our altitude], FL360. [The B787] was directed by ATC to descend and maintain FL340. Within a few minutes we were assigned the same clearance. Shortly after leveling at FL340, our aircraft entered a rapid, shuddering turbulence, followed by a rapid roll to the right. We both immediately put our hands on the controls and recited the upset recovery call outs. We disconnected the autopilot, though the autopilot may have disconnected by itself, and autothrottle. We both fly with our FPV (Flight Path Vector) up so we could see immediately, intuitively that we weren't stalled, but our push was slight, not even half a G, which added to our effective counter roll rate. Prior to our response to the upset, the autopilot had already put in aileron control forces counter to the roll, but the aircraft was still rolling to the right. As we took control, the aircraft reached approximately 40 degrees before the aircraft responded to our control inputs, then rolled left to approximately 20 degrees. Based on the fact we were at FL340 we left the thrust where it was positioned, possibly a slight reduction, as the energy state was good and a large thrust change was not necessary. Our altitude loss was minimal and the descent was very shallow. The recovery point at which we managed our flight path divergence started at approximately FL337, only a 300 FT loss. Rudder may have been used - Indicated by both an overshoot, subsequent bank to the left and a report from the flight attendants that we not only rolled, but yawed. We advised ATC that we had encountered wake turbulence which had caused our descent. They offered us direct HLYWD moving us from the wake of the preceding aircraft. We then checked on the Flight Attendants and passengers to ensure there were no injuries. The seat belt sign had been off and there was a passenger in the lav, but no injuries were reported. The First Officer and I debriefed the event but, because ATC started our descent onto the Arrival, I failed to make a PA to the passengers. After landing, I waited at the flight deck door to thank the passengers. I saw that the event was more impactful than I had realized and a PA would have gone a long way to reassure the passengers and Flight Attendants.
Synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported an upset at FL340 descending into LAX in trail of a B787.

Narrative: Just prior to pushing, I was handed a Notice to Crew (NOTAC) for aircraft batteries in compartment D. I signed one and kept it, signed the other and returned it. I didn't look at it closely and didn't realize until cruise that the release was supposed to note it as well.
Synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported aircraft departure with flight release missing required 'Hazmat cargo' amendment note.

Narrative: Flight was deviating off the ZZZZZ arrival due to thunderstorm activity. Subsequently cleared direct ZZZZZ and told to descend to 5,000 feet. While it is possible both the Captain and FO (First Officer) heard the wrong altitude, the FO read back 5,000 feet. Even though the published altitude is 6,000 feet, this did not seem unusual to us as we were flying below storm overhangs and had barely flown any of the arrival up to this point. After reaching 5,000, the controller asked why we were at 5,000. We informed him that was our cleared altitude. He informed us 6,000 was the minimum vectoring altitude.
Narrative_1: On arriving into ZZZ, we were taken off the ZZZZZ4 arrival due to thunderstorms in the terminal area. Upon contact with Terminal Radar Control we were issued radar vectors. The Air Traffic Controller stated that we would rejoin the arrival at ZZZZZ. We were told to fly heading 090 and cleared to descend from 9,000 to 6,000. The clearance was read back and confirmed by both of us. Shortly thereafter the controller gave us a further descent down to 5,000. The clearance was read back and confirmed by both of us. After the clearance was read back, ATC never intervened on the altitude that we read back. ATC then told us to fly direct to ZZZZZ. Whilst we were level at ZZZZZ at 5,000, ATC stated that [the next fix] had an altitude of 6,000 ft. I stated that we were cleared by him down to 5,000. There were no traffic conflicts.
Synopsis: Flight crew reported descending 1000 feet below minimum altitude on approach as cleared by ATC.

Narrative: During approach into ZZZ while receiving vectors was cleared to 9,500 feet MSL and told cleared for the ILS XX and to maintain 9,500 feet until established. Selected APP and aircraft captured GS and LOC and was descending on the app with GS and LOC locked on. Got a call from approach at 8,100 feet letting us know we were low and to climb up to 8,600 feet I immediately disconnected the auto pilot and initiated a climb while maintaining LOC. After crossing ZZZZZ I then recommenced my descent and flew visually using the PAPI as my guidance. Landed the aircraft within the touch down range and stopped on the runway. CA taxied aircraft to gate. During taxi we were informed by approach that the GS had issues and they thought it had been fixed. We initially intercepted the GS and LOC approximately 20 miles out. At approximately 2 miles out the GS was back in line with the PAPI.
Narrative_1: We were doing the ILS Z Runway XX into ZZZ. Night time, good visibility, no clouds. ATC had us at 9,500 feet, turned us to intercept final outside of ZZZZZ and cleared us for the approach. Autopilot was on. We were flaps 1 about 190 knots at the time and about 22 miles on final. We intercepted the localizer and the glide slope at about the same time. At which point we were busy setting touch down zone, putting flaps down and gear. A moment later ATC gives us an altitude low warning, climb immediately to 8,600 feet. The flying pilot ( first officer) immediately disconnected auto pilot and initiated climb. We were around 8,100 feet, on the glide slope, auto pilot on when this was initiated from what we could tell. We had just passed ZZZZZ (FAF, but 17 miles out). The controller mentioned they had some glide slope problems just a week or two prior, and asked us if we were ok to proceed visually. Still being over 10 miles out, runway and PAPI in site, and glide slope still showing slightly below us, we proceeded visually with reference to PAPI and GS. The problem may have been from the auto pilot intercepting the LOC and GS at the same time and possibly overshooting the GS as it sometimes does when far out and possibly exasperated by configuration changes. This all happened about 15 to 20 miles from touchdown. Or it could have been from a faulty GS signal that they have had problems with previously.
Synopsis: Flight crew reported descending below minimum altitude on approach and climbed back to correct altitude. ATC advised flight crew that there had previously been problems with the glide slope.

Narrative: Air return due to pirep telling us we had a 6 foot flame coming out of engine 2 on takeoff.Mid-way down the runway for takeoff, a regional aircraft 'other carrier flagged', stated 'using the afterburners, huh?' Since we were empty (no Passengers, and not much fuel), we were accelerating quickly, and thus his comments made sense. Upon rotation, the Tower asked the regional aircraft, 'what was that you said'. To which he responded, 'looks like (Company) is using afterburners, a six-foot flame was coming out of the back of the #2 engine'. Upon reaching clean up altitude, we ran all the appropriate checklists, and returned back to ZZZ. The fire trucks were called by ATC, and they performed an inspection upon taxiing clear of the runway. We were cleared to taxi to the gate, and the event was entered in the logbook, and Maintenance and Dispatch, and the Chief Pilots were notified.The regional aircraft could have been more clear in his comments, and we could have aborted the takeoff at low speed.
Synopsis: Air carrier flight crew reported another carrier flight crew commented about flames exiting engine tailpipe during takeoff roll. Flight crew returned to departure airport.

Narrative: Halfway through our flight our B-Flight Attendant asked to come into the flight deck and talk with us. When she got to the flight deck she indicated that there was a very strong cleaning/bug spray smell in the aft galley. Additionally, our C-Flight Attendant was complaining of coughing and having a hard time taking a deep breath because of the strong cleaning smell. Our A-Flight Attendant didn't smell anything. No Passengers were indicating concern and we didn't smell anything. The Captain asked the Flight Attendant (F/A) if she was medically concerned, and if so, we would patch through to medic so she could communicate her concern. All the F/As indicated they were feeling OK and did not want to contact medic. They just wanted someone to look at the aircraft in ZZZ. At that point the Captain told her we would put the packs to high to help eliminate the strong cleaning odor. We also contacted Dispatch through ACARS to discuss the situation and see if there was an anti-microbial spray completed the night before. Additionally, we informed Dispatch that the F/As were not comfortable taking the aircraft on our next leg. Dispatch wanted a patch through ARINC to get F/As, operations and medic on the line for a conference call. During their discussion, Dispatch sent us an ACARS message to divert to ZZZ1. As a result, we notified ATC of our intention to divert. The Captain notified the F/As and Passengers of our intent, as well.As a precaution we accomplished the Smoke, Fire, or Fumes QRC and referenced QRH Smoke, Fire or Fumes Checklist in case the situation escalated. Dispatch notified us the aircraft had been sprayed the night before with antimicrobial spray. We communicated with our A-Flight Attendant on what to expect on landing, taxi, and at the gate. We kept in constant communication with the A F/A to constantly reassess our situation. On our descent into ZZZ1 medic recommended the two Flight Attendants having issues breathing use the portable oxygen. With that information, we [advised] ATC to have Medical Personnel standing by. We then accomplished all appropriate checklists and landed uneventfully.The anti-microbial spray the night before was a bit much. That needs to be more regulated. I think the call to divert was a good call, but happened very fast. Our Crew day also ended up being super long with this diversion on our first leg. We were OK to continue after the diversion, but that kind of day, with what we went through, is probably not completely safe.
Synopsis: B737-700 First Officer reported Flight Attendants were experiencing physiological symptoms from 'very strong ' cabin fumes. After consultation with Dispatch it was determined to divert for maintenance action.

Narrative: During takeoff roll, FO (First Officer) seat became unlatched horizontally, causing FO to slide aft. As pilot monitoring, I assumed control of the aircraft and steered us back to runway center line until FO was ready to assume control again. Seat not properly locked horizontally. Latching mechanism possibly in need of adjustment. Double-checking seat lock with a good 'shove' prior to departure. Also closer maintenance inspection of seat latches may be warranted.
Synopsis: Captain reported assuming control after First Officer's seat slid back and prevented him from reaching the flight controls.

Narrative: Immediately after takeoff, the horizontal trim failed. Neither pilot could activate the electric trim. The manual trim wheels were used to keep the aircraft in a trimmed condition, though with a significant amount of difficulty possibly due to the trim motor clutching against the manual inputs. The Stabilizer Trim Inoperative QRH procedures were followed. [We advised ATC] and the flight returned to ZZZ for an uneventful flaps 15 landing.I don't know why the electric horizontal trim failed. I do know that the manual trim was significantly more difficult to operate during this event than it had been in previous instances where I've had to use the manual trim wheels. The aircraft was never too far out of trimmed condition, but a strong binding was felt as we rotated the trim wheels. It was suggested to me after the event that this binding sensation was in fact the trim motor 'clutching' against the manual inputs. I'm not a strongman, but I worry that two smaller, weaker pilots might have found themselves in extremis.Figure out why the manual trim wheels felt as if they were binding, and correct that design condition.
Narrative_1: Everything that occurred prior to the time we became aware of the Stab trim failure was normal and uneventful. Shortly after Takeoff, the Captain said his stab trim didn't seem to be working and asked me to check mine. My stab trim was also inoperative. There were no other secondary issues. We continued with the departure while reviewing/going through the Stabilizer Trim Inoperative procedure. Once we had gone through the QRH procedure, we [advised ATC] and returned uneventfully to ZZZ where we wrote up the problem. We were given a new airplane about an hour later and continued our trip to ZZZ1. Cause, unknown maintenance issue.
Synopsis: Flight crew reported horizontal trim became inoperative with binding when attempting to use manual trim wheels. Flight crew elected to perform an air turn back.

Narrative: We were climbing out of DEN on the EEONS 8. Crossed HIDEF at 10,000 feet and started the climb again. We started to pick up wake turbulence from the 777 in front of us through about 11,000 feet. We received a call from ATC for traffic northeast of us as we were coming through 11,500 feet. We started looking for the traffic and when I looked back inside we were going through 12,000 feet about 1-2 miles prior to SHOBO. We began correcting back to 12,000 feet. Max altitude was about 12,300 feet. No call or mention of the deviation from ATC.
Narrative_1: While climbing out on flight from DEN via EEONS8 departure from 34L, we were given a traffic call from ATC as we neared SHOBO. At the same time, we encountered wake turbulence from a heavy aircraft on the same departure. As Pilot Monitoring, I was looking north for traffic as the aircraft was responding to the turbulence and controlling the aircraft. Simultaneously, we neared SHOBO, which has a no higher than 12,000 feet restriction. PIC called altitude at approx 250 feet above the restriction, and smoothly leveled, then began descent to maintain 12,000 feet until passing SHOBO, then resumed climb. No ATC comm was received during this time.
Synopsis: B737NG flight crew reported a distraction from wake turbulence contributed to climbing through an altitude restriction departing DEN in trail of a B777.

Narrative: Crew departed late due to brake accumulator issues on previous aircraft, and a potential one on this aircraft.Ground Ops were completely normal and the FO (First Officer) had no problems deploying the flaps to 3 for takeoff.Takeoff was normal and as we were turning to an assigned heading, we reached the cleanup altitude. I called for flaps 1 and noticed that the FO had some what I felt was minor difficulty bringing the flaps up to 1. This is not unusual, a hand slips, or the lever used to move the flap handle out of the detects isn't gripped correctly for easy retraction. I thought little of it.When I called for flaps UP, the raising was again delayed, and I noticed my FO reaching around with his right hand to put both hands on the flap lever to get it up. We talked about him having trouble getting them up, and I flew the aircraft only to ensure that I did not over speed the flaps. Eventually he was able to get them up which I saw on the speed tape on the PFD and I verified on the display, and flap handle position.We discussed what had happened a bit but decided to focus on safely exiting the terminal area and getting to altitude since the aircraft was now in the safe, and proper configuration. We made a plan to contact Maintenance Control at cruise and notify them of the problem and get advice about continuing the flight.After reaching altitude, the FO told me what he had encountered and explained how difficult it was to move the lever that released the flap handle from the detent to raise the flaps.A phone patch was initiated with dispatch and Maintenance Control and we discovered that our radio 2 wasn't able to receive over long distances. We ended up substituting radio 3 for radio 2 and temporarily disabling ACARS to complete the phone patch. Maintenance Control was very helpful on the phone patch and felt like he knew what the problem was. Maintenance Control was asked if he felt the aircraft should continue to ZZZZ, and he wanted it to go to a maintenance hub. As a Captain, I agreed with that thought process and asked the Dispatcher to bring in the Ops Manager so that we could all agree on a plan of action. We could have landed the aircraft at ZZZZ if there had been a flap malfunction, but the aircraft would have been stuck there quite a while.Eventually after consideration of landing lengths, the close to overweight landing weight of the aircraft, and the potential for wet runways in ZZZ1, that the best and safest place to divert the aircraft would be ZZZ1 in case the flaps would not deploy normally. Consideration was based on the worst case, flaps up scenario.Destination was changed with ATC once the plan was agreed upon by all parties and the phone patch was terminated and ACARS restored.Maintenance Control was asked via ACARS if we should leave the flaps down after landing and they asked them to retract them as much as we could.Fortunately, the landing in ZZZ1 was uneventful. The flaps deployed normally. Upon taxi-in. The flaps were retraced to position 1, where the handle binding began to be very difficult to overcome.Upon arrival at the gate, after shutdown, I tried to move the lever that releases the flap handle from the detent and found that it was impossible to move with just one hand.
Narrative_1: We were doing a flaps 3 takeoff from [Runway] XXL. After the acceleration altitude, and above flap retraction speed, the pilot flying called for flaps to 1. I noticed, while moving the lever from 3 to 1, that the flap lever was nowhere near as smooth and free moving as it usually is, rather, it was quite difficult to move. As we accelerated through flap 1 retraction speed, it took considerable effort to get the lever out of the detent. I mentioned it to the captain who quickly made sure to raise the nose and not over speed the flaps as I used both hands to get the flap lever compressed and moved to the up position. The flaps moved as expected, with no issues, the flight control page showed normal, and the hydraulic page showed normal. We continued the climb out of ZZZ, and when reaching a safe altitude, I took the controls and radios with ATC, while the captain initiated an incredibly detailed conversation with dispatch and Maintenance Control. After exhausting every bit of information we could give, and every insight Maintenance Control had, the decision was made with dispatch and everyone in planning that they were talking to, to divert to ZZZ1 instead of potentially having a flight control issue on landing in ZZZZ, on a shorter runway, at an international station, and then leaving the plane there. We didn't [request priority] but asked approach to slow down early to get the flaps out and make sure they extended. We had planned every contingency for having to go around and then [request priority] if they didn't, and were ready to run whichever QRH abnormal procedure would have applied based on where the flaps ended up. On the approach, the flaps came down just fine and a normal landing was made. After landing, we planned, with maintenance approval, to attempt to retract the flaps but to stop if they locked again and not force anything. The lever was much less stiff from flaps full to flaps 1 than earlier, but again locked at the detent there. We left the flaps at 1 into the gate, let ramp know to tell anyone they could, and had maintenance meet us there. Sounded like they were going to replace the entire flap lever section.
Synopsis: Flight crew reported difficulty in raising the trailing edge flaps and elected to divert instead of risking a grounded aircraft at an outstation.

Narrative: This event was a near midair collision in ZZZZ. On Aircraft X ZZZ to ZZZZ. Weather at ZZZZ was not a factor even though there was a significant storm cell over the final approach fix to Runway XX. ZZZZ was reporting 10 miles visibility. While making approach into ZZZZ we were told to go around due to previous aircraft reporting a pothole with gravel on approach end to Runway XX. Tower immediately closed the runway. We then went around and did published missed procedure. We entered holding at 8,000 feet at ZZZZZ per instructions. After we exited holding (now at 6,000 feet) the controller gave us instructions to go direct to ZZZZZ1 fix and begin RNP approach into Runway YY. We loaded the approach to the opposite Runway YY since the pothole was on the approach end of the Runway XX and proceeded to ZZZZZ1 on about a 200 heading. Then unexpectedly, the controller gave us a vector of 090. In hind sight, we think this vector was meant for another aircraft. The new heading of 090 ended up sending us directly for another aircraft at same altitude. TCAS began with a TA then an RA. At same time controller frantically gave us a new vector. After properly executing the resolution advisory, we narrowly missed the conflict aircraft and proceeded back to ZZZZZ1 and did the RNP to Runway YY for normal landing. We never saw the conflict aircraft however they did have us in sight, and I don't recall who the conflict aircraft was. There were two jets in holding. We think the controller got our call sign confused with someone else for the 090 vector. English as a second language may have been a factor in this event. Both the F/O (First Officer) and myself remember hearing our call sign in the 090 vector. In the end it was TCAS that saved the day.
Synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported a near midair collision while executing a go-around and took evasive action at a foreign airport.

Narrative: As weight left the wheels, my primary and secondary nav, heading, DG, compass failed. Along with the failures I had a PWS (Predictive Wind Shear) fail message and a TCAS fail message. My flight director failed as well. As we continued to climb, FO flying the aircraft, I began to troubleshoot the problems. I ran 2 checklist as they did not correct the issues. I opted to return to ZZZ. At that time I requested priority handling. I continued to communicate with company, FAs and passengers. The FO flew the ILS to [Runway] XXR. We landed and taxi to the terminal.
Synopsis: B737 NG Captain reported loss of navigation systems and instruments on lift off. Captain elected to return to the departure airport.

Narrative: While at cruise en route to ZZZ, we received a TO Data Available message via ACARS. Shortly after, Dispatch notified us that the HAZMAT we had onboard (we had proper paperwork for the HAZMAT) was not included in the Zero Fuel Weight (ZFW) calculations. We reviewed the new Takeoff Data for the correct ZFW and made the adjustment to the FMC, and calculated new landing data for that weight. The rest of the flight proceeded as normal.
Synopsis: B737-700 Captain reported Dispatch notification during cruise stating Hazmat cargo weight not included in the aircraft Weight & Balance data. Weight & Balance data corrected and flight continued.

Narrative: I was First Officer (FO) on Aircraft X operating to ZZZ. We were conducting the ILS XXR circle to XY approach when we received an abnormal landing gear indication. When I lowered the landing gear, the annunciator panel showed 3 red lights along with 3 green lights. The overhead panel showed 3 green as well. We briefly discussed continuing the landing as there was some confidence the gear was down. The discussion continued until around 500 ft. and I felt strongly that we shouldn't be making such consequential decisions that close to the ground without running a checklist. We performed a go-around, ran the checklist, got the gear down without the red lights, and landed successfully.
Narrative_1: ILS XXR circle XY at ZZZ. Lowered gear just prior to FAF (Final Approach Fix). 3 red, 3 green illuminated. After evaluating with First Officer (FO), executed go-around on XY due to gear disagree. Standard missed. Ran checklists. Vectored for longest runway... ILS XXR. Extended gear on 10-mile base. All indications normal. Executed normal landing. Taxi to gate to find puddle [of] hydraulic fluid at left main. Possibly unrelated.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported an issue with the landing gear indications.

Narrative: After pushback from Gate XXX and given our taxi instructions 'XX-XY-XZ etc...' to XXL for departure, we commenced our single-engine taxi. While I was taxiing at a slow speed, taxi light on, I noticed a truck that appeared to be stopping on the roadway across Taxiway X between XZ and XY to give way to our aircraft. However, the truck did not stop and they rolled right through Taxiway X without giving way to our aircraft. I applied brake pressure to prevent the plane from hitting the truck. Due to the slow taxi speed, we did not think the braking action to prevent the collision was too firm to knock anyone down or warrant a drastic brace from anyone if they were up. We notified ATC about this taxiway incursion and they asked if there was an Operations car on frequency to go after the truck. We took off, were in cruise, and were past the CP (Critical Point) - [middle of the flight] - when we set up for the first bathroom break. I went out first and I asked [the] First Class Flight Attendant (FA), 'If everything is all right back here.' They responded, 'Yes.' I went to the bathroom, came back up to the cockpit, and was talking to the Purser who also said everything was 'fine' as well. When the First Officer (FO) came back he then informed me that [the] FA informed him that when I had to brake to not hit the truck, she hit her right side against the forward galley wall with some of the quarter turn edging. I then called back and asked if she needed medical help in ZZZ1. She replied that she was "icing it and took Tylenol and she would not need medical attention in ZZZ1." I asked the other FAs if they were all right; one stated that they didn't even feel the braking action and two others stated they felt it as they were standing but everyone else was fine. To be clear, the first time I was told something was wrong was past the CP. Before departure I briefed the FAs that if there is anything wrong or abnormal, even if we are in sterile cockpit, do not hesitate to call up and let us know. Also, during the flight, no calls to see if [there were] medical personnel on board to help with an injury were made by the FA crew.Prior to the top of descent when we set up for another bathroom break, the Purser came in and I asked him how [the] FA was doing. He said, 'She seems fine, she wants to go home, she's just a little sore.' When I went out, I asked how she was doing. She stated, 'She wanted to call in enroute injured, but then wanted to deadhead home.' I told her, 'I don't know that they will be able to deadhead her home, but if she is enroute injured please let me know and I will contact Dispatch.' She then said she was 'enroute injured.' I said, 'Do you want medical treatment in ZZZ1.' She said, 'No.'I then texted Dispatch that we had an FA who was enroute injured and would call them when we landed per the reporting requirements. I also requested priority handling and asked the paramedics to meet the aircraft to evaluate her, just to be safe. We landed without incident. When the paramedics came on board, [the] FA refused additional medical care from them and stated to the FO, 'Why did you call them out, you didn't need to do that.' Appropriate reports were made per the manual to the Dispatcher [and others].
Narrative_1: During our flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1, most of which was uneventful, we had a minor injury on taxi out of our galley Flight Attendant (FA), but we were not notified until after the CP (Critical Point), [middle of the flight]. On taxi out we had to stop taxi for a truck that did not stop as we were taxiing X XY XZ from Gate XXX. As we came to a stop at the XX XY intersection, we at the time were more concerned about the truck that did not stop, and believed that we did not stop too abruptly for the truck but just more startled that it did not stop. Hindsight, we did not hear any clunking or hitting - and although we stopped slightly faster than normal, we did not realize that [the] FA may have been knocked off balance a little bit. We did make a call to Ground to let them know that the truck did not stop but we quickly continued our taxi not thinking too much of the incident. While the initial incident where [the] FA hit her arm may not have been that bad, it sounded like it got worse as we flew with some aching and building pain, so she let the flight crew, us, know about her sore arm and sore neck.As the flight continued, we reached radio/ACARS reception into ZZZ1 when [the] FA decided that the pain was too much and she was in flight injured and would not be able to work the return flight leg from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. As I continued to fly, the Captain (CA) coordinated with Dispatch and attempted to call ZZZ1 Operations to let them know the situation. After the CA was given all the information and was notified that she was incapacitated and unable to work the return flight, the decision was made to request priority handling [and] have paramedics meet us at the gate when we arrived to check on [the] FA.At top of descent the decision was made by [the] FA that her arm was hurt too much and after coordination with [the] FA, Dispatch, and calling Operations, we were approximately over ZZZ2 and the CA decided to request priority handling as a precaution due to an incapacitated crew member and in the best interest of the crew member's health. Our flight landed and taxied uneventfully and [the] FA [was] checked out by the airport paramedics. As we left the flight, we wished FA a speedy recovery; she seemed in good spirits.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported that a Flight Attendant sustained a minor injury due a braking event on the runway to avoid a truck not giving way to the taxiing aircraft.

Narrative: Captain (CA) & First Officer (FO) commented on a dirty sock smell on taxi out, no other abnormal indications. Upon adding takeoff power, left side of cockpit filled with a smokey/steamy mixture and acrid smell. Captain rejected. Maintenance (MX) advised there was an engine wash performed night prior and the aircraft engines were not run up properly after the procedure. We ended up having MX onboard for the runup who had us perform duties from a checklist that should have followed this engine wash including a run up of at least 5 min at 70% N1. The odors were still present during this time. If MX had been performed accurately the night prior, this could have been avoided. And, unfortunately, this routine wash is performed under a 'work card' making it invisible to pilots during a preflight in any MX accounting systems or via the aircraft logbook.
Narrative_1: At approximately 90 KIAS, smoke came out of cockpit floor, under Captain's side, and rejected takeoff. Uneventful. Cleared off runway stopped and had emergency equipment check for fire. All clear and taxied to gate. Maintenance said engine wash were performed overnight, probable cause of smoke/steam on takeoff roll. Maintenance did a high power engine run, delayed flight and re dispatched after maintenance cleared aircraft. Maintenance crew did an engine run, at gate, versus high power one the night prior. According to mechanic, a duct clamp was installed improperly in the E&E bay; residual water and duct clamp coming off on ducting might have contributed to what appeared to be smoke/fumes/vapor on takeoff roll after takeoff power was applied. [Reporter recommends Maintenance] perform high power engine run after every engine wash. If non-high power engine run, performed by maintenance overnight (info only entry to AML should be recorded so as to keep flight crews informed).
Synopsis: B737-800 flight crew reported smoke and fumes emanating from left side of the cockpit during takeoff roll. Flight crew executed a rejected takeoff and maintenance was requested.

Narrative: Climbing through approximately 500 ft. AGL in a right turn to 360, the departure heading selected on the MCP by the FO (First Officer) prior to takeoff, the FO's flight director, FD2, failed; the MCP (Mode Control Panel) altitude window indicated 50,000, not the pre-takeoff selected altitude of 3,000, and the FO's command bars biased out of view. The PF continued the climbing turn using PFD (Primary Flight Display) raw data in night-time VMC conditions. Cross-checking respective PFDs revealed no flags or indications as to the specific failure.In the busy initial climb segment, confusion as to the cause of current flight instrument condition gave way to confidence in the raw data. Directing the PF to continue to climb using raw data, I attempted to select 3000 ft. on the MCP; the altitude knob spun freely without any effect on the window. I then turned off the FD1 and FD2, reselected 3000 ft. in the MCP altitude window, confirmed the heading bug was at 360, selected heading, and turned the FD switches back on, FD2 first, in an attempt to restore FD2 guidance for the PF. Immediately upon switching on FD2, the MCP altitude returned to 50,000 and no command bars appeared on the FO's PFD.Switching to Departure Control, ATC gave us direct routing to the first fix, ZZZZZ, and continue climb to 11,000. I asked ATC for a heading, mentioning our concern that our navigation might be unreliable. They provided a 010 heading which when selected, had no effect on the FO's heading bug. Changing heading on the MCP failed to change the bugs on the FO's ND (Navigation Display) and PFD compass displays. I confirmed compass heading on the wet compass corresponded with both the Captain's and FO's compasses. They asked if we needed to declare an emergency; I declined as we had good raw data and were still diagnosing the malfunction.I attempted a second reset of FD2 with the same negative result. Leveling at 11,000, the PF reported the autothrottles were not holding commanded airspeed; we disengaged the autothrottles. Turning both FDs off again and selecting FD1 on provided accurate command bars on the Captain's PFD. We agreed that continuing using raw data was possible, and that full FD capability was available from FD1. I transferred aircraft control to myself and agreed with my FO's suggestion of going to the QRH for additional troubleshooting/procedural steps. A satisfactory QRH procedure to handle this malfunction was difficult to find and both FMS1 on the Captain's ND and FMS2 on the FO's confirmed FMC operation. We asked ATC for direct down range and confirmed FMS accuracy using FD1 guidance of MCDU1 entered direct routing. I engaged the autopilot and autothrottles and we continued on course using LNAV/VNAV.We discussed the status of the aircraft and the conditions at our destination, ZZZ. We elected to continue to ZZZ where we completed the trip without incident. I submitted an electronic logbook entry and called Maintenance Control after arrival. Approximately 35 minutes into our hour-long flight, I realized we had not requested [the] planned climb above our initial cruise altitude, FL310, and that contingency fuel had been burned during a slower climb than normal. Burn, alternate, ZZZ1, and 45-minute FAA fuel was still available, though a missed approach would have compelled diversion to ZZZ1. The FD2 diagnosis and distraction lead to the initial loss of SA regarding erosion to our fuel state. Beginning descent and approach planning brought for our new fuel and prepared us for contingencies. Communication throughout was key to understanding the status of the aircraft and mitigated the initial startle and confusion at such a low altitude early flight stage.
Narrative_1: We were cleared for takeoff by ZZZ3 Tower with instructions to turn to heading 360 and maintain 3,000 ft. The pilot flying which was me, the First Officer, put 360 in the MCP and deselected LNAV. We took off and as we were climbing through about 500 ft., the command bars disappeared and altitude went to 50,000 on both the PFD and MCP. We leveled at 3,000 on heading 360. ATC gave us climb to 11,000 and direct to a fix. The Captain told him we needed a heading we were having trouble with the flight director. ATC gave us a head of 010 and climb to 11,000 ft.The heading bug on the First Officer's PFD and MFD was stuck on heading 360 but was 010 on the MCP and on the Captain's displays. The Captain checked the PFD heading with the compass and it matched. We had no flags on the PFD or MFD. The Captain turned off both flight directors and then turned them both back on with the First Officer's being the master. When he turned it back on, the altitude went back to 50,000 and we could not change it. The command bars never came back. We saw that the Captain had a flight director and that his heading bug would turn with the MCP. The Captain then turned the FDs off and put his FD as the master. When he did that, the altitude went back to normal. On the FO's (First Officer) displays there was still no FD and the heading bug was stuck on 360 but now the altitude was correct. We continued the flight to ZZZ with the Captain flying.
Synopsis: B737 flight crew reported that shortly after takeoff, the First Officer's flight director began malfunctioning, leading to the MCP and heading bug also being inoperative.

Narrative: Outside the marker [Runway] XXR Captain received call from purser about chemical type smell moving forward from aft cabin. Noticed it on extreme short final but took measures to alleviate, if possible, the stated smell and monitored for reduction or increase. The landing in gusty conditions required focus there. On landing APU selected to start on final was on line and directed APU bleed air to packs and selected recirculate [fans] off immediately causing cessation of the smell and acknowledged alleviation in command. Smell was barely noticeable but a tad acrid then removed on taxi in. Recirculate [fans] back on blew it out completely. Never a need nor concern for use of cockpit oxygen. No persons affected nor did anyone use O2. No injuries. Event terminated at gate with a write up and briefing of mechanics plus filling out of required maintenance 4 page review by Captain.
Narrative_1: On approach in ZZZ the Captain received a call from the lead Flight Attendant about an acrid chemical smell moving forward from the aft cabin. By that time we could smell it in the cockpit as well. We turned off the recirculate fans to stop the spread of the smell, which helped, but then focused on the landing. We started the APU on short final and turned off the engine bleeds after exiting the runway, using the APU to power the packs. After turning off the engine bleeds the smell dissipated and we turned the recirculate fans back on. No oxygen was used or needed by the crew or passengers. We parked safely at the gate and briefed me and made a maintenance write up.
Synopsis: B777 flight crew reported a fumes event on final approach during landing. After executing a safe landing flight crew took measures to alleviate the fumes followed by requesting maintenance.

Narrative: We were seven miles behind a 747 on approach to Runway 9 in Miami, flaps 5, 170 knots on glidepath, when the aircraft abruptly went into 30 degrees left bank. We commanded full right aileron and there was no response for an unknown amount of time (possibly three seconds). We regained wings level flight only to encounter another abrupt 30 degree roll to the left with lack of aircraft control. After much discussion, my First Officer and I were worried that after such a 'minor incident' (seven miles behind a 747) that the event should cause such a severe loss of aircraft control. We both agree that the incident should be investigated.
Narrative_1: We were 15 miles out on the localizer to Runway 9 at 5000 feet. We were seven miles in trail of a B747. We encountered wake turbulence and the aircraft yawed to the left 30+ degrees for 3-5 seconds. We inputted right aileron with no results. The aircraft returned to level flight on its own and immediately went into a 30+ degree left bank turn for 3-5 seconds.
Synopsis: B737 NG flight crew reported momentary loss of control during a wake turbulence encounter on approach to MIA in trail of a B747.

Narrative: At FL390, pressurization in cabin started to increase. Started a descent and went through the checklist. Shortly afterwards the cabin went to 15,000 feet and O2 masks were deployed. Had requested priority handling with Dispatch and ATC. Alerted FAs (Flight Attendant) of the problem, what to expect. Landed in ZZZ1, intended destination. Debriefed crew, Maintenance, Dispatch, [and] union. Everyone said it was done by textbook procedures.
Narrative_1: AT FL390 we were cleared to descend and passing through FL360 we noticed the cabin altitude increasing. We told ATC and initiated an immediate descent. Complied with ECAMs and QRH procedures. Briefed FAs (Flight Attendant) and safely landed aircraft. Debriefed with crew, Maintenance, Dispatch, passengers, and emergency medical support staff.
Synopsis: A320 flight crew reported loss of cabin pressure control and requested priority handling and proceeded to land at destination airport.

Narrative: Departed SJC for ZZZ, encountered aircraft upset at FL 364 due to close proximity and below Boeing 777 at FL 370. No injuries or aircraft damage were apparent.
Synopsis: B737 Captain reported an upset climbing through FL364 after encountering wake turbulence from a B777 at FL370.

Narrative: On takeoff roll, Runway XX, with gusty left crosswinds, the aircraft suddenly and without warning, 'skidded' left. Corrected the ground track and continued the takeoff without further incident. FAs (Flight Attendants) reported being aggressively shoved sideways in their seats.
Synopsis: B737-800 Captain reported the aircraft suddenly skidded to the left during takeoff roll due to gusty crosswinds requiring corrective input.

Narrative: Enroute from ZZZ to ZZZ1, shortly after leveling off at cruise altitude, we received an IMBAL (imbalance) message and saw that our right fuel tank had 1,000 lbs less than the left tank. We had just turned off our center fuel pumps a few minutes prior. We performed the IMBAL checklist which then led us to the Fuel Leak Engine checklist. By this point it was decided that the safest course of action was to return to ZZZ. We requested priority handling and were cleared direct to ZZZ and were given a descent clearance. We shut down the #2 engine per the Fuel Leak Engine checklist. We also performed the One Engine Inoperative Landing checklist, the Non-Routine Landing Considerations checklist, and the Overweight Landing checklist. I was the Pilot Flying until downwind, at which time the Captain took the controls and landed the aircraft. We stopped on the runway and had the firefighters check out the aircraft. Everything looked ok to them and we were cleared to taxi to the gate. The Captain made an AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook) entry for the suspected fuel leak and overweight landing.The only causal factor was the mechanical irregularity of the right fuel tank showing 1,000 lbs less than the left, which gave us the IMBAL message.
Synopsis: B737-800 First Officer reported a fuel imbalance message in flight, causing an in-flight shut down of the #2 engine and a return to the departure airport.

Narrative: During climb out, FA (Flight Attendant) called on intercom to report a very loud banging noise behind the wing area, aircraft right side, row 31. FA said it sounded like someone pounding on the fuselage with a sledgehammer repeatedly. We leveled off at FL280 immediately and reduced speed from 280 KIAS to 250 KIAS. I asked the FO to look for a nearby field with good weather. FA recorded the noise via video on her cell phone and brought it to the cockpit. After reviewing the video, we decided to divert to ZZZ. We notified dispatch and coordinated with the FA's and informed the passengers. During the descent and configuration of the aircraft for landing at ZZZ, with the flaps at 5deg, I called for Flaps 10 while the aircraft speed was at 209 KIAS. I immediately said 'delay that stay at flaps five.' I believe the FO moved the flap handle out of the 5 detent and returned it immediately. The flaps remained at 5 degrees and I continued to slow the aircraft. I called for gear down an Flaps 15, flaps 25, flaps 30 landing checklist. I noticed the stick shaker indicator on the airspeed tape was in an unusual position and cross checked the configuration to find the flaps were at 5. We were at approximately 1200 feet when I announced 'going around', but did not hit TOGA as I did not want GA thrust. At this point, the FO and I were convinced that the two problems were related; that there was some structural damage to the flaps.We climbed to 5,000 feet and referenced the Checklist for FLAPS - TRAILING EDGE FLAPS DISAGREE. We returned the flap lever to 5, then selected 2. The flaps retracted to 2. The checklist directed us to 'Proceed normally.' We had a discussion about what that meant and were not comfortable with extending the flaps again, with suspected mechanical damage to the flaps already existing. We got a phone patch with Maintenance Control and dispatch on HF and discussed the two issues and our checklist. They had no additional advice. We discussed the plan to land in the current flap configuration (flap 2), using the flap up speeds with Maintenance Control and dispatch. The FO had already assessed the landing distance and we referenced the FLAPS- TRAILING EDGE FLAPS UP LANDING checklist. We landed on RWY XXL at ZZZ, at VREF 40 + 40 + 5. I used auto brakes 3, and rolled to the end of the runway. We had the fire/rescue look us over for damage prior to proceeding to the gate. They reported a large cable hanging from the satellite antenna. The PSEU (Proximity Switch Electronics Unit) light came on after landing. The FO and I debriefed the events in detail post flight and during the next two flights. It was not until the following morning, that I realized that in all likelihood, I caused the flap malfunction by calling for flaps 10 at 209 KIAS. The SATCOM antenna seal failure noise was significantly concerning, and I assumed the flap issue was directly related.
Synopsis: First Officer reported a SATCOM antenna became dislodged on take off, repeatedly striking against the fuselage. Flight crew elected to divert for a precautionary landing.

Narrative: It was the FO (First Officer)'s leg into ZZZ. He had briefed the ILS approach which was the landing runway on the ATIS. A flap 40 degree landing was planned. The weather was VFR at the field with a cloud base at roughly 4,000 ft. MSL. ATC had us on a left downwind and turned us on a 90 degree base to final for Runway XXR. The FO had a 2.0 mile ring around the FAF ZZZZZ in the box to be fully configured for landing by then. And to the best of my recollection we were fully configured by the FAF. Runway XXR was in sight and ATC cleared us for the visual approach which was backed up by the ILS XXR. As we turned on to final for the Runway XXR at ZZZ, an accelerated red airspeed zipper came up on the bottom of the speed tape. There was an 'airspeed low' aural warning. The FO pushed the power in immediately, a stick shaker was felt, and the red airspeed zipper came down for the top of the airspeed tape. The FO disengaged the autopilot. There was very narrow gap on the upper and lower red zippers on the airspeed tape and the FO flew between the narrow gap. The FO stated, 'I'm not sure what is going on'. The chain of events happened at a very accelerated pace. Then the aircraft accelerated and the red zippers opened up and I called out ' watch your speed'. I remember seeing the aircraft accelerate near 159-160 kts. and I saw the red zipper on the top of the airspeed tape at 162 kts. In recovery, the aircraft climbed approximately 200-300 ft. We had Runway XXR in sight and the FO was in good position to land. I asked the FO if he was good with landing or if he wanted to do a go-around. The FO elected to continue the approach. Considering what we had just experienced, I felt that was a good choice. The FO continued the visual approach flying on the ILS XXR glide slope and localizer. At 1,000 ft. the FO made the 'stable' call out. At 500 ft. I made the 'stable' call out. We experienced no more airspeed red zipper indications or aural warnings for the remainder of the approach. The FO had a good landing. Upon landing I saw that the speed brakes did not automatically deploy so I manually deployed them. I noted after clearing the runway that due to the distractions, I failed to finish the 'below the line' checklist which I later mentioned to the FO. After the flight the FO and I decided to call Maintenance Control to discuss what had happened to us. Maintenance Control notified me that our Aircraft X had a 'history' of unreliable airspeed and that the FO's pitot tube was changed out. The Maintenance Representative voiced concern that it may be that our aircraft had a much 'bigger' maintenance issue and he wanted to pressure test the pitot system before releasing the aircraft. I put the 'write-up' in the maintenance book. I notified the outbound crew of what had happened and that my understanding was that Maintenance was on the way. ZZZ Operations was notified as well.I agreed with the Maintenance Representative that Aircraft X possibly had a bigger Maintenance issue at hand. When I called out 'watch your speed' as the airspeed was approaching 160 kts., the First Officer had the same indication and matched mine. I have never seen anything like this event ever. So it seems possible that the airspeed was correct but the red zippers were not correct. Due to the distractions on final approach, I did not complete the Before Landing 'below the line' checklist and this did not register until touchdown when I had to manually deploy the speed brakes.I did not complete the Before Landing 'below the line' checklist. A go-around could have possibly helped in this situation but I do feel now as I did then, that the safest thing to do was land the aircraft straight ahead.
